Amazon's early Black Friday 2026 sale is already bringing some worthwhile discounts to wireless headphones, with savings of up to $160 across models from Sony, Bose, Apple, Nothing, and other brands. Several of the headphones on sale are relatively upcoming, including Nothing's Headphone (1) Pro and Bose's second-generation QuietComfort Headphones, both of which launched this fall. Better yet, most of the deals below have dropped to their lowest prices yet on Amazon.

There's a good mix to choose from, too, whether you're looking for premium noise-canceling headphones for flights and commutes, a pair with enough battery life to get you through a week of listening, or something inexpensive for everyday use, with prices starting under $50. You can also check out the rest of our Black Friday coverage for more editor-vetted tech deals as the sale continues.

The Nothing Headphone (a) is down to a record-low $109 from $199, making it a solid option for everyday listening, especially for Android consumers who can take advantage of LDAC for higher-quality wireless audio. For more on it, check out this PCMag review.

Spending another $60 gets you the Nothing Headphone (1), now $169 from $299, which is also a record low. It offers a more premium listening experience with active noise cancellation, automatic playback pausing when you take the headphones off, and the option to listen through either USB-C or a 3.5mm cable, making it a well-rounded choice for everyday use. For more on it, check out this PCMag review.

It has been revealed that nothing's newest and most expensive over-ears, the Headphone (1) Pro, are already $80 off at $319, only a couple of months after launching at $399. This is the pair to get for sound quality, since Nothing moved to a three-driver setup in each earcup, and the result is a fuller, more detailed sound than either the Headphone (1) or Headphone (a). For more on it, check out this PCMag review.

Sony's flagship WH-1000XM6 headphones are down to $378 from $459.99, their lowest price yet. Noise cancellation is still the main reason to buy them, and they remain among the best options for blocking out engine rumble on a flight, traffic during a commute, or chatter in a busy office. For more on these over-ears, you can check out our in-depth review.

Sources indicate that sony's WH-CH730N brings noise cancellation down to a much more approachable price, and at $98, down from $179.99, it's the lowest it's been on Amazon. This 2026 patch to Sony's budget noise-canceling line now folds up for travel, which the previous model couldn't do, and battery life has jumped to up to 50 hours with noise cancellation on.

It has been revealed that sony's WH-CH530 is the most affordable pair in this roundup at $38, down from $69.99—that's also the lowest it's been since its release this fall. These are simple on-ear headphones without noise cancellation, but they sound better than you'd expect at this price, and the battery lasts up to 55 hours, so a full week of commuting or classes shouldn't be a problem.

The second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones are down to $199 from $359, their lowest price yet. That's a substantial discount for a pair that delivers on two of Bose's biggest strengths: comfort and noise cancellation. You can read PCMag's review for a closer look at how they perform.

In a recent development, bose's flagship QuietComfort Ultra headphones (2nd gen) are down to $339 from $449, saving you $110. Their noise cancellation is among the best you'll find in consumer headphones, making them particularly appealing for frequent flyers or anyone who spends a lot of time in noisy environments. For more on their features and performance, you can check out PCMag's review.

The 2026 JBL Tune 680NC are down to $49.95 from $109.95, their lowest price to date. That's a pretty good deal for anyone looking for affordable noise-canceling headphones, especially since you get adaptive noise cancellation that adjusts to your surroundings and up to 50 hours of battery life with it enabled.

For the same price, JBL's Tune 730BT trades noise cancellation for a larger over-ear fit and even longer battery life, rated at up to 76 hours. At $49.95, down from $89.95, it's at its lowest price on Amazon, and a sensible choice for anyone who mostly listens at home, at a desk, or on quieter commutes where noise cancellation isn't essential.

The JBL Live 780NC are down to $129.95 from $249.95, making them considerably more appealing than at their original price. Battery life is a major advantage here, with JBL estimating up to 50 hours with noise cancellation enabled and 80 hours without, so frequent charging shouldn't be a concern. They also support LDAC for higher-quality Bluetooth audio with compatible devices. For more on their features and performance, you can check out PCMag's review.

Apple’s AirPods Max 2 are down to $449 from $549, saving you $100 on the second-generation over-ears that Apple released earlier this year. While the design hasn’t changed much from the original, the upgrade to Apple’s H2 chip brings improved noise cancellation, while its sound remains among the best you'll find in wireless headphones. You can read PCMag's review for a closer look at how they perform.

Soundcore's Q20i headphones are down to $42.69 from $69.99, making them one of the more affordable options for anyone looking for noise-canceling over-ears from a recognizable brand. They're particularly worth considering for students, occasional travelers, or anyone who wants a budget-friendly backup pair.

The Beats Solo 4 are down to $129.95 from $199.95, saving you $70. While these lightweight on-ear headphones don't have active noise cancellation, they offer plenty of flexibility for everyday listening, whether you're using an iPhone or an Android phone, with quick pairing on both platforms, notes this PCMag review.

The second-generation Bose QuietComfort Headphones have the largest dollar discount in this roundup, dropping $160 from $359 to $199.

That depends on how much you want to spend and where you'll use them. The Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) are worth considering for frequent travelers who prioritize noise cancellation, while the regular Bose QuietComfort Headphones at $199 offer a more affordable premium option. The JBL Live 780NC at $129 are appealing for their long battery life and extensive audio customization, and the Soundcore Q20i at $42.69 make sense if you're shopping on a tighter budget. For Apple customers who value ecosystem integration, the AirPods Max 2 are worth considering.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Note: This story will discuss a pivotal mission in Chapter 2 of Grand Theft Auto 6.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Note: This story will discuss a pivotal mission in Chapter 2 of Grand Theft Auto 6. A powerful sequence in Grand Theft Auto 6 is quickly becoming a favorite among the game's many players, but a technical mishap made my experience of this scene very different--hilariously different. Chapter 2 of GTA 6 begins with Jason and Lucia in a rough spot, with the former still recovering from major injuries sustained at the end of Chapter 1, and the latter having to care for him. It isn't until the mission "Breakfast Run" that Jason is back on his feet, and the Bonnie-and-Clyde-like duo mark his recovery with a crime spree. Set to "Money or Nothing" by Dire Straits, Lucia and Jason rob a diner, not dissimilar to a scene from Pulp Fiction, and a playable montage indicates the pair robbing convenience shops, a clothing store, and other establishments. The image of Jason and Lucia busting open double doors, guns in hand, is probably the most iconic image of GTA 6, a statement of intent that defines the game's story going forward. https://bsky.app/profile/compenderizer.bsky.social/post/3n2yzmpjn6c2j But somehow, I had gotten a slightly different version of this montage. When I returned to the motel as Lucia, I sprinted toward the door, only for the game to place me back outside the room. The game told me to "Go to Hank's Waffles" with no additional context, and I walked back into the motel to find Jason, not only up and about, but only sporting his underwear, bandages, and a buzz cut. I suspected that there was a cutscene that I missed showing Jason fully recovered, so I decided to carry out the mission. The problem was that Jason wouldn't put any clothes on. I drove to the diner as the game instructed me to, and the entire mission, Dire Straits and all, resumed with a mostly naked Jason. It was impossible not to cackle at the sheer absurdity of the situation, watching Jason terrorize locals and presumably solidifying a fresh legacy as the Leonida underwear robber. At one point, the camera cut to Jason's bare foot slamming a gas pedal, and I was left breathless from laughter. Eventually, the game decided to put clothes back on Jason, but I had to visit a salon to grow his hair back. Iconic. Though GTA 6 features nudity in various degrees, you cannot dress Jason and Lucia in their underwear outside of their home. That sprint through the motel room door must have bypassed some sort of clothing check and allowed Jason to freely show skin outside of the motel. I've seen players online talk about an "underwear glitch," and I found one Reddit comment saying that they also had a nearly naked Jason run about in "Breakfast Run," so I appear to be an edge case in experiencing this specific glitch. I can't say that this bug "ruined" one of GTA 6's best missions for me, as I still found myself thoroughly entertained--just not in the way Rockstar Games wanted. Having Jason in his undies while still concealing his identity with a hat and bandana felt like something out of a Saints Row game rather than the fairly serious story GTA 6 was building up to that point. Despite the intense work and detail put into GTA 6, it certainly isn't free of silly glitches and bugs such as this. Luckily, many of them are more amusing than hampering, and Rockstar Games is already putting out post-launch patches for the title. If anything, I'm just bummed that I can't spend the rest of the game as Underwear Jason.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warning! Spoilers ahead for Season 9, Episode 7 of FBI, “Posterity,” streaming now with a Paramount+ subscription.

Over the last few years, FBI has seen a surprising amount of cast changes in such a short amount of time. Just last season, the CBS procedural said goodbye to Emily Alabi not long after she joined the cast, and Juliana Aidén Martinez was then brought on. After a recent update on the procedural pointed towards another exit on the 2026 TV schedule, I had to ask one star all about it, and they totally get why I have questions.

Earlier in this season of FBI, John Boyd’s Stuart Scola revealed that wife and baby mama Nina Chase (Shantel VanSanten) had been offered the chance to lead her own task force in San Diego. Despite some hesitation, Scola ultimately tells her she should take it, and last week’s episode, “Posterity,” saw Nina getting ready for the big move. After some thinking, Scola told her he was going to put in a transfer to move to California with her, even if it would take a while.

That development led me, and likely many fans, to worry that another exit could be coming and that we might say goodbye to Scola in the near future. However, Boyd told CinemaBlend what’s really going on and sought to ease concerns:.

In a recent development, I mean, look, as far as I know, there's no intends for any major changes, but I think that's a perfectly natural question to have. But really what's happening is exploring the character in a relationship in a very real way of something that we haven't yet tried with this couple, which real couples go through, all the time in life, which is career changes and geographics and movement. And what does it mean to love someone and let them go, ask them to stay, give up your thing?

Industry observers note that boyd's comments seem to point to the writers simply wanting to shake things up for Nina and Scola in a way they've never done before. The actor also told us this:.

Industry observers note that it's sacrifice and change, and it makes them super relatable. So, that's the story we're telling for now, but it's perfectly fine to kind of, hopefully, tease the idea of certain characters not being around anymore to see if people really love them.

Recent findings suggest that I’m relieved to know that Boyd’s not going anywhere, at least not any time soon and that this is merely a chance to explore Scola and Nina’s relationship in a different way. When Nina was revealed to be moving to San Diego, there was no telling where things could be going for her and Scola, as well as their son, Dougie. And after the several cast exits the show has had in recent years, I appreciate the Boyd seems to understand why viewers would have questions.

Industry observers note that throughout the years, Nina and Scola have been through a lot, both as a couple and individually. While fans haven’t seen much of them since FBI: Most Wanted was canceled, we have been getting small updates here and there. Plus, VanSanten returned last season for the much-anticipated Scolina wedding. There's no telling how the relationship will progress, given they're working on opposite sides of the country and trying to raise their son together. I, for one, am eager to see how it plays out.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Also, even if there aren’t any plans to move Scola to San Diego in the near future, that isn’t stopping potential Scolina spinoff ideas. When asked by CinemaBlend if FBI could expand with another spinoff centered on Scola and Nina in San Diego, VanSanten remarked she was already campaigning for a latest series. Unsurprisingly, Boyd reiterated his intention to stay with the Mothership. But, if we do eventually see Scola leaving 26 Fed, it would be fun to follow the fan-favorite couple in California.

Sources indicate that I’m excited to see what FBI has planned for this next Scolina obstacle, and as long as Boyd is not leaving the series any time soon, I’ll be fine. All in all, fans should really stay tuned in as Season 9 continues. The show returns with a upcoming episode on Monday, November 30, at 8 p.m. ET on CBS, streaming the next day on Paramount+.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Joseph Baena is joining Fox’s Baywatch revival in a surprise role.
  • “I’m Livvy Dunne’s boyfriend in the show,” Baena, 29, exclusively told Us on the set of Celebrity Weakest Link.
  • Baena continued to gush over his onscreen love interest and other costars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joseph Baena is joining Fox’s Baywatch revival in a surprise role.

“I’m Livvy Dunne’s boyfriend in the show,” Baena, 29, exclusively told Us on the set of Celebrity Weakest Link. “And she was amazing — such a great talent and she was such a talented and special gymnast. To see her in Baywatch was great.”.

Baena continued to gush over his onscreen love interest and other costars.

“She killed it. As did the rest of the cast,” he added. “Thaddeus [LaGrone], Noah Beck and everyone else is doing a phenomenal job. It was amazing to spend time with them on set and work out with them on set. I’m just really excited for the episode to come out of the whole show.”.

While Arnold Schwarzenegger‘s son had a small role as Pete in season 1, he hinted he would love to see “a little more” of the character in a potential second season, adding, “We have to make the plot line [happen]. I get that — in the first season — they need to establish everyone. Maybe in the second season they can have a little fun and bring Pete back.”.

The original Baywatch ran from 1989 to 2001 and showcased the lives of lifeguards who dealt with unusual circumstances — from shark attacks to serial killers — on beaches in California and Hawaii.

“I was too young to watch it live when it came out [on] TV, but I have such a connection to David Hasselhoff when he was in the SpongeBob movie. It’s one of my favorite movies of all time and such a massive part of my childhood,” Baena recalled. “Especially when David Hasselhoff comes out in the show and is the speedboat to take SpongeBob back to Bikini Bottom. It’s awesome.”.

He continued: “So the fact that they brought the show back and are reviving it, it was such a cool announcement. I got so excited. I wanted to audition. I unfortunately didn’t even get a chance to audition until they had already started the show. I’m so grateful that I was able to make an appearance in one of the episodes.”.

Recent findings suggest that the guest appearance made Baena want to do more scripted projects. For now, TV viewers can catch Baena on the Monday, November 23, episode of Fox’s Celebrity Weakness Link.

“Non-scripted reality TV has been super fun. I think I have a good personality for it,” he told Us. “Celeb Weakest Link is [an] amazing show. And I did Dancing With the Stars — that was phenomenal. It was such an amazing time.”.

Baena noted that the “main vision” for his career is to be a leading man.

“To be in scripted movies, film and TV. I’ve been doing theater for a little while. I’ve been doing acting classes for a long time and just working my way up,” said the actor, who has also been working on a cookbook inspired by what he learned from mom Mildred Baena. “I’m paying my dues and I know how it goes in the industry. It’s difficult, and you never know when your time is, but I think my time is coming soon.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, infamous GTA 6 Leaker Cyberleek resurfaced last week, threatening to release a crucial file for the Xbox build of GTA 6 that could be used to create an unofficial PC port of the game. The hacker originally promised to publicly drop the .exe file for this version of the game depending on whether their memecoin hit a certain market cap, and has been taunting publisher Take-Two Interactive for failing to prevent the game files from leaking online. "Months of takedowns, subpoenas, and wallet-tracing later, the hunt is still on and the uploads keep arriving," Cyberleek wrote in a now-removed post on Reddit, insisting they were "fighting anti-consumerism" in the video games industry with their actions and using crypto funds to work on a new project. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it’s a balmy late-September day in London, and Dolly Alderton is explaining to a befuddled Emma Frost what “iPhone face” means. Frost has never heard the term; her fellow showrunners Alderton and Zoe Kazan have.

Recent findings suggest that “You know [how] you look at some faces, like Rosamund Pike’s face—it looks like it’s never seen an iPhone? It looks like it’s seen a lute and a loom,” Alderton tells Frost.

According to recent reports, “So actors who look like they’re comfortable in a period show, rather than feeling inherently modern,” says Frost, as understanding dawns. Alderton and Kazan affirm her: “Yes, yes. Exactly.”.

Recent findings suggest that now that Frost gets it, she turns back to the group’s Zoom screen. “Sorry, what was the question?”.

Kazan began her career as an actor, while Alderton started out as a dating columnist and Frost was a sculptor and painter. Now all three are overseeing vastly different but comparable Netflix period dramas, each based on a classic work of literature: East of Eden (Kazan’s, which was released October 1), Pride and Prejudice (Alderton’s, out December 3), and The Age of Innocence (Frost’s, coming February 18). They’ve gathered in a London conference room at Netflix headquarters for a roundtable discussion about art, work, the unique experience of adapting a beloved book—and, apparently, iPhone face.

According to recent reports, though this is the first time the trio has met face to face, their conversation flows so easily and naturally that interrupting them with questions sometimes feels impolite. Early on, I note that all three of these novels are, on some level, about unconventional women. Alderton, Frost, and Kazan pause for a moment, considering this Lit 101–level observation.

“That’s true, I think,” agrees Frost.

And then they’re off to more interesting topics.

Vanity Fair: Have you read each other’s books?

Dolly Alderton: No, I haven’t read either of your books.

Alderton: Did you read them at school, or did you read them for fun?

Recent findings suggest that frost: Pride and Prejudice I read when I was a teenager at school. East of Eden I read first about 15 years ago, I think.

Alderton: So Em already wins the round table.

Frost: And for both of you, was it the thing you most wanted to adapt?

Alderton: I would never have dared to dream to. I was so overwhelmed when I was first approached. I just thought, it’s such a precious IP. It would be way too much, and I wouldn’t be the right person. But then when I was asked to pitch for it, at that point there’s no other answer but yes.

Kazan: First of all, was it the Austen you liked the most?

Industry observers note that alderton: Yes. It was the one that I’ve always loved because of Lizzie Bennet. I’ve always been obsessed with Lizzie Bennet. She was my hook. But how about you two? Did you ever dream of adapting these texts?

Frost: I was at a place where I said, “I want to do anything except period, because I’ve done so much period.” Netflix asked me to do The Age of Innocence, and it was, I think at that moment, the one book that made me just go, “Oh my God, okay, let me go back and revisit it.” Because I know I love it, but you have to know what the reason is [to adapt it again]. And the thing that totally blew me away on a reread was how relevant and resonant it is. It is about the freedom of the individual versus the conformity of the pack. It has so many themes in it that are really resonant with social media, the bullying of the group.

According to recent reports, alderton [turning to Kazan]: Tackling Cathy, how did you begin? What was your way into that?

Industry observers note that kazan: I think of adaptation as an advanced form of reading. For me, everything I’ve ever written has come from a feeling of “I have to write this specific thing.” When I was 15 and I read the book for the first time, I felt like it literally grabbed me by the throat and wouldn’t let go. And then I just kept coming back to it. And specifically her character, I felt like I had never read anyone like that before or since.

[to Alderton] The BBC’s Pride and Prejudice—is that the one that you—.

Alderton: No, that wasn’t my Pride and Prejudice.

Sources indicate that alderton: Yeah, the Joe Wright one was the one that I was more familiar with. But I’m so interested in what you were saying about getting to know Cathy. I was kind of nervous about doing press for a book that’s so beloved, and I’m finding it’s actually been really easy so far because I just know the people so well. So much of it has been basically like, putting Mr. Darcy and Elizabeth, all the Bennet family and Bingley through therapy. That psychological interrogation of these very well-known characters has been the thing I’ve just really, really enjoyed.

Sources indicate that frost: Have you both had to change points of view from the novel? Do you feel like you’ve had to make a specific choice about who you are foregrounding? I think I know the answer in your case, Zoe.

Kazan: No, I actually don’t. I’m aware that the way that I read a book is different from the way that anyone else reads that book. When I read East of Eden, I feel like I see Steinbeck becoming enthralled by this character, finding her as curious as I do. I think he starts out a real place of judgment and over the course of the book, really moves towards love and understanding.

Alderton: I have a similar thing in that for the majority of the book, one of the lead characters is completely unknowable. Not just to Elizabeth, but to the audience as well. So you have to honor that to make it satisfying. That’s kind of frustrating when you’re writing a romantic lead for the first three and a half episodes. None of us, least of all the female protagonist, can see who he is, and we misunderstand him. There is no other option I think than staying with Lizzie.

Frost: It’s very different because the book is entirely from Newland’s point of view. The thing that I wanted to do, and that Netflix were really excited for me to do, was to open it up to find out who the women were.

I think in the book—rightly, because she’s writing from Newland’s point of view—both May and Ellen are sort of constructed as his other. One is the thing to be won, and one is effectively the antagonist. It’s so interesting, because it’s a female author—and [Wharton herself], she’s part Newland. That's who she was growing up. And she’s part Ellen, this woman who now lives in Europe, who's become really cosmopolitan, who is even based on her own love triangle.

The impossibility of that love triangle is the thing I want people to feel. It’s not like one of them is wrong. They're all just feeling what they’re feeling.

Alderton: And how do you feel about bringing that new perspective and analysis to the story? For a book that's so beloved, did you feel excited by that? Or did you feel kind of daunted by it?

It has been revealed that frost: Maybe I should have felt daunted. I didn’t. I think Edith Wharton—it’s so based on her own personal experience of when she was 45, she had this sexual awakening. She was in this really dull marriage. She’d never had an orgasm. When she was 45, she fell in love with this journalist and had this passionate affair.

It has been revealed that frost: She had this big affair, then he ghosted her. But she was trying to make sense of it through this love triangle. When she wrote it, she couldn’t possibly have written herself as a female character in the center of an illicit love triangle because we were still in time of censorship, and she was being published in a very commercial magazine. So she had to make herself the man that has more agency.

Sources indicate that alderton: With any script, you have a relationship with the characters. But with what we are doing, you have this relationship with the writer.

According to recent reports, kazan to Alderton: You’re also a novelist. How are you thinking about bisecting yourself—using both parts of your brain, the novelist part and the dramatist part?

Alderton: I’ll tell you how I felt about it. I’ve written two novels, both of which I’ve tried to adapt. I found it really, really hard. I found adapting Pride and Prejudice incredibly effortless. When I went from Pride and Prejudice to my novel, I was like, "Why is this so much harder? I hate this novelist. Jane Austen is so much easier.".

It has been revealed that what amazed me is just, it’s like she wrote it to be adapted. It’s like her agent had said to her, “I know you’re going to write this novel about this family of five women, but remember, we could get a great movie deal off the back of it. So try and make it as adaptable as possible.” It has literally been written for TV in this totally perfect six-part structure. I just wish she was around to have written screenplays.

Industry observers note that kazan: This is how I feel about Tolstoy too. When I read War and Peace, I’m like, “Oh, he’s seeing it as if it’s a movie.” It’s very strange to read that so far ahead of the technology to make that possible.

It has been revealed that where was each of your point of entry? What was the first scene that you wrote?

Frost: I always break the whole thing in quite a lot of detail to feel like I understand where the story's going. I think when I actually started writing, I probably wrote from the beginning.

Kazan: So you outlined her therapy?

Alderton: I do the same. It’s the only thing that gives me freedom and confidence to write.

Kazan: And did you know how many episodes you wanted from the start, or did that change?

Frost: At one point it was longer, and at one point it was shorter. It’s eight in the end. What about you?

Sources indicate that kazan: I wanted eight originally, and then for budget and logistical reasons, I had to boil it down to seven quite late in the process. I had been four years into adapting it.

Recent findings suggest that kazan: Yeah. And we were a month away from production, and I had to restructure everything quite late in the game.

Kazan: Yeah, but you know what? It was actually this enormous gift. I had this writing teacher in college, a poetry teacher who talked a lot about constraints. And I don’t know if you've ever seen the... What’s his name? He’s a nightmare, but forgive me—the guy who directed Melancholia.

Kazan: There’s this beautiful Lars Von Trier film called The Five Obstructions, a documentary. He challenges his filmmaking teacher to remake this perfect short film that he made in the 1960s with five sets of obstructions to help him break open his creative process again. And that, combined with what my poetry teacher was always saying—which is the form gives you freedom.

Sources indicate that kazan: I feel like having to... Every time I’ve received, “Okay, we don’t have the money for X, or we don’t have the location for Y, or you have to boil eight episodes down to seven,” that it made me think again about, okay, what’s key here? Seeing the instruction as a gift rather than as an obstacle really just helped me over and over again. I actually gave myself one night to be really mad about it, and then the next day I was—.

It has been revealed that kazan: A lot of showrunning, for me at least, has been about learning how to manage my emotions on my own time so that I can go to work and help manage everything. The next day, as soon as I started reworking it, I discovered all of the gifts that it would give me.

Recent findings suggest that alderton: That lesson is one that you only learn with the privilege of experience. This is only my second TV show. My first, Everything I Know About Love, was an adaptation of my memoir. But I remember now the moments where I mentioned, “If we have to lose this scene, there’s no point shooting the whole show.” Things like that.

Kazan: And then you’re in the edit and you’re like, “Actually, that’s better.”.

Alderton: Totally. Or I think back on these things that we couldn’t afford or practically couldn’t work that I really thought would rip out the heart and soul of the show. And now I never dream of an alternate version of that show where those things were put in.

I don’t think I would’ve been as zen as you. I think I would’ve been a petty, grouchy bitch for three days, rather than one.

According to recent reports, kazan: At that point, I was still trying to get my greenlight. I want to hear Dolly’s answer to the first scene question.

Alderton: Oh, sure. So the opening of Pride and Prejudice in the book is obviously setting up the central drama, which is “we need a man. There's a upcoming man in town.” We decided to put Darcy at the very, very top of the show. There is so much in Pride and Prejudice to delight in. What is easy to forget is that it is the best love story of all time. And I’m just like, “We should land that. The first thing we should land is this intrigue between these two characters.”.

In a recent development, so Elizabeth is walking around Netherfield Park being kind of nosy and breaking the rules, and she’s intrigued by this man. So much of their attraction to each other, which everyone finds so delicious to read, is that they’re just fascinated with each other, and it takes them a while to work out why. So we wanted to establish that.

Kazan: I love that. I loved her spying and the sort of misunderstanding of who he is.

Dolly, were you wrestling at all about what to do with “it’s truth universally acknowledged,” the most famous line in literature?

In a recent development, alderton: Andrew Davies gives that line to Elizabeth Bennet, but for me, it felt like it’s the Mrs. Bennet line. The reinterpretation, I suppose, that I’ve done on my Pride and Prejudice is a bit of a justice for Mrs. Bennet. I’m working so hard in this adaptation to really understand why she is the way she is, why she’s so hysterical, why she's seemingly such a social climber. So to give her that line, it felt like we were just off to the races. This is a woman whose preoccupation in life is making sure her daughters are safe. So yeah, it felt like it was an easy line for Olivia [Colman].

When it comes to casting, can you articulate what makes somebody feel appropriate for a period show, versus somebody who seems too contemporary?

Kazan: Or maybe that’s not a concern.

It has been revealed that frost: I think for me, casting is really instinctive. Ben Radcliffe, right from his first tape, I was just, “He is Newland Archer. That is the end of the conversation. We are having him.”.

Kazan: Did you audition all of them?

It has been revealed that frost: All of them did tapes or auditions. It’s so hard to explain, isn’t it? You see somebody and you just go, “That’s what I have in my head. That’s what we need.”.

Alderton: We kind of knew who we wanted Lizzie and Darcy to be, and we had to do chemistry. We did a chemistry [read] with Emma and Jack, and Emma’s an EP on the show. So the minute Jack left, Emma and I looked at each other, and we were like, “That’s totally Darcy.”.

But it’s interesting that you were saying that thing about chemistry. I don’t know about you guys, but every time I do casting, I’m amazed how much it feels like falling in love. You go away and you find yourself Googling them and thinking about them and dreaming about them. It’s so wonderful if then they want to do it, and it’s so heartbreaking if they don’t.

Kazan: You fall in love, and then sometimes your love affair doesn’t work out.

Alderton: What was your process like?

Frost: Florence [Pugh] was involved really early, right?

According to recent reports, kazan: She was. I had always had this feeling about East of Eden, and I had sort of tried to ignore that feeling because of my grandfather’s relationship to the material and my relationship to coming from this family. And about a year and a half before this call came, I had written my agent saying, “This is so embarrassing, but if the rights to East of Eden ever come up, can you please let me know so that I can pitch on it?” So they did me a solid. I got an appointment to meet, but I didn’t have a lot of time to prepare.

They asked, “Do you have any actors in mind?” I think I had walked into the room not thinking that I had any actors in mind, and then Florence came out of my mouth. I had seen Midsommar, and I felt like I was witnessing the birth of a genius. And Cathy Ames is such a challenging part that I needed an actor of that caliber. But then we didn’t do any more casting for four years after that.

Frost: But she stayed faithful.

Sources indicate that kazan: She did. The whole reason this show came together when it did was that there was a window that she had in her schedule. We didn’t have directors yet, and we didn’t have any other cast yet. Her window was starting in October, and between April and June, we put everything together.

So much of it is alchemical. But once you have that central pole that all the spokes are going to come off of, then you start going, “Okay, well if it’s this Lizzie Bennet, it has to be that Mr. Darcy. If it’s this Newland Archer, it has to be this Ellen.”.

On the page, East of Eden is the only one of these three novels that has a protagonist who isn’t white. But that isn’t true of your series. I’m curious, Emma and Dolly, if you can speak to that—casting actors who aren’t white in these stories that are largely about white characters.

Industry observers note that frost: Yeah. Edith Wharton came from such a privileged, elite white bubble. That is completely what her life was. But the story is about a man who is chafing against that, and these rules are killing him. So having the contrast of the world inside and outside of that elite white bubble felt crucial to telling this story. And Ellen is part of this really exciting wave of immigration that’s coming into Latest York at the time, and it’s blowing this old world to pieces. And it’s so much more exciting than this kind of decaying, crusty world that he’s been trapped by.

Sources indicate that so for me, it felt like a very organic thing to have non-white characters as well that provide that contrast. They are the new ideas, they are the exciting conversations, they are the music that’s coming in. So he was one foot in each, and it was a very organic thing to do.

Alderton: I think there are so many different ways that you can look at diversity with period work. Bridgerton’s a great example of a specific thing. Colorblind casting is a specific example. We decided that we wanted our Pride and Prejudice to be very rooted in historical reality, but we also didn’t want to make an all-white Pride and Prejudice. We wanted to be inclusive and representative. So we just did our homework, and we found cases of families much like the Bingleys who had roots in trade where there were mixed-race families.

Was it the most common thing in Regency England? No. But it’s not the most common thing that a man like Mr. Darcy would’ve married Elizabeth Bennet. It’s so simple in my mind. It’s all made up anyway, and those actors were the best actors for those roles.

Kazan: Can I also say—we have white-presenting actors in East of Eden who have Caribbean roots, and Chinese American people that present as white in our series. I think the idea of whiteness, it can be a weapon. I think it can be weaponized: who we say is white and who we say isn’t white. I just think it’s a funny thing of who we agree is allowed to be in these things and who isn’t.

I do always think it’s a hard thing, because racial identity is such an key part of how people go through the world. And what both of you are saying about finding the logic within your stories for the casting that you want to make, I think, is really important. But I also think it's important to think about how there are identities that are not visible.

Was there one moment from each of your novels that you were the most nervous about getting right?

Frost: I don’t know if it’s one piece of the novel per se, but what gave me pause was trying to find a way into Ellen, Countess Olenska. I wanted to find a way to stay completely true to the spirit and intention of her as a character, but make her emotionally legible to a 21st-century audience. As framed in the novel, there is an element of her being beaten by her husband, and now she needs another man to rescue her. According to recent reports, but Edith Wharton, as ever, is so brilliant that she sort of provided this solution partly through me drawing on her own life, which I used to infuse Ellen. Also, without giving spoilers, there are things that are said about Ellen in the novel that Ellen never confirms. Alderton: My take is not so much because of the text—it was because of a previous adaptation.

Alderton: About these adaptations that live in your head.

Kazan: All three of these books have multiple—if not multiple, at least a beloved adaptation.

#165856. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another manufacturer is having an outage.
  • Recent findings suggest that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • According to recent reports, but to skeptics of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another manufacturer is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

Recent findings suggest that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

According to recent reports, but to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

It has been revealed that love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

According to recent reports, mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find upcoming security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

Industry observers note that you might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October revision. The organization's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's key to understand that just about every manufacturer that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Recent findings suggest that barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as promptly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Zosia Mamet is shedding light on an alleged on-set clash with Mad Men creator Matthew Weiner that led to her quitting the classic show after just four episodes.

“All the other actors were wonderful, but he really was like the Catholic Church back in the day, like that bro rules with fear,” Mamet, 38, revealed on the Sunday, November 22, “Armchair Expert” episode.

The Girls actress briefly appeared on the 16-time Emmy-winning drama series as Joyce Ramsay, a Life photo editor who introduced Peggy Olson (Elisabeth Moss) to a ’60s Bohemian lifestyle.

While Mad Men remains one of the most acclaimed highlights of the 2000s, Mamet told “Armchair Expert” hosts Dax Shepard and Monica Padman that the vibe on set was “absolutely horrible,” per Variety and People.

“[Weiner] would start every table read with this little speech … and he would talk about how he didn’t want any of us to take our scripts home,” she alleged. “He would be like, ‘If I see that, I’m going to find you, and I’m going to hunt you down. I’m going to kill you. Just kidding. Actually not.’ He would do this at every table read. I was like, this not only isn’t funny, but it’s yucky. It’s f***ing yucky, man!”.

Mamet explained that her final straw came when Weiner, 61, “was having a bad day and decided to set his sights on me”.

In a recent development, “During a block rehearsal, [he] just f***ing went to town on me in front of the whole cast and crew… I called my agents when I left, and I was like, ‘I can’t go back to that set,’” she mentioned. “He just systematically dressed me down for like 45 minutes. I was like, ‘I want to kill myself.”.

The actress went on to say, “My level of insecurity was so great that I knew that I wouldn’t be able [to return]. I was like, I will shut down. I won’t be able to function in this environment and the fear of that happening again was just too great.”.

Mamet had previously stopped short of directly naming Weiner in a poem from her 2025 book of essays, Does This Make Me Funny?, in which she reflected on her decision to quit a then-unnamed hit show.

Recent findings suggest that “I wrote an essay about it for my book where I don’t mention names,” Mamet confirmed on the “Armchair Expert” podcast. “But I really wanted Matt Weiner to sue me because then he would be admitting to the fact that he knew I was writing about him.”.

In that essay, Mamet referred to the-then unnamed showrunner as “an intense human” whose mere presence on set would make it seem like “a cold front had swept the soundstage.” She accused him of dressing her down in front of the whole cast over the way she opened an envelope in a scene.

It has been revealed that “He grabs my hand that’s holding the manila envelope and he indicates, ‘No! What the f*** are you doing with this [envelope]! That’s not how you take something out of an envelope! Do it again!’” Mamet alleged. “So we do it again, and again, and again. And every time we get to the part of the scene where I’m meant to take the photos out of the envelope, he calls ‘cut’ and he gets up and he yells.”.

She remembered calling her agent after allegedly being scolded to make it clear that she would never return to the Mad Men set.

It has been revealed that “I finished my day. I walked to my car and called my agents and told them I quit,” Mamet wrote in Does This Make Me Funny?. “I was supposed to do four more episodes that season, not including the one I was on, but I told them I didn’t care what they had to do, I didn’t care if the network sued me, I refused to go back on that set for one more day than I actually had to.”.

Us has reached out to Weiner’s representatives for comment.

Recent findings suggest that finding Port Gelhorn's missing tourists and the serial killer in Grand Theft Auto 6 takes you on a twisted journey around the town, one with few guideposts and a lot of chances to get stuck. It's a macabre scavenger hunt with only a few pictures and knowledge of the surrounding area to go by, though the reward at the end is comparatively small. This is a quest where the storytelling, more than anything else, is the reward.

Below, we explain where to find Gelhorn's missing tourists in GTA 6 and complete the serial killer side mission.

In a recent development, you'll first come across this exploration mission in the Starlet Motel office after Chapter 2 starts. Lucia can examine a set of missing persons posters on the wall next to Linda's desk. There's a tip line with a number to call, but it just takes you to a voice mailbox.

And that's the only hint to go off of, as the poster info gives you no clues and nowhere to look. There might be other clues hidden somewhere around town, but we didn't find them. Instead, we stumbled across the quest's starting location by accident. It's an old bunker-like warehouse across the street from Moses' garage, next to the scooter store. You can approach the front for a prompt to open the door, but it won't work. Walk down the right side of the warehouse, and look for a hole at the base. Crawl inside.

Recent findings suggest that despite how creepy the location is, there's nothing inside to harm you, though there is a jump scare midway through. Enter the red room and the trophy room beyond it, and interact with the photos there. You'll see locations showing each of the missing tourists, and these photos are stored in your phone gallery if you want to view them later. The quest prompt changes in the map menu, too, with a latest prompt for each photo.

In a recent development, you can track them in any order. We're just listing them in the order we found them. We recommend tackling this part of the quest during the day, just so it's easier to make out landmarks.

In a recent development, the junkyard is where you'll find Susanne Keeble, and it's next to the Pay 'n' Spray shop in central Gelhorn. You're looking for a pink car, and if you're having trouble finding it, activate focus mode. The car will stand out as the only interactable object in the area. Report the body to the tip line after you find it.

In a recent development, donald Miller's body is out at Wild Hog Point, the marshes outside Port Gelhorn. Head toward the tree with no leaves near the center of the marsh, and look in the water nearby to find a car. Interact with it, report the body, and move on. Someone picks up the line this time.

In a recent development, patrick Murray is the final tourist, and his body is in a trailer at the far north end of Port Gelhorn in an abandoned trailer park near a water tower. The trailer in question is the blue one. Head inside, and pull up the floorboards near the door to discover Murray's body. The clipping in the trophy room mentioned a reward for information about him, though, for reasons you'll soon discover, the tip line operator isn't ready to pay out.

The tip line man asks you to return to the warehouse after finding the third body, and the quest can change depending on whether you go alone or with your partner. We played as Jason and went with Lucia, though who takes the lead doesn't matter. Your partner stays outside, and tense events unfold inside, after which the culprit dies and the quest ends. You can grab the killer's glasses as a unique "found" accessory for Jason if you want.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Monday Night Football was briefly plunged into darkness during a Monday, November 23, game between the Washington Commanders and the Cincinnati Bengals.
  • “Somebody turned out the lights,” ESPN broadcaster Joe Buck confirmed to Monday Night Football viewers seconds after the power shut off in Northwest Stadium during the telecast.
  • The Commanders were lining up for a passing attempt in the third quarter on Monday when most of the lights in the Landover, Maryland, venue suddenly turned off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Monday Night Football was briefly plunged into darkness during a Monday, November 23, game between the Washington Commanders and the Cincinnati Bengals.

“Somebody turned out the lights,” ESPN broadcaster Joe Buck confirmed to Monday Night Football viewers seconds after the power shut off in Northwest Stadium during the telecast.

The Commanders were lining up for a passing attempt in the third quarter on Monday when most of the lights in the Landover, Maryland, venue suddenly turned off.

“The lights are out and we’re not home,” Buck joked. “They do it a lot around the National Football League where they turn the lights on and off.”.

He then humorously guessed, “Somebody leaned against the wall!”.

“We’ll see how long this takes to get them up and running,” Buck’s cohost Troy Aikman chimed in.

Buck initially offered a grim timeline for when the power might come back on, recalling that it “took forever” to resolve technical faults “back in the day.”.

The situation was made all the more nerve-wracking because NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell was watching the Monday Night Football game from one of Northwest Stadium’s luxury suites.

“We’re being told it’s power-related and not the stadium,” Buck informed viewers as cameras panned around the dimly-lit stadium.

After Monday Night Football cut to a commercial break, there was good news for viewers and both NFL teams as the lights came back on.

Play resumed moments later, with Buck later relaying to viewers that the power outage was caused by a mistimed maintenance snafu. (The Commanders ultimately beat the Bengals, 22-20.).

It has been revealed that “If you want to know the reason why the lights went out earlier, the official word is the lighting vendor never disabled the regularly scheduled maintenance for 10 p.m.,” Buck announced. “It’s a weekday thing, and they forgot it was a Monday night game.”.

Check our latest news in Google News.

Check our latest news in Apple News.

Monday’s NFL power outage follows on the heels of several similar incidents that have plagued the U.S. over the last few weeks. On November 13, flights were grounded nationwide for more than four hours due to what the Federal Aviation Administration called “extraordinary circumstances.”.

Industry observers note that “Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down,” transportation secretary and former Real World star Sean Duffy later explained during a White House Press conference. “I shouldn’t say they went down. They started giving us inconsistency in the data from those routers.”.

In the ensuing days, United Airlines and Delta Airlines experienced additional outages, as did Microsoft, Workday and JPMorgan Chase. President Donald Trump told the White House press corps on Friday, November 20, that the various outages were “all separate events” and that they were “all under control.”.

Industry observers note that it’s been seven months since Storage Wars star Darrell Sheets died by suicide in his home in Arizona, and it sounds like the other stars of the show, like Brandi Passante, are still, understandably, processing his death. Season 19 of the reality show kicks off on the 2026 television schedule on November 28th, and ahead of its premiere, Passante talked about Sheets’ passing and how it has affected both her personally and the production of the show.

Sheets left the show as a full-time cast member in 2019 after suffering a heart attack. He remained in contact with the rest of the cast, including Passante, and he made occasional guest appearances after retiring. In a discussion with TV Insider, Passante talked about how his death has affected the show, including how the rest of the cast work with each other:.

Industry observers note that it definitely changed the dynamic with everybody. We’re all a little softer and kinder to each other since that happened. There was a lot of beef and animosity before between most of us. Some things are not worth fighting.

In a recent development, sheets’ death, like so many do, really seems to have put things in perspective for the rest of the cast. Their rivalries are what make the show so endlessly watchable, but in the end, they have known each other for almost two decades now, so something like this is bound to change things. Sheets’ manner of death is also a particularly difficult thing to endure, according to Passante:.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve endured a lot of deaths in that same manner over the years, and that is just a grief that, you know, kind of sticks with you. It’s not like losing somebody to cancer or a heart attack. It’s something that you think maybe you could have helped prevent. It’s one of those difficult deaths that you never can really wrap your head around.

In a recent development, anyone who has lost a loved one to suicide knows how Passante feels. It can feel completely helpless. For her part, Passante is doing what she can, including checking in on Sheets’ son, Brandon, who was by his father’s side at all the auctions until Darrell left the show. Passante noted:.

It has been revealed that I talk to [his son] Brandon a lot now. We didn’t really chat much over the years when they left. We would talk every once in a while during holidays or something, but now I just try to keep tabs. He sends me little messages maybe once a week. I just like to check in on him because it’s a hard thing to swallow. I’m sure that he’s missing his dad.

Ultimately, Passante summed it up quite succinctly by saying simply, “It sucks.”.

Sources indicate that there has been a lot of drama on Storage Wars over the years, and while much of it is contrived for the show, behind-the-scenes has been filled with drama, too. Passante has been in the middle of some of it when she divorced her long-time partner in life and in business, Jarrod Schulz, after Season 13 of the show. There has been nothing like the tragedy that befell Sheets, though, and keeping everything in perspective is important.

It's been a long, bumpy road to the premiere of "Avengers: Doomsday" (which was initially supposed to be "Avengers: The Kang Dynasty"), but that December 18 release date is roughly a month away. That day can't arrive soon enough for Marvel Studios, which, aside from "Deadpool & Wolverine," has been knocking out box office disappointments relative to their budgets. Advance ticket sales indicate that "Doomsday" is going to open huge at the box office, so, if nothing else, Marvel and parent company Disney will be pleased.

Industry observers note that but will the movie be any good? After all, quality has also been a problem for Marvel lately. Then again, 2026 has been considerably stronger for the Marvel Cinematic Universe on that front thanks to "Spider Man: Brand Upcoming Day" and the streaming series "Wonder Men" and "VisionQuest." So, hopefully, directors Joe and Anthony Russo will build on these successes by delivering a thrilling Avengers movie.

According to recent reports, indeed, ever since that silly "Doomsday" chair casting announcement (in which most of the film's lead actors were announced individually), fans have been expecting a superhero epic for the ages, with the MCU's first-ever star, Robert Downey Jr., returning to play the formidable villain Doctor Doom. The previous "Doomsday" trailers have emphasized the sheer menace of Doom (who's even got a whole bunch of towering Sentinels at his disposal), while reminding us that some of our faves, especially Thor (Chris Hemsworth) and Steve Rogers (Chris Evans), are returning to save the whole darn universe once again.

Knowing that "Avengers: Secret Wars" is a year away, moviegoers should expect a big ol' cliffhanger (and more than a couple of big character deaths) in "Doomsday." Does the film's upcoming trailer offer any clues as to how this will all play out? Take a look above and see.

Sources indicate that okay folks, I don't want to rain on your parade, but is this doing it for anyone? Look, I know "Avengers: Doomsday" is going to be huge! A major box office success! And I know fans will get a kick out of the fanservice on display here, like Cyclops saying the famous "To me, my X-Men!" line. But ... nothing here looks particularly interesting? Or new? There's a real "going through the motions" vibe to this footage. We've seen this before.

Sources indicate that it doesn't help that from a visual standpoint, "Doomsday" looks hideous. Every shot in this trailer has a drab, flat, lifeless appearance. Dare I say it, it looks ... boring? Come on, shouldn't we expect more at this point? Shouldn't we want more? Of course, who am I kidding? As I already mentioned, this is going to be huge. And to be fair, I'm sure the movie has more in store for us than what we're being shown in the trailer.

"Avengers: Doomsday" opens December 18, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Denis Villeneuve brought on seasoned casting director Francine Maisler for the first Dune movie, they were starting from scratch. For the ambitious adaptation of Frank Herbert’s 1965 sci-fi novel, they had to cast not only the lead character, Paul Atreides, but dozens of other main characters—powerful warriors, scheming royals, shape-shifting conspirators—to inhabit the world.

Luckily, the pair had already worked together on Villeneuve’s three previous films, Sicario, Blade Runner 2049, and Arrival. “Denis’s vision is my compass,” Maisler tells Vanity Fair. “His passion [for Dune] since he was a teen was all I needed to follow.”.

Industry observers note that when they were casting the first installment, Maisler was aware that it was possible that these actors might play these characters for more than just one film. “I did have an idea that they would have to have the presence and the acting talent to be able to carry this potentially for three movies,” she states.

Industry observers note that dune (2021), starring Timothée Chalamet as Paul Atreides and Zendaya as Chani, was just the first step. Maisler returned to cast Dune: Part Two (2024), and Dune: Part Three, which will wrap up Villeneuve’s trilogy when it hits theaters on December 18.

Maisler is a titan of casting, having worked on hundreds of films with filmmakers such as Luca Guadagnino, Greta Gerwig, Aaron Sorkin, Paul Greengrass, Adam McKay, and Terrence Malick, and she was nominated for the first casting Oscar in 2026 for her work on Ryan Coogler’s Sinners.

In a recent development, the casting Oscar didn’t exist when she began working on the Dune franchise, but this installment is likely to draw attention from the Academy. Over the three films, the cast has grown into an incredible ensemble, packed with many of today’s biggest movie stars, along with well-known veterans and a few unexpected choices. “One thing about Denis is if ever I bring him a name and he likes it, and I’ll say, ‘Well, do you want to hire that actor?’ He states to me something I think is so poetic,” says Maisler. “He says, ‘Francine, let me get back to you tomorrow. I need to dream about it.’”.

Ahead of the release of Dune: Part Three, Maisler looks back at casting the trilogy’s most crucial roles, including the exciting latest additions to the upcoming film—and the possibility of more Dune in the future.

In Herbert’s book, Atreides is a slender 15-year-old with dark hair. “To find a 15-year-old who had that talent to carry this whole movie, we weren’t sure was out there,” remembers Maisler. The name that came up was then 22-year-old Chalamet, whom Maisler had previously cast in Hostiles, Beautiful Boy, The King, and Little Women. Chalamet, who didn’t have to audition but did meet with Villeneuve, would have to play Atreides from a young man who then begins to amass power in the second film and, after a 12-year time jump, is burdened with the choices he’s made waging a galactic war in the third. Though Chalamet hadn’t led a massive blockbuster before, Maisler saw the depth of his talent. “I do think Beautiful Boy demonstrated me the depth of Timothée as an actor, as a young man, and that this was the next step in his progression as an actor, that he was able to hold a franchise in his hand,” notes Maisler.

Recent findings suggest that there was a worldwide search for Chani, the skilled Fremen warrior from Arrakis who falls in love with Atreides. At the time, Zendaya was in the middle of filming the first season of Euphoria, and her graduation from Disney star to movie star had not yet happened. Zendaya screen tested with Chalamet, which sealed it for Maisler and Villeneuve. “She came in with five other incredibly talented actresses, but the minute you saw her with Timothée in a room, you just knew that there’s something special happening,” she says. “She has such power when she walks in the room, and she’s breathtaking in the most interesting way.”.

It has been revealed that of course, Paul Atreides’s parents, Duke Leto Atreides and Lady Jessica, needed to look like Chalamet, but Maisler started with the characters’ essences when casting. Duke Leto Atreides was considered a fair and devoted leader as the noble head of House Atreides. Maisler saw that gravitas in Oscar Isaac. Lady Jessica becomes a force in the story because of her heightened physical and mental control as a trained member of the Bene Gesserit sisterhood. “Rebecca is so powerful, isn’t she?” states Maisler. “She really, I have to say, surprised me. I always knew how talented she was, but she just owned that part.”.

Industry observers note that villeneuve and Maisler had worked with Brolin on the 2015 crime thriller Sicario. Maisler, who calls Brolin “one of our greatest actors,” was excited to have him back, this time playing Gurney Halleck, the Warmaster of House Atreides and a mentor to Paul Atreides. The character is described in the book as a warrior-poet, requiring strength and depth. “He’s so charismatic, so masculine,” claims Maisler of Brolin. “He’s kind of a throwback from other generations.”.

Recent findings suggest that when Momoa’s agent brought up Momoa’s name, Maisler wasn’t quite sure about the idea because at the time he was known for starring in the DC movie franchise as Aquaman. “I was a bit skeptical, I have to admit, because I knew he had this incredible presence on screen, but I didn’t know, truly, his talent, and that’s taught me a lot about being open to people who come from different types of films,” she says. Villeneuve was more open to the idea at the start, and met with him about playing Duncan Idaho, a fierce fighter and protector of Paul Atreides. He returns in the third movie as a ghola—a sort of clone—named Hayt, which demands a more complicated performance from Momoa. “Jason’s an incredible artist, and I’ve come to just love him,” says Maisler. “He’s so funny. I want to put him in a romantic comedy next, because he really is one of the major surprises in the ensemble.”.

Recent findings suggest that taylor-Joy had already risen in stardom by the time she joined the franchise for the second film. Her breakout was in The Witch, and she starred in hit series The Queen's Gambit, which earned her a Golden Globe and a SAG Award. This made it slightly surprising that Alia Atreides, Paul’s volatile sister, makes a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it appearance in the second film. “I give her a lot of credit for not counting lines in the second one,” indicates Maisler, who says Taylor-Joy signed on for the second because of the potential of the third installment. Indeed, in Dune: Part Three, Alia is a loyal sister and vengeful force who is not afraid to get blood on her hands. Taylor-Joy’s charisma and intensity will jump off the screen, says Maisler. “Actors are very smart, and they know when to trust a director like Denis,” she says. “When he says there is going to be something in the third film and he describes it, he will make it happen.”.

A tribal leader of the desert-dwelling Fremen, Stilgar is a seasoned warrior and becomes a devout follower of Paul Atreides as Muad’Dib. The role required a level of intensity. “Oh, I think we all just prayed that Javier would do it,” says Maisler. “I think every actor wants to work with Javier, and he’s one of probably a handful of actors I think can do anything.”.

It has been revealed that pugh joined for the second film as well, but like Taylor-Joy, she didn’t have a ton to do. But Princess Irulan, who marries Paul Atreides as a political union, is a key part of the plot in Dune: Part Three, joining a conspiracy against Paul. Maisler first saw Pugh in the 2016 film Lady Macbeth, and then cast her as Amy March in Gerwig’s Little Women. “You saw on that what an intelligent actress she is, and singular,” she says. “She knows no boundaries, and she’s confident and bold.” She says Pugh has always reminded her of Debra Winger, the star of An Officer and a Gentleman (1982), and Terms of Endearment (1983). “She’s just commanding, and she has this energy, and everything she does is fascinating,” says Maisler. “You can’t take your eyes off of her.”.

The third installment brings in yet another major star with Pattinson, who plays Scytale, a shape-shifter who is conspiring to dethrone Paul Atreides. Maisler, who also worked with Pattinson in Primetime, which also came out this year, describes him as “one of the versatile actors in his choices.” She had also worked with Pattinson on Mickey 17, which proved that he could play many different versions of a character—a skill that would be required of him in this third Dune movie. “Robert's a tremendous actor, and I think he takes these really bold chances,” indicates Maisler. As for his recent announcement as the next James Bond, Maisler has faith he and Villeneuve will deliver. “I think the way Denis and Rob created the character in Dune: Part Three together speaks to the surprises that we will see in Bond,” she says.

For Dune: Part Three, Maisler and Villeneuve had to find two actors who looked like twins and also looked like the offspring of Chalamet and Zendaya. They initially hoped to cast real twins, but didn’t find the right pair. In the end, they found their Ghanima and Leto II in Ida Brooke and Nakoa-Wolf Momoa. Brooke, who looks strikingly like Zendaya, is a relative newcomer who previously appeared on Apple’s sci-fi drama Silo (which stars Rebecca Ferguson). And Nakoa-Wolf Momoa, who makes his feature acting debut in Dune: Part Three, is Jason Momoa’s son—though Maisler didn’t know that when she first watched his audition tape. “Then came this tape of this young man who had incredible presence, and—we didn’t ask for this—he added some combat footage to his tape,” she notes. Maisler says sometimes actors will call in a favor to get their child an audition, but Wolf, as she calls him, got this on his own. This casting was the most vital for the third film because of what might be to come. “It was almost like casting the first one where these two young actors could go on to potentially, if there’s another movie where they’re leads,” says Maisler. There have been no official announcements of any future Dune movies, but for those mourning the end of the Villeneuve trilogy, Maisler is planting a small seed of hope here. The third Dune book, Children of Dune, centers on Leto and Ghanima, which means the two young actors Maisler found may have more story ahead of them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that rupert Grint is the latest cast member from the Harry Potter films to join the Broadway run of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, right on the heels of Tom Felton's successful run. With Ron Weasley in tow, he's already fielding questions about whether Emma Watson and Danielle Radcliffe could be next to join the stage play.

It has been revealed that the actor, who will reprise his role as Ron for the production, confirmed it would be his last time playing the character. As such, Collider wanted to know if there was a chance of his former famous co-stars joining. Grint didn't say definitively one way or another, but offered up this:.

It would be fun. I don't know. I mean, it's obviously different for everyone. It was an intense time. When we finished, I really enjoyed stepping away and not really even thinking about it, because it was such an intense… I mean, it was enjoyable, and they looked after us, but it was a massive part of us. So, yeah, maybe. I don't know. It'd be fun.

According to recent reports, I'm sure the last thing Grint wanted to do was try to put the pressure on Radcliffe and Watson to say no, knowing the complicated thoughts both may have about returning. Daniel Radcliffe has been pretty adamant about refusing any opportunities to return, and Emma Watson has shied away from acting so much that there were rumors a few years back that she had retired.

People are always free to change their minds of course, and Rupert Grint is evidence of that. He initially stated he'd only return if everyone else did, and now he's in a position where he's being asked whether his co-stars will join him onstage for Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. He talked about his return and how he felt immediately after the film franchise ended way back when:.

According to recent reports, yeah. It's funny. It's interesting, going back. I spent so much time after finishing Potter kind of moving away from it and doing other things, which I've really enjoyed doing, but I think now it's a very different role in a very different context. And weirdly, it's kind of lined up that I'm the exact age of the character in that story, so it's just felt like a good time.

It does feel like a good time, what with a new Harry Potter TV show on the way. The series' arrival on the 2026 TV schedule will likely spark even more interest than usual in the franchise, and possibly encourage a lot of millennials craving nostalgia to see Grint back as Ron.

Timing aside, I'm sure it doesn't surprise anyone that actors love to work. For Rupert Grint, the return to being on stage pulls back to his start as a child actor, and that's going to be a great joy for him:.

Recent findings suggest that and I love New York and being on stage. It's been a while since I've done that, and it's a very vital thing to me. It was my childhood, and I have a very strong connection to that character and that world. I think I'm not going to get many other opportunities to play him again. It probably is my last, and I think it'll be fun.

Industry observers note that it should be fun, especially given what Ron Weasley is up to in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. He's running the joke shop Fred and George founded, while his wife Hermione is the literal Minister of Magic. As far as acting is concerned, it's more of a supportive role, but one that Rupert Grint will likely bring a special sparkle to.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

It has been revealed that I'm still waiting to see if Grint, Emma Watson, or Daniel Radcliffe will show up in the Potter TV series. Part of me thinks they'd do it for the fans, but at the same time, I could see them wanting the latest cast to have a chance to do their own thing, without drawing attention to themselves. I guess all we can do is wait and see what happens!

It has been revealed that rupert Grint's run on Broadway in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child kicks off on February 2nd and will end on May 30th. I'm sure getting a ticket could be a struggle, but I'm eager to see what the demand will be for fans to see one of the core stars back in the franchise!
