📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in 1959, Gregory Peck starred in a surprisingly bleak dystopian sci-fi movie about the end of the world. Perhaps unsurprisingly, given its subject matter, "On the Beach" was a box office disappointment, despite the fact it also starred Ava Gardner, Fred Astaire, and a pre-"Psycho" Anthony Perkins. But as Turner Classic Movies notes, "the film struck a chord with the public and for decades remained the definitive dramatic portrayal of the aftermath of a nuclear attack.".

Sources indicate that peck made his film debut in 1944's "Days of Glory" and, amazingly, earned an Oscar nomination for his work in John M. Stahl's "The Keys of the Kingdom" that same year. While that film proved to be his breakthrough, it wasn't until the 1950s that he truly ascended to megastardom, becoming one of the biggest leading men in Hollywood. He started the decade by irritating 20th Century Fox chief Darryl F. Zanuck, who wanted Peck to shave his mustache for the 1950 Western "The Gunfighter," before going on to star alongside Audrey Hepburn in the romance classic and one of the best movies of the '50s, "Roman Holiday.".

It has been revealed that he also appeared alongside Ava Gardner in 1952's "The Snows of Kilimanjaro," before reuniting with her for 1959's "On the Beach." While their prior collaboration had been a romantic adventure outing, "On the Beach" was a decidedly more gloomy affair in which humanity was wiped out almost entirely, while the survivors waited to be killed off by radioactive winds. Not exactly, "Roman Holiday," then. Still, the film has its share of romance and adventure, even if it does end on a fairly dreary note.

Industry observers note that "On the Beach" isn't always cited as one of the best Gregory Peck movies, and is a bit of an underrated entry in his filmography that deserves more attention. For one thing, the film is directed by Stanley Kramer, the legendary filmmaker who also oversaw "The Defiant Ones," "Guess Who's Coming to Dinner," and "It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World." All of Kramer's movies tackled social complications, and with "On the Beach" the problem was nuclear war. The film arrived in an era in which such a thing was an ever-present threat and like many other filmmakers after him, Kramer wanted to hammer home the absurdity, horror, and tragedy of it all.

Sources indicate that he did so by adapting Nevil Shute's 1957 novel "On the Beach," in which nuclear war erupts, wiping out most of the major nations and leaving clouds of radiation across the northern hemisphere, which begin to drift South towards Australia. Kramer's movie version uses the same premise, though unlike in the book, we never learn who actually dropped the bombs that wiped out life in the Northern hemisphere. Instead, we simply learn that Gregory Peck's Capt. Dwight Towers and the crew of his American nuclear submarine USS Sawfish are arriving in Melbourne to escape the nuclear fallout in their homeland.

Towers is greeted by Australian naval officer Peter Holmes (Anthony Perkins), who invites him to a party. There, Towers meets regretful nuclear scientist Julian Osborn (Fred Astaire) and Ava Gardner's Moira Davidson, with whom Towers falls in love. Soon, it transpires that the nuclear fallout everyone expected to float down to Australia might not make it that far south, and Towers sets out with his submarine crew to investigate.

Industry observers note that without giving away the ending, "On the Beach" doesn't wrap up on all that happy a note. Stanley Kramer remind viewers that there's "still time" via a banner that literally indicates as much. But it happens to be flapping away in a deserted Melbourne in a way that calls to mind the end of "Oppenheimer," in which the titular scientist ponders how the nuclear destruction of our species is inevitable regardless of how long we stave it off.

Industry observers note that that might have something to do with the film's disappointing box office. After all, it couldn't have been a lack of star power. "On the Beach" was also shot on-location in Melbourne and was, as The Sydney Morning Herald noted in 2019, "the biggest film ever made" in the city. Stanley Kramer, meanwhile, was on a roll following the success of 1958's "The Defiant Ones," and "On the Beach" earned positive reviews. It should have been a bigger hit and should definitely be more widely remembered than it is today.

In a recent development, many films designed to remind audiences of the devastating threat posed by nuclear weapons have come in the wake of "On the Beach." In 1966, the BBC released the horrific mockumentary "The War Game," which was summarily banned by the Government of the United Kingdom for its disturbing depiction of nuclear attack and the ensuing fallout. Then there was 1983's "The Day After" and 1984's "Threads," the apocalyptic TV movie that shook Britain to its core. More recently we've seen movies like "House of Dynamite" provide a realistic look at how a nuclear attack might unfold. But Gregory Peck's 1959 film was one of the first to really deal head-on with the threat of nuclear annihilation and deserves to be remembered for it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Marshals" Season 2, Episode 7, "Under the Influence," sees Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton and Arielle Kebbel's Belle Skinner go undercover in an off-grid cult. During their time there, Kayce is confronted by the cult's charismatic leader, who forces him to relive the loss of his infant child — a moment from "Yellowstone" that was both tragic and, in the eyes of many fans, ridiculous.

Sources indicate that kayce Dutton has been haunted by his "Yellowstone" experience since the very beginning of "Marshals." The youngest Dutton scion has seen it all (including the worst things the Dutton family ever did on "Yellowstone") and has been trying to put it all behind him since Taylor Sheridan's neo-Western series wrapped up back in 2024. Unfortunately, as Brett Cullen's Chief Deputy U.S. Marshal Harry Gifford observed in "Marshals" Season 1, "Duttons are born with dysfunction in their blood," and "Under the Influence" forces Kayce to confront one of his most painful memories. That memory just so happens to be linked to one of the most controversial storylines in "Yellowstone" history.

In a recent development, "Under the Influence" sees ATF agent Sam Colby (Adam Joel) go missing after embedding himself in Moonstone Farm, a homesteading cult led by the mysterious and intense Eric Savard. This character is played by Beau Knapp, who delivers a surprisingly compelling performance as the Moonstone figurehead. (The show should bring him back ASAP.) After Kayce and Belle infiltrate the farm, Savard emerges to welcome them at a community meeting that quickly turns sinister when the cult leader forces Kayce to relive the trauma of losing his infant son. It's clearly a rough time for both the Dutton boy and for fans, who have to be reminded of this contentious "Yellowstone" moment.

It has been revealed that in "Under the Influence," Eric Savard confronts Kayce Dutton and asks him what he's lost. After a few lies, Savard pushes Kayce, and he's left with no choice but to draw from his real-life experience. "My son," he notes. "He was barely an hour old. I wasn't even there." This is a reference to "Yellowstone" Season 5, in which a pregnant Monica Dutton (Kelsey Asbille) decides to drive herself to the hospital during early labor. Why? Well, that remains one of the biggest points of contention, as it seems she and Kayce had no birth strategy whatsoever. Meanwhile, Tate Dutton (Brecken Merrill) could have driven her but didn't, and for some reason, calling an ambulance was completely out of the question. All of this led to Monica driving herself, almost hitting a buffalo, swerving, and crashing head-on into an oncoming truck.

Sources indicate that the result was the loss of baby Dutton, who was set to be named in honor of Kayce's father, John Dutton (Kevin Costner), who himself suffered a terrible and controversial death in "Yellowstone" Season 5. Baby John passed away roughly an hour after the crash, which is what Kayce references in "Under the Influence.".

Sources indicate that baby John remains one of many "Yellowstone" characters who should never have died. His passing not only seemed avoidable but like a quick way to get some drama out of the show's final season and nothing more. Fans have since criticized the whole thing (check out Reddit to get a sense of their distaste), and it stands as one of the show's least effective storylines. Now, "Marshals" has tried to revisit it for some drama of its own. But like most things in this CBS spin-off, there's not really much beyond a surface-level reference.

Earlier in "Marshals" Season 2, we saw a flashback in which a young Kayce Dutton looked in the mirror at a fresh Yellowstone brand on his chest. This is the brand his father, John, used to bring relatives and ranch hands into the "Yellowstone" brotherhood, forever tying them to the ranch. That same brand is shown in "Under the Influence," wherein Kayce is pulled off a man he's fighting only for his shirt to open, revealing the unmistakable Yellowstone mark.

"Marshals" Season 1 had trouble figuring out what it was about, juggling storylines and never seeming to explore any one of them in too much depth. That's mostly remained the case for Season 2, but there does seem to be a bit more of a focus on Kayce reckoning with his past. The second season of "Marshals" began by putting a twist on a "Yellowstone" tradition, namely by using animal imagery to evoke Kayce's inner emotional state. The character would encounter a Buffalo on his property at times when he was trying and failing to mentor Tate Dutton and steer him away from embracing what Tate calls "the Dutton way." Since then, we've seen a small but noticeable increase in scenes showing Kayce reflecting on his family's past.

Recent findings suggest that "Under the Influence" might be the most significant in that respect, as it ends with Tate moving out of East Camp and Kayce drinking again after having abstained for years. What's more, Ash Santos' Andrea Cruz asks Logan Marshall-Green's Pete Calvin about Kayce's story, to which Pete replies it's not his place to tell. At this point, it seems as though the show's writers might actually be interested in going a little deeper into Kayce's Yellowstone trauma, and that's a good thing.

Then, on the dishy Amazon Prime series "The Girlfriend" that aired in 2025, Cooke starred alongside Robin Wright as the absurdly named Cherry Laine, a flirtatious and openly sex-positive woman who starts dating a man with an overprotective mother (Wright).

Recent findings suggest that cooke is a versatile actress, and like Dormer, she's able to wield her beauty like a sharp weapon, which would make for an extremely fun performance as Moneypenny. Recent findings suggest that michaela Coel is probably the most offbeat choice to play Moneypenny in a future James Bond project, but do me a favor and walk with me here. Callister" episode of "Black Mirror" to the psychosexual A24 drama "Mother Mary" alongside Anne Hathaway, and she's uniformly excellent in every single one of her performances.

Coel, who also has an Emmy for her guest performance on the Amazon Prime series "Mr. & Mrs. Smith" (and should have several for "I May Destroy You"), is a truly formidable actress who can hold her own against A-listers like Hathaway and Ian McKellen in 2025's "The Christophers," and I think she'd add a serious edge to Moneypenny that would just elevate this role. We don't know what future Bond movies will do with the character after Naomie Harris brought her into modern times, but after Harris, Coel is certainly a worthy actor to pick up the mantle and deliver her own sly, cunning take on Moneypenny. Seriously, if you have any doubt, go watch Coel in "Mother Mary" and tell me you wouldn't love to see her defiantly flirt with Pattinson's James Bond.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in an action movie, there’s nothing worse than an underwhelming final battle. While Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings was one of the best post-Avengers: Endgame movies of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, its final battle became a disconnected CGI fest that was hard to follow. For Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Secret of the Ooze, the sequel’s fun energy was undermined when a mutated Shredder died after collapsing a dock onto himself without a fight ever even starting.

Industry observers note that it can be hard to stick the landing with that final boss fight, especially after a movie has been good up until that point, and a lame final battle can undermine everything that came before it. Fortunately, James Cameron’s 1986 action thriller Aliens — leaving Netflix on Dec. 1 — does not suffer from this issue, even after setting an impossibly high bar for itself.

After Ellen Ripley (Sigourney Weaver) defeated one Xenomorph alien aboard a spaceship in Ridley Scott’s 1979 horror thriller Alien, Cameron blew up the franchise by having Ripley visit a planet full of those same creatures and fend off dozens of them with the help of a platoon of Colonial Marines.

Spoilers ahead for the end of Aliens.

Towards the end of Aliens, after Ripley rescues the young girl named Newt (Carrie Henn) from an alien nest filled with eggs, Ripley encounters the Xenomorph queen, a massive creature far larger and more frightening than any of the aliens she’d encountered thus far. After a momentary hesitation, Ripley proceeds to turn her blowtorch on the eggs and blow up the egg sack attached to the queen, while the creature writhes in pain. After Ripley escapes with Newt, the queen tears herself free from the egg sac​​​​​​​ and pursues the duo, who narrowly escape.

Sources indicate that what follows is one of the great fake-outs in cinema history. Bishop (Lance Henriksen), the loyal android, retrieves Ripley and Newt in a dropship, and they escape as the alien-infested planet below is nuked.​​​​​​​ They return to the main ship and all seems well until​​​​​​​ the queen, who had stowed away on the scout ship, tears Bishop in half and comes after Ripley and Newt. Newt hides under the floor panels and the queen nearly gets her​​​​​​​ until Ripley reappears with an exosuit cargo loader and the two have an epic brawl for the ages.

Discussing the queen in a 1987 interview, Cameron explained,​​​​​​​ “The queen was an opportunity to take a design stance that was beyond the first film — create a new organism, basically.”.

She was a creature that Cameron designed himself, building upon the work of artist HR Giger, who designed the Xenomorph alien for the first film.

According to recent reports, “I had an image of what I wanted this thing to look like, which was, obviously, inspired by Giger's approach,” remarked Cameron. “I wanted to continue with that design philosophy, but I wanted to give it certain other characteristics in terms of size and speed and grace and certain feminine characteristics that the alien warrior didn't have. So I just sat down and drew a few different versions of it. And, actually, the first full sketch that I did of it is pretty remarkably close to what we finally wound up with.”.

Special effects wizard Stan Winston​​​​​​​ then led the team of effects artists that created the most complex animatronic monster made up to that point​​​​​​​. It took up to 16 puppeteers to control the queen, with some parts moved by hydraulics and others by rods and cables​​​​​​​. And, because this was 1986, none of that operating equipment could end up in the shot to be removed later digitally. What we see in the movie is precisely what was filmed during production.

Perhaps the most impressive thing about the Xenomorph queen, though, was just how perfectly it built upon everything else in the film. When compared to the single alien in Ridley Scott’s original film, Aliens was already full of surprises just by the sheer volume of creatures, but the queen managed to perfectly pay off the entire film with a terrifying design and an incredibly tense battle with Ripley. Four decades later​​​​​​​, it’s still one of the best final fights in cinema history, and certainly worth revisiting before the film leaves Netflix.

According to recent reports, aliens is available to stream on Netflix until Dec. 1. It's also on Hulu and Disney Plus.

One Variant Of Marvel's Doctor Doom Is A Descendant Of A Brutal Historical Villain

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in the 2000s, Marvel Comics launched "Ultimate Marvel," a reboot that brought its lead characters into the 21st century.
  • According to recent reports, "Ultimate Fantastic Four" also reimagined the FF's nemesis, Doctor Doom.
  • Recent findings suggest that "Ultimate Fantastic Four" #7 (by Warren Ellis and Stuart Immonen) depicts Victor's childhood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the 2000s, Marvel Comics launched "Ultimate Marvel," a reboot that brought its lead characters into the 21st century. "Ultimate Fantastic Four" pivoted from from the classic "astronauts bathed in cosmic rays" origin (which is so 1960s). Instead, the "Ultimate" FF were teen geniuses transformed in a teleportation experiment.

According to recent reports, "Ultimate Fantastic Four" also reimagined the FF's nemesis, Doctor Doom. Renamed Victor Van Damme, this Doom was part of the Baxter Building think tank and was also transformed in the Four's accident. This Doom has no armor, but literal metal skin. (You can see that both the 2005 and 2015 "Fantastic Four" films took from "Ultimate Fantastic Four" for their Dooms, to their detriment.).

Recent findings suggest that "Ultimate Fantastic Four" #7 (by Warren Ellis and Stuart Immonen) depicts Victor's childhood. On his tenth birthday, Victor's father revealed to him that they are descendants of Vlad Țepeș, or Vlad the Impaler/Vlad Dracula, the infamous 15th century king of Wallachia. Van Damme Sr. explains to his boy:.

Sources indicate that "Vlad Dracula understood that truth is inborn. That men of greatness must bend an ignorant world to their truth by any means necessary. And so he bent Wallachia to his will. He was cruel, but cruelty is no vice. It is a tool of necessity.".

From that moment, Victor was told he must be a man who bends the world to his will. His father instructs him to memorize his family line from Vlad down, beating him whenever he fails. Doom being the descendant of royalty, coming from money, and being imparted from childhood with lessons that a great leader is a ruthless one are all massive changes to his character. Victor von Doom acts like an aristocrat, but unlike Victor Van Damme, he came from nothing.

In a recent development, doctor Doom is an Eastern European king, beloved by his own people but seen as monstrous by outsiders. He's a monarch in Vlad the Impaler's image, so making Doom a literal descendant of Vlad fits. But "Ultimate" Doom does not live up to his family legacy.

Sources indicate that his first "kingdom" is a camp of squatters in Copenhagen. Clad in green rags (instead of a regal cloak), Doom compares his fresh skin to "Wallachian armor," but he didn't forge it himself. His metal body can form sharp spikes, like the kind on which Vlad impaled his enemies. Reed Richards, much pettier and hotheaded than his classic self, scratches Victor with one of those spikes and leaves a scar: "Impaled on your own sword, Victor.".

Vlad is associated with dragons; his father, Vlad II, was a member of the Order of the Dragon knighthood, and known as Vlad Dracul, or "Vlad the Dragon." (Vlad III's infamous moniker can mean "son of the dragon.") "Ultimate" Doom brands his followers with dragon tattoos made up of mind-controlling microfibers.

Dracula can also mean "son of the Devil." Doom's metallic body has cloven hoof legs, echoing goatlike depictions of Satan. But "Dracula" or not, Doom doesn't drink blood — and neither did the real Vlad the Impaler. Pop culture has reforged Vlad into the historical basis for Bram Stoker's "Dracula" and its vampiric villain. Later "Dracula" adaptations like Francis Ford Coppola's 1992 "Dracula" film or the action-horror manga "Hellsing" explicitly depict Dracula as the same person as the historical Vlad.

Sources indicate that "Ultimate Fantastic Four" indulges this, too. Victor's father tells his son that Vlad let his enemies believe he drank blood. As Doom, Victor brands his subjects on their necks, and controls them like vampires do familiars.

Dotor Doom echoes both the historical Vlad and the literary Dracula; his fictional nation, Latveria, is a pastiche of the gothic Transylvania seen in "Dracula" movies. (Many "Fantastic Four" adaptations also insert Doom having an infatuation with Sue Storm that he never has had in the comics, like how many "Dracula" films make the Count and Mina Harker lovers, not monster and victim.).

Sources indicate that "Dracula" is often paired with Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein," especially thanks to Universal and Hammer's films of both. Doom melds "Dracula" with "Frankenstein." He shares Dr. Frankenstein's name, Victor, and both men's lives are defined by the death of their respective mothers. Victor Frankenstein tried to create life in grief over his mother's death, while the machine that blew up in Doom's face was an attempt to contact the "nether world" and his mother's soul.

According to recent reports, as the classic Doom stands in the shadow of these villains, historical and literary, Victor Van Damme in "Ultimate Fantastic Four" stands in Doom's. "Ultimate Doom" almost feels like a purposefully-inverted villain, taking Doom down a peg yet only highlighting the strengths of the original.

Classic Doom was born into a poor Roma tribe. The world told him he was lesser and he made himself into a king to prove it wrong. "Ultimate" Doom was taught from childhood that the world was his birthright, but he isn't strong enough to carry it — like Kendall Roy if he was a Eurotrash super-villain. Classic Doom created an armored second skin to hide himself and his supposedly scarred face from the world. "Ultimate" Doom's flesh hardened like a chrysalis, turned brittle, and cracked off, leaving only metal — as if a heartless tin man with the features of the Devil is all he ever was.

According to recent reports, cristian Mungiu's Palme d'Or-winning, Sebastian Stan-starring film "Fjord" will be available to rent on digital platforms beginning November 24, 2026. Given that this is a few days before Thanksgiving, "Fjord" will be the perfect film to watch with the extended family, and won't inspire any kind of snippy, angry political discussions whatsoever.

Recent findings suggest that that, of course, is sarcasm. "Fjord" is, in fact, very, very political. According to /Film's review, "Fjord" is a clumsy, one-sided, and very ideologically weighted drama that is presented as unbiased through its efficient visuals and realistic style, but which is very biased indeed. Even in a room of people who are politically aligned, either to the left or the right, "Fjord" will inspire discussion. Or an argument. Watch it with your politically opposed family members, and let the sparks fly.

"Fjord" tells the story of the Gheorghiu family, which consists of stern Romanian father Mihai (not listed as one of Stan's best roles on /Film's countdown of them) and Norwegian mother Lisbet (Renate Reinsve), along with their two teens, two elementary-school-age kids, and an infant, who move from their long-term Romanian home to the small Norwegian town where Lisbet grew up. The Gheorghius are conservative Christians, which is very different from the local community, mostly made up of non-adherents.

When the Gheorghiu parents are unexpectedly accused of physically abusing their children, Norwegian Child Protective Services immediately takes the kids away (like, in an afternoon), leaving the Gheorghius having to find any kind of legal recourse to get them back. They will eventually have to explain themselves in court. The Gheorghius aren't wholly innocent, confessing to spanking their kids from time to time.

According to recent reports, the progressive government of Norway is presented as being full of harridans and busybodies who are hellbent on removing children from their well-meaning parents. "Fjord" presents a political conflict between conservative and liberal ideologies. The Gheorghius attempt to gin up support for their cause by calling in conservative protestors and staging their legal struggle as a bias against Christians. By Romanian social norms, a light spanking is seen as socially appropriate, but the Norwegian government is determined to keep the Gheorghiu kids away from Mihai and Lisbet. The movie sides with the conservative characters, making the entire film feel like light social propaganda.

"Fjord," however, won the Palme d'Or at Cannes, as well as the François Chalais Prize, the FIPRESCI Prize, the Prize of the Ecumenical Jury, and the Prix de la Citoyenneté. It is also beloved by most critics, racking up a 91% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 165 reviews. Justin Chang's review in The Fresh Yorker noted that some of the villains in "Fjord" are unrealistically larger-than-life, but that it was ultimately subtle. He wrote:.

"Is 'Fjord' guilty, as some have charged, of stacking the moral decks in the Gheorghius' favor? We are presented with a few potentially hissable villains ... Yet Mungiu has an uncommon ability to temper bluntness with nuance.".

Industry observers note that as soon as it's easily available to rent online, one can watch "Fjord" for themselves and see if it's politically charged, naturally neutral, or morally complex. Cristian Mungiu tends to handle politically difficult issues with frankness and directness; he reminded us of the necessity of abortion with his 2007 drama "4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days." You, however, are the one can must decide if "Fjord" is as powerful.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Time is as cruel to sci-fi television as it is to humans.
  • Fortunately, Prime Video's The Expanse is a rare exception.
  • It has been revealed that perhaps in a decade, even the visuals from The Expanse will start feeling dated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Time is as cruel to sci-fi television as it is to humans. As more time goes by, it becomes hard not to notice how sci-fi reveals that were once considered masterpieces are slowly decaying into tomorrow's relics. Good sci-fi storytelling alone remains timeless. However, from a visual and legacy standpoint, many TV shows of our time struggle to sustain what they started.

Fortunately, Prime Video's The Expanse is a rare exception.

It has been revealed that perhaps in a decade, even the visuals from The Expanse will start feeling dated. The CGI from earlier seasons already seems a little rough around the edges. Yet, overall, The Expanse can still stand well against some of the biggest major-screen productions. The reason being that its visual language emphasized grounded physics and industrial grit instead of extreme photorealism.

When it comes to The Expanse's themes, it feels more relevant than ever. Its portrayal of manufactured class divides, information war, and humanity's unchecked ambition reflects real concerns surrounding today's world. Beyond its themes and visuals, however, there is another aspect that ensures the Prime Video sci-fi show ages like George Clooney.

Way too many sci-fi shows have landed in the ever-growing graveyard of the streaming era's cancelations. This has happened to a point where many viewers have even given up on getting too invested in shows. After all, one can never know when the proverbial plug will be pulled.

The Expanse, too, almost became a victim of the same trend. Despite earning immense acclaim after landing on Syfy, it was canceled after just three seasons. History could have repeated itself. The Expanse could have become another forgotten sci-fi series that fell short of reaching its full potential.

However, this is when fan-campaigning and Amazon eventually saved the day.

Sources indicate that more often than not, fan campaigns go unnoticed. When the economics stop making sense, streaming services and networks care little about fan campaigns from cult audiences. In The Expanse's case, though, fans did everything from flying a place over Amazon Studios to launching a miniature Rocinante into near-space.

In a recent development, as a result, The Expanse was saved by Amazon, and Jeff Bezos himself unveiled its return. He mentioned (via Forbes),.

It has been revealed that "I just got word that The Expanse is saved. The show is extraordinary, and these guys are unbelievably talented.”.

While Prime Video, too, could not eventually sustain the show's run beyond season 6, it is hard not to be grateful that The Expanse got to last so long. Some of the best aspects of the series emerge after season 3, which shows how it would not have been half as good if Prime Video had not given it a second chance.

Recent findings suggest that unlike many canceled sci-fi shows, The Expanse has a reliable 6-season arc with a solid legacy. It continues to age so well because it got the opportunity to reach its full potential.

According to recent reports, lined up with the same team as The Expanse, Prime Video is adapting Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck's The Captive's War book series. Naren Shankar of The Expanse fame is returning as the showrunner, while director Breck Eisner is also set to helm the series. Reports suggest that even Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck​​​​ are actively involved in the series' writers' room.

In a recent development, with so much going in The Captive's War's favor, it is hard not to hope that it will get the same treatment as The Expanse. Unlike The Expanse, The Captive's War only consists of a trilogy of books. Owing to this, if its creators adapt only one book per season, the show could wrap its run in just three seasons.

However, given how unpredictable streaming cancellations have become, one can only pray that it will last long enough to cover its entire source material. Given the strength of its production team and source material, though, The Captive's War could have a strong three-to-four season run before concluding its story.

If all goes well, the upcoming Prime Video sci-fi series could also match The Expanse's legacy and maybe even pave the way for its return after season 6.

In a recent development, the Expanse is a sci-fi series set in the distant future where humanity has spread out across the solar system, but the alliances between the three most potent governing bodies have reached a state of cold war. A mixed-up crew finds themselves at the center of a dangerous intergalactic conspiracy that threatens to bring war to the colonized worlds.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • From 1980 until 1995, no one was safe from the dark wit of Gary Larson, not even Mickey Mouse.
  • Here are the 10 best Disney parodies featured in Gary Larson’s The Far Side.
  • Recent findings suggest that jiminy Cricket, Pinocchio's conscience in the 1940 Disney classic and the ghost of Christmas Past in 1983’s Mickey's Christmas Carol, finds himself in a glass jar in this comic strip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From 1980 until 1995, no one was safe from the dark wit of Gary Larson, not even Mickey Mouse. For 15 years, while he was publishing his beloved single-panel comic strip The Far Side, Larson satirized just about everything, including popular culture. And while Disney didn’t own Marvel, Star Wars, the Muppets, and so many other brands back then, the tech giant was still a huge target that Larson took aim at several times.

Here are the 10 best Disney parodies featured in Gary Larson’s The Far Side.

Recent findings suggest that jiminy Cricket, Pinocchio's conscience in the 1940 Disney classic and the ghost of Christmas Past in 1983’s Mickey's Christmas Carol, finds himself in a glass jar in this comic strip. I assume this guy is an entomologist, or at least a bug collector.

Industry observers note that as funny as this idea is on its own, there are a few dark details here that add to the macabre humor​​​​​​​. For one, the guy is singing the Pinocchio song “When You Wish Upon a Star,” which makes me wonder if he intentionally lured Jiminy to him. Also, if you look closely in the jar with Jiminy, he’s being kept in some sort of water or solution, with his hat floating on top of the liquid. Is Jiminy already dead?

Pinocchio's conscience isn’t the only one to feel the wrath of Gary Larson. So does the wooden boy himself in this hilarious 1992 comic panel which is all about the worst possible time for Pinocchio to become a real boy.

According to recent reports, A year after the lion comic, Larson returned to Pinocchio and made him a victim of yet another feline​​​​​​​. Honestly, if I were a cat, I would definitely turn Pinocchio into a scratching post. He’s perfect for that.

In a recent development, this strip is a play on the word “Mousketeer” — at least, I think it is. This feels like one of those Far Side comics that is more of a rough idea than a perfectly defined joke. Still, the visual alone of this kid on a pirate ship is enough to get a laugh.

In a recent development, I realize that Peter Pan isn’t just a Disney property, but the 1953 animated film is the most famous version of the character, and I’m guessing that’s the version Larson had in mind in 1982 when he depicted Peter Pan having just flown into a window. To be fair, Peter Pan never struck me as the brightest Disney character, so I buy that he might fly himself into a window.

It has been revealed that larson poked fun at another Peter Pan character a decade later, when he indicated Captain Hook with a career counselor who is helping him decide between a job in piracy or being a massage therapist. While it’s obvious that he becomes a pirate, I do wonder if Hook might have been happier had he gone the other way (although his patients might have suffered).

Yet another Peter Pan character is featured in this one. If I were the frog​​​​​​​ that managed to catch Tinkerbell, I’d forever have bragging rights at the pond. Good for this frog. He earned it.

Recent findings suggest that the Incredible Journey is a 1963 Disney film based on a 1961 novel by Sheila Burnford. It’s about three lost pets — two dogs and a cat — who travel a long distance​​​​​​​ to reunite with their human family. Kids of the 1990s (like me) may be more familiar with the 1993 remake Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey starring Don Ameche​​​​​​​ and Michael J. Fox as the dogs and Sally Field as the cat.

To make fun of this movie, all Larson had to do was team up three ridiculously mismatched animals: a cow, a squid, and a snake.​​​​​​​.

Recent findings suggest that if Goofy were my pilot, I would also be very worried​​​​​​​. Have you seen how bad skiing goes for that guy? It’s not good. I also kind of wonder how he even got a pilot’s license.

Larson was a master at finding the worst possible scenario to put a character into. Pinocchio on safari is a great example of this, as is Dumbo in a mid-air collision.

Tom Hardy And Gary Oldman Had A Batman Reunion In This Forgotten Western Gangster Movie

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when you think of Tom Hardy and Gary Oldman working together, chances are you think of 2012's "The Dark Knight Rises," in which they played Bane and Commissioner James Gordon, respectively.
  • Today, Hardy and Oldman happen to be on two of the best demonstrates on TV.
  • Unfortunately, the pair don't actually share any scenes in the film, but their respective presences help elevate the whole affair, which is well worth a watch for the quietly intense performance from Hardy and the signature flourish of a performance from Oldman.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when you think of Tom Hardy and Gary Oldman working together, chances are you think of 2012's "The Dark Knight Rises," in which they played Bane and Commissioner James Gordon, respectively. But this generation-spanning British duo have crossed paths on screen multiple times throughout the years, including in a movie that debuted the same year as their Batman team-up. Yes, "The Dark Knight Rises" was one of two films in 2012 to give us a Hardy/Oldman collab (as well as a weird Tom Hardy accent). The other was "Lawless," a Southern Gothic gangster outing that's been mostly forgotten, but was a fairly substantial deal at the time.

Today, Hardy and Oldman happen to be on two of the best demonstrates on TV. The former plays the perpetually embattled mob fixer Harry Da Souza on "MobLand," and the latter plays the perpetually disheveled Jackson Lamb on "Slow Horses." But the duo have worked together on four separate projects throughout their careers, beginning with one of the greatest spy movies ever made: 2011's "Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy." Asked by Digital Spy about working with Oldman on the John le Carré adaptation, Hardy had nothing but praise for the man. "Gary Oldman is my hero, that's it," he said. "He's right up there." The actor went on to say he's "stolen everything" from Oldman, with whom he'd re-team a year later on "Lawless.".

Unfortunately, the pair don't actually share any scenes in the film, but their respective presences help elevate the whole affair, which is well worth a watch for the quietly intense performance from Hardy and the signature flourish of a performance from Oldman.

"Lawless" is directed by John Hillcoat, who made his breakthrough by overseeing one of the best dark Westerns ever made: "The Proposition." That 2005 effort was written by Nick Cave, who also penned the script for "Lawless," based on Matt Bondurant's historical novel "The Wettest County in the World." It's a lot less brutal than Hillcoat's 2005 effort, and boasts a typically compelling score from Cave himself.

Recent findings suggest that similarly compelling are the performances. A month prior to the film's release, in August 2012, Tom Hardy had simultaneously terrified and bewildered moviegoers as Bane in "The Dark Knight Rises," famously delivering his best known weird accent through a face covering worn by the ruthless brawler. But he didn't disappoint in the accent department as Virginian bootlegger Forrest Bondurant, either.

"Lawless" follows Forrest and his two brothers, Jason Clarke's Howard Bondurant and Shia LaBeouf's Jack Bondurant, as they run a bootlegging operation in 1931 Virginia. When U.S. Marshal Charley Rakes (Guy Pearce) arrives from Chicago, he decides to be far less lenient with the brothers than local law enforcement, forcing the trio to defend their livelihoods. Throughout it all, Hardy emanates a quiet intensity as Forrest, rolling a toothpick over his tongue and delivering lines that are quite often incomprehensible. But his screen presence is undeniable — which makes it even more of a shame that he has no scenes with Gary Oldman's gangster character, Floyd Banner.

Sources indicate that gary Oldman is only in "Lawless" very briefly, though he does get one of the best scenes, pumping a car full of lead while casually chewing on a cigar. We don't get to see Tom Hardy appear alongside the man from whom he claims to have "stolen everything," but luckily the two "Dark Knight Rises" stars reunited one more time for crime drama "Child 44" in 2015 and shared several scenes (though they ultimately failed to save the movie as a whole).

According to recent reports, "Lawless," meanwhile, debuted at the 2012 Cannes Film Festival ahead of its theatrical release in August of that year. I remember the film being somewhat of a major deal due to Hardy's "Dark Knight Rises" role, and the fact "Lawless" was his first big film post-Bane. When I say "big deal," I mean relative to the movie being a small-town Southern Gothic drama and period piece; it was never going to draw in the crowds the way Christopher Nolan capping off his Batman trilogy did.

It has been revealed that that said, the film did make $54.6 million on a $26 million budget and earned solid reviews. Today, "Lawless" sits at 67% on Rotten Tomatoes, though some critics seemed baffled by Hardy's accent. Still, "Lawless" is arguably one of Tom Hardy's best movies, giving the actor plenty of screen time to showcase his trademark combination of sheer aggression and insouciance (which has been on full display in "MobLand" of late). A scene in which Hardy's bootlegger sits lazily on his porch, barely paying attention while his brother roughs up two police officers, is just a lot of fun to watch. Had Oldman and Hardy had any screen time together, it might have been a true must-see.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that christmas levels up any romance, making it just that much sweeter, more spectacular, more special somehow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that holiday romances are a phenomenon unto themselves. They take a familiar romance trope and set it during Christmas, the most magical time of the year. Romance is heightened at Christmas because the holiday is all about giving and sharing love. Thoughtful gifts under the tree show people they care, mistletoe encourages couples to kiss, and families gathered around the fire are the perfect setting for a proposal.

Industry observers note that christmas levels up any romance, making it just that much sweeter, more spectacular, more special somehow. Watching Christmas romances is a great way for audiences to feel the warmth and sentiment of the season. Netflix has a wide catalog of holiday romances, some better than others. These Christmances are among the best.

Vanessa Hudgens plays two roles in this The Princess and the Pauper-inspired holiday film, where a duchess and a baker decide to switch lives a week before Christmas just to get a break from the spotlight and the humdrum, respectively. This leads them to fall in love with their respective love interests, with each couple being one-half royalty and the other commoner—but both are as whimsical as the other.

Industry observers note that as one of the first Netflix Christmas romances, alongside A Christmas Prince, that truly kicked off the annual tradition and influx of specials, The Princess Switch, is really an honorable mention that we must acknowledge. It has all the precursors of what we recognize as a Netflix Christmance: the over-saturated style, simplistic plots, and guilty pleasure tropes we will always end up blushing at. —Jasneet Singh.

According to recent reports, when hotel heiress Sierra (Lindsay Lohan) has an accident and gets severe head trauma that causes her to lose her memories, single dad Jake (Chord Overstreet) decides to house her in their bed and breakfast until she recovers or someone comes to claim her. As the two sweetly fall in love, we await the moment Sierra regains her memories, especially that of her fiancé.

As Lohan's comeback from her hiatus from acting, Falling for Christmas is a treat for everyone, as we applaud her ability to promptly regain her stride. The plot is easy to follow along with, but Lohan is truly the main star here, sharing holiday cheer and sparking up the warm embers of Christmas love with the charismatic Overstreet that we can cozy up to. It's one of the best Christmas rom-coms on Netflix to date. —Jasneet Singh.

One of Netflix's first forays into Christmas romance, Christmas Inheritance is about as classic and cheesy as a holiday romantic comedy can get, but this inherent cheesiness adds to the film's charm. The film follows a spoiled Fresh York City socialite (Eliza Taylor) who must visit her father's small hometown in order to inherit his manufacturer. However, in the process, and after forging an unlikely connection with a local inn manager (Jake Lacy), she ends up learning a valuable lesson on the importance of hard work and supporting one another.

Sources indicate that the film may be doing the furthest thing from reinventing the wheel as far as Christmas rom-coms are concerned, but for what was one of Netflix's first outings with the genre, the film helped pave the way for many more Christmas movies to come. Taylor and Lacy have some genuine on-screen chemistry, the plot has a basic but effective message of being kind around the holidays, and Andie MacDowell does a great job as the standout supporting character.

Brooke (Hudgens) may not believe in fairy tales, but when handsome knight Sir Cole (Josh Whitehouse) arrives from 700 years ago, she’s surprisingly game to help him break his curse with a Christmas Eve quest.

It has been revealed that these two may be from different centuries, but they bond over watching Netflix Christmas movies and kneading bread so suggestively it leaves viewers blushing. The Knight Before Christmas may be a little schmaltzy, but it’s also cozy, sweet, and perfect for this season’s streaming.

In a recent development, while the wide array of English-language films that Netflix releases often comes to mind when considering their Christmas romance films, the platform has amassed such overwhelming global capital that it has released prominent original Christmas films from filmmakers and regions all around the world. One such standout that frankly deserved to get more recognition in North America is Christmas As Usual, a Norwegian production tackling the clashing cultures of India and Norway amidst a chaotic Christmas engagement party.

The must-see Scandinavian film plays into the classic conventions of other Christmas in-laws films, with the distinct flavor and passion for both of its respective cultures and the beauty that can come from the blending of cultures. Ida Ursin-Holm and Karan Gill make for a charming central couple, with their love and connection being clear from the very beginning of the film, largely having to deal with hurdles that attempt to get in the way of their love.

Industry observers note that dressing like an elf to photograph kids on Santa’s lap isn’t exactly Abby’s (Kat Graham) dream job, but it pays the bills. In The Holiday Calendar, Abby’s best friend Josh (Quincy Brown) is back in town, which helps ease the pain of the recent loss of her grandmother, who left her an antique advent calendar as her Christmas inheritance. The calendar seems to predict the future with small gifts that point Abby toward a new love interest, Ty (Ethan Peck).

The Holiday Calendar is a low-angst love story. Graham is absurdly talented, and her chemistry with Brown feels natural and authentic. Together, they elevate the material. The story features a warm and supportive social circle, including a wonderful turn by Ron Cephas Jones as Gramps. Watching with mulled wine and faux fur-lined slippers is optional but recommended.

The recently cheated-on Layla (Christina Milian) decides to go to the Pentatonix Christmas Eve concert to reunite with a man she had met the previous year. However, in the struggle to get her hands on these sold-out tickets, she recruits Teddy (Devale Ellis). Throughout their seemingly impossible quest, the two gradually fall in love, but it is not without its challenges.

Though the desperate search for tickets to an a cappella group seems wholly nonsensical, the sweet chemistry between Milian and Ellis shines through. They share cozy moments that make any lover of Christmas romances giggle and smile warmly. Meet Me Next Christmas has a strange premise, swoon-worthy co-stars, and a dash of Christmas magic — what more could you ask for? —Jasneet Singh.

A Christmas Romance entirely centered around the joy and whimsy that music can provide during the holiday season, Christmas With You tackles the difficulties of impostor syndrome and fading star power and how the holiday season and genuine love can help put things into perspective. The film sees a pop star (Aimee Garcia) granting a young fan's wish by visiting her Quinceañera, meeting her in person, in the process forming an unexpected bond with her musician father (Freddie Prinze Jr.).

Both Garcia and Prinze Jr. are fan-favorite stars of the past, so having them return and have joyous fun in this film was certainly a treat for fans of these iconic stars. The film itself makes great use of its central music and themes to be all sorts of fun in its execution, although it shares many similarities with another prominent streaming rom-com, Marry Me, only with more approachable Christmas energy over the whole thing.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

According to recent reports, you do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

Industry observers note that you have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

It has been revealed that meeting the in-laws is already stressful enough, but in Our Little Secret, Lohan's Avery finds out her boyfriend's sister is dating her ex-boyfriend, Logan (Ian Harding), and vice versa. Instead of divulging this straight away, the two skirt around the truth, leading to hilarious situations and covert alliances. But it turns out the spark between them has yet to be extinguished; they just need to confront the baggage from their shared history first.

According to recent reports, lohan and Harding fall into easy banter, making their mishaps and conflicts all the more engaging amid the tension of the familial relationships. The film taps into the awkwardness of visiting those relatives during the holiday season, but ultimately, the comedy winds down to a wholesome sentiment of family and love. —Jasneet Singh.

According to recent reports, like so many people around the holidays, Peter (Michael Urie) in Single All the Way dreads going home for the holidays to be bombarded with questions about his single status. In the grand tradition of romance tropes, Peter convinces best friend Nick (Philemon Chambers) to go home with him, posing as his boyfriend. Little does he know that his mother has a blind date waiting for him, who just happens to be her hunky fitness trainer James (Luke Macfarlane).

Recent findings suggest that urie ably leads a charming extended cast, including icons Kathy Najimy and Jennifer Coolidge. The script is better than average for a romance, with actual, genuine laughs built in and thanks to a mother who dubs herself ‘Christmas Carol,’ the holiday cheer and setting are top-notch. A movie with three heartthrobs is just the gift that audiences deserve, and a gay Christmas romance is even more rare and welcome.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Effective immediately, Nvidia’s Board of Directors just voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as President, CEO and board director — just 11 days after he resigned amid an explosive espionage and extramarital affair scandal, and a mere six days after the firm insisted it had no intention of bringing him back.
  • In a recent development, if you blinked over the last two weeks, you might have missed the entire post-Jensen Huang era of Nvidia.
  • So what changed between last Tuesday’s firm “no” and this morning’s unanimous “welcome back”?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Effective immediately, Nvidia’s Board of Directors just voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as President, CEO and board director — just 11 days after he resigned amid an explosive espionage and extramarital affair scandal, and a mere six days after the firm insisted it had no intention of bringing him back.

In a recent development, if you blinked over the last two weeks, you might have missed the entire post-Jensen Huang era of Nvidia. It is the kind of corporate whiplash that makes Sam Altman’s infamous five-day OpenAI ousting look like PTO. To make sense of how the world’s most consequential chipmaker pulled off a full-speed reverse, you have to look at the sheer chaos of the last 25 days.

So what changed between last Tuesday’s firm “no” and this morning’s unanimous “welcome back”?

Industry observers note that according to Nvidia’s official announcement, two things broke the deadlock: a series of sitdowns where the board became “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead,” and — crucially — a green light from Washington.

The board explicitly noted that it “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

Combine that quiet federal clearance with an internal employee revolt, vocal backing from the White House and a brutal month on the stock ticker, and the board’s math became pretty simple.

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Jones mentioned in Monday’s statement, thanking Colette Kress for holding the fort as interim CEO before returning to her full-time CFO duties.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Huang, for his part, struck a notably humbler tone than the usual keynote bravado I’ve seen in person a few times.

In a recent development, "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment... Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can't wait to get back to work." — Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO.

Industry observers note that before you get too excited with “WE ARE SO BACK” responses and “stonks” GIFs, read the fine print at the bottom of Nvidia’s press release. Huang may have his title back, but he’s walking back into a very different corporate structure — and the legal storm hasn’t magically evaporated:.

If you were hoping that two weeks of boardroom chaos at Nvidia would pop the AI bubble and magically bring back $90 DDR5 kits (like me), I have some bad news: Jensen Huang’s comeback just put the AI infrastructure train right back at full throttle.

With Wall Street cheering his return and Washington clearing the runway, hyperscalers aren’t tapping the brakes on data center spending anytime soon.

That means Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron have zero reason to pull wafers off high-margin data center memory and send them back to everyday PC builders — especially with Trendforce expecting DRAM prices to climb another 10-15% this quarter and stay tight well into 2027.

Does that mean the dream of RAMageddon dying is gone? Not quite — it just changes your game initiative.

If you see a legitimate Black Friday deal that actually undercuts pre-crisis pricing, treat it like an escape hatch. Waiting for “cheaper RAM next spring” is a gamble that’s looking worse by the hour.

There is one genuine silver lining. While DRAM stays squeezed, Trendforce’s latest forecast shows NAND flash prices finally turning the corner and starting to dip as early as Q1 2027 — so unless you spot a genuinely fair Black Friday deal, don’t let retailers gouge you on storage right now.

Nvidia’s rebound might keep AI demand humming, but it doesn’t bail the memory giants out of their California antitrust lawsuit or stop the mainstream backlash over inflated PC prices.

Jensen getting his desk back is great news for Nvidia shareholders. For the rest of us just trying to buy a computer without paying an absurd memory tax, the message is simple: grab the real Black Friday bargains while they exist, ignore the fake red discount stickers, and buckle in — RAMageddon isn’t packing its bags just yet.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on paper, The Hunger Games and The Walking Dead are two distinct franchises.
  • It has been revealed that loosely based on the French graphic novel Le Transperceneige and Bong Joon Ho's movie of the same name, Snowpiercer has a distinct post-apocalyptic setup.
  • Finding shelter in a constantly moving train does not sound too bad when the planet outside is frozen beyond repair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on paper, The Hunger Games and The Walking Dead are two distinct franchises. But picture a dystopian world where the apocalypse is not ruled by zombies but by monstrous humans themselves. Even the games they play among themselves to increase their class divides are more political and terrifying. There lies the premise of a compelling 40-episode sci-fi thriller.

It has been revealed that loosely based on the French graphic novel Le Transperceneige and Bong Joon Ho's movie of the same name, Snowpiercer has a distinct post-apocalyptic setup. Some indicates, like The Walking Dead, are open world survival thrillers. Others, like Silo, unfold in underground bunkers. Snowpiercer primarily takes place in a titular train that endlessly circles Earth.

Finding shelter in a constantly moving train does not sound too bad when the planet outside is frozen beyond repair. In Snowpiercer's world, however, the man-made divides and horrors inside the train are far more disturbing than the thought of freezing to death. Owing to this, it seems fair to compare Snowpiercer with both The Hunger Games and The Walking Dead.

Sources indicate that panem, in The Hunger Games, weaponizes spectacle and controlled scarcity to exploit the lower classes. They quietly aggravate the existing divides between oppressed districts while ensuring the Capitol remains safe and sound. A similar system can be noticed in Snowpiercer. Just like Panem's districts in The Hunger Games are numbered based on economics, humanity is divided through a train's cars in Snowpiercer.

According to recent reports, while the elite accommodate the front cars of the trains and enjoy every luxury, the ones at the back rot in inhumane conditions. Much like President Snow in The Hunger Games, the train's creator, Wilford, also has a cult-like following where he is almost treated like an overarching deity. Similar to Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss Everdeen, Snowpiercer also finds its reluctant rebel in Andre Layton.

He emerges from the depths of the lower classes but, like Katniss, realizes that overthrowing a tyrant is far easier than leading a deeply divided population without becoming a tyrant yourself.

Similar to the characters in The Walking Dead, the ones in Snowpiecer, too, gradually experience moral erosion in their post-apocalyptic world. Alliances keep shifting, and, instead of uniting against one common evil, the people get lost in their own petty conflicts and selfish desire to survive. Despite these overlaps, though, Snowpiercer finds its distinct voice through its detective noir drama.

In a recent development, overall, Bong Joon Ho's Snowpiercer is an absolute masterpiece. The show does not even come close to being as gripping and intense as the award-winning film. However, the series still makes good use of its long runtime to expand the world-building from the movie. While the movie rapidly moves from one car to another, the show carefully reveals how everything from water supply to food production works.

Industry observers note that instead of jumping from one action set piece to another, the show paces itself and introduces gripping mysteries to keep viewers hooked. The movie is star-studded, with Chris Evans, Tilda Swinton, Ed Harris, Song Kang-ho, Jamie Bell, and Octavia Spencer serving as its leads. Even the show, however, boasts memorable performances from Jennifer Connelly, Daveed Diggs, Rowan Blanchard, and Sean Bean.

Industry observers note that all in all, the Snowpiercer show never comes off as a forced extension of the original movie. It also does not try too hard to draw any connections to the film, which helps it etch its own solid identity like The Hunger Games and The Walking Dead.

Snowpiercer is set aboard a perpetually moving train that carries the last survivors of humanity after Earth is frozen into an uninhabitable wasteland. As passengers remain divided by a rigid class system, former detective Andre Layton is drawn into a murder investigation that exposes growing unrest and ignites a struggle over who should control the future of the train.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Actor Brent Spiner is most famous for playing Data, the emotionless android who wants to learn humanity, on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." If an actor is part of a "Star Trek" main cast, they're essentially geek royalty for life. Spiner has parlayed that into, among other things, occasional guest roles on a handful of superhero cartoons. Spiner played the Joker in two episodes of the "Young Justice" cartoon series and that's not even the only Batman villain on his voiceover resume.

According to recent reports, spiner appeared as the Riddler/Edward Nigma in an episode of "Justice League Action," except in the episode, the Riddler had reformed. "Justice League Action," which aired 52 episodes from 2016 to 2018, was essentially a more kid-friendly "Justice League Unlimited." Episodes were 11 minutes long, and would feature three or four DC heroes from a larger rotating cast starring in adventures.

"Justice League Action" is not part of the DC Animated Universe that began with "Batman: The Animated Series" and concluded with "Justice League Unlimited," but its style is adjacent due to creative team overlap: Alan Burnett was one of the producers on "Justice League Action" and Paul Dini wrote several episodes. It also reused some DCAU voice actors, like the late Kevin Conroy as Batman and Mark Hamill as the Joker.

Industry observers note that in the show's Riddler episode, the Joker has kidnapped Batman and left clues to his location all over Gotham. Wonder Woman (Rachel Kimsey) and Green Arrow (Chris Diamantopoulos) are hopeless at solving riddles, so the Riddler offers his services. Declared sane and recently freed from Arkham Asylum, the Riddler has reinvented himself from a super-villain to a private detective, using his riddle-solving skills to fight crime instead of to cause it. The episode is, accordingly, titled "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective.".

Sources indicate that there are two dominant interpretations of the Riddler; a cool, collected trickster who condescends to everyone less intelligent than him, or a short-fused, hyperactive showman. You can divide different Riddler actors across those lines fairly neatly: John Glover in "Batman: The Animated Series" is the former, Frank Gorshin in the 1960s "Batman" show and Jim Carrey in "Batman Forever" are the latter.

In fact, many Bat-historians would argue the violently murderous modern Joker owes more to Gorshin's Riddler, who flies off the handle and often loses control of himself to sadistic laughter. How amusing, then, that in "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective," the Riddler joins the case to save Batman because he's angry at the Joker for stealing his act of leaving clues at crime scenes.

Spiner's Riddler is cool and smug — definitely closer to Glover than Gorshin. His costume, a green suit and bowler hat with a question mark cane, is the one that Glover's Riddler wore in "Batman: The Animated Series" as well. It's the classic "refined" Riddler look, being more respectable than his original jumpsuit costume, and one that fits a Nigma who is trying to rebrand himself a respected professional. But the Riddler's design otherwise still has classical villainous features: triangular eyes with significant black eyebrows, pointed nose and chin, etc.

Even as Nigma helps Wonder Woman and Green Arrow, he talks down to them. He may be working on the side of good, but he's still only solving mysteries to prove how smart he is.

Overall, "Justice League Action" is a pretty light and comedy-heavy series. The riddles that Nigma decodes in the episode are logic leaps in line with the '60s "Batman" TV show. There's also the episode's last twist that the Joker actually orchestrated this scheme to get revenge on the Riddler, not on Batman. Why? Because the Riddler once stole his donut in the Arkham Asylum cafeteria.

In the climax of "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective," the Joker traps Riddler. He asks him a riddle ("What has four eyes but doesn't see?") and, if the Riddler answers it, that will activate the death trap that holds Batman hostage. The Riddler tries to stop himself but he compulsively answers the riddle ("Mississippi"), leaving Wonder Woman to save Batman.

Recent findings suggest that the Riddler rarely appeared on "Batman: The Animated Series" because his riddle gimmick made plots too complicated for a half-hour, action-driven cartoon. But that show still planted the seed for "E. Nigma, Consulting Detective." In his third and last appearance as the main villain, "Riddler's Reform," Nigma tries and fails to go straight. When Paul Dini wrote "Detective Comics" in the 2000s, he revisited that idea by making the Riddler a private detective who reluctantly partners with Batman.

"E. Nigma, Consulting Detective" in "Justice League Action" takes its title from Dini's "Detective Comics" #822, even though Dini didn't write the episode (Jonathan Callan did). The Riddler endangering Batman with his compulsion is the same conclusion the status quo-bound comics eventually reached: Edward Nigma is too selfish to ever fully reform.
