Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series (★★☆☆☆).

One to avoid this time around — it makes coffee, but there's not much to say about it. It costs far too much money for the quality of espresso that it spits out, even if the device itself does look pretty special.

Read the full Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series review.

We review a lot of espresso machines at Tom's Guide. Very few of them make it into our buying guides, but you can see a comprehensive list of other models we've tested at the bottom of this guide.

When it comes to testing espresso machines, there's a lot of room for human error. In order to minimize this, I work closely with a team of true coffee experts, from former baristas to serious home baristas. Every review you'll read on Tom's Guide will be from a true espresso enthusiast who can tell their flat whites from their cappuccinos and their arabica from their robusta.

Industry observers note that we consider a huge range of factors when evaluating espresso machines. Here's a non-exhaustive list of the things we test for:.

Ease of use: You shouldn't have to be a pro to work an espresso machine. These appliances are designed to make life easier, so while it's fair to expect a learning curve if you opt for a manual machine with lots of hands-on features, we mark machines down for any quirks or fiddly features that will make day-to-day use harder for the average buyer.

Recent findings suggest that ease of cleaning: Some machines are splashy, messy, and get greasy from the touch of a button. These are workhorses, sure, but they're also meant to look nice, so we evaluate whether they spill grounds, splatter milk, or will require any major upkeep with each review.

Value for money: Even a budget espresso machine can be expensive, so we always consider whether a machine is priced competitively when putting it to the test. If we wouldn't recommend our friends spend their money on a machine, we wouldn't recommend it to you, either.

Grinding: If a machine has an in-built grinder, we put it through the same testing that we use when evaluating the best coffee grinders. After all, the quality of your grinder plays a massive part in achieving a good extraction. It's the single most important part of any espresso-brewing process. We evaluate the range of grind sizes on offer with every machine (you'll want a very fine consistency, but this will vary depending on the bean you use), as well as how much coffee a machine grinds automatically. A lot of enthusiasts brew using ratios, so we like to weigh the grounds before we brew for good measure.

Brewing: Albeit an crucial step, this is also the simplest to test. Whether a machine can brew well is dependent on the performance of the grinder, but we know we've got a quality coffee if it brews at that sweet spot between 190 to 200°F (88 and 93°C) and we get between 25-30ml of espresso. We use a coffee scale to test this, just to be extra thorough.

Recent findings suggest that taste test: Metrics aside, it's all in the taste-test. We buy high-quality coffee (presently, we're using a subscription to Hard Lines' specialty coffee) that's freshly-roasted to give our machines the best possible chance of brewing a brilliant espresso. And if it tastes too bitter or too tart, we know it's not the beans' fault! If the coffee tastes too grassy, it suggests the machine doesn't brew hot enough, and if it's burnt-tasting, that's a sign that it's not got good temperature regulation and is scorching our grounds.

Milk steaming: Steam wands need to be powerful, ergonomic and responsive. A great wand will not only heat your milk but also help to create a powerful vortex, which will add texture and incorporate air into your milk jug. I'll get more into how to use a steam wand below, but you best believe that if former barista Erin can't get a good texture from a steam wand, there's no hope for a home user.

Super-automatic espresso machines will often feature milk dispensers that automatically froth your milk and pour it into your mug. This is really convenient if you don't like the idea of learning to steam milk by hand, but just so we're clear, these machines don't steam your milk. They simply heat it and inject some bubbles as they pour into your cup. It gets the job done, but it's not going to compete with a coffee shop-quality flat white.

Longevity: You need to be prepared to look after an espresso machine. They block easily if you don't descale regularly, and your group head and steam wand will need to be flushed out periodically. This aside, we've also tried machines that simply don't feel like they're built to last. Where possible, we like to hang onto a top pick for prolonged home use and testing. That way, we can enhancement our guide if it doesn't seem built to last. Our number one, the De'Longhi La Specialista Opera, is right now living with Erin as her home machine, allowing us to continue to evaluate its position in this guide.

It has been revealed that this question used to be a lot more simple to answer: there's manual, and there's super-automatic! However, things have changed a lot in the last few years, and now there's an increasing number of machines that sit somewhere in between.

In truth, it would be easier to characterize types of espresso machine as a spectrum, all the way from lever pump machines like La Pavoni to one-touch super-automatics like Jura.

But to make life easier, I've divided the domestic machines in this guide into three categories:.

Espresso machines are pretty complicated, which is why I did a dedicated Specialty Coffee Association course before compiling this guide. While I’ve tried to make it as accessible as possible, there is some terminology you might need to learn to understand the reviews below. Here are the ABC's of espresso machines.

If you’re completely new to espresso machines, the thing you have to ask yourself is: “how much time do I want to spend, how much skill do I have, and how much am I prepared to put into this?".

I posed this question to Lucy Dunstan, Product Manager at SMEG and La Pavoni. “It’s quite simple really, it’s all about extracting the flavor from your coffee,” she told me.

Sources indicate that “There’s a scientific process for making an espresso. It has to be between 88 and 93°C [190 to 200°F], you have to put about 9 bars of pressure on it, and you want to extract between 25 and 30ml of liquid. So what all these machines do is offer a way of controlling that process.”.

Industry observers note that there are so many variables that stand between your machine and a perfect espresso. This includes the beans you use, how you grind them, the volume of grounds in your portafilter, the pressure you use when tamping, the temperature stability of your machine, the water pressure exerted, the volume of water pushed into your puck… that’s a non-exhaustive list, and it’s before we even get into milk steaming!

There are so many variables that stand between your machine and a perfect espresso.

Here’s what I wish I’d known when I bought my first espresso machine: The more automated features you opt for, the fewer variables you’ll need to worry about. “Sometimes with espresso machines, an entry-level price will actually require more skill,” states Dunstan.

“If you’re completely new to espresso machines, the thing you have to ask yourself is: how much time do I want to spend, how much skill do I have, and how much am I prepared to put into this? So you’re either someone who doesn’t have a lot of time to spend on making your coffee, or you want to delve into that world where you’re getting hands-on.".

There's an unfortunate irony with espresso machines. You can get good espresso with a cheaper machine, but to do so, you'll need to learn the ins and outs of how these machines work. For the entry-level buyer without much knowledge, you'll often have to spend a lot more on a super-capable machine that will take all the hard work out of the equation.

According to recent reports, it doesn't make much sense, right? Coffee enthusiasts can get away with spending $200 on a basic espresso machine because they've got the skill to use it properly, but if you're just dipping your toes in the water? Well, prepare to spend at least $500. It's no wonder why so many people opt for a pod machine like a Keurig or a Nespresso!

Fortunately, the market is catching up. An increasing amount of espresso machines feature assisted settings that will remove some of the variables that can mess up your espresso. This includes automated grinding that controls the volume of coffee dispensed into your portafilter, automated tamping for an even pressure, and even hands-free steam wands that will texture your milk for you.

Sources indicate that the majority of the machines I've included in this machine fit into this automatic category in some sense. I think they're the best option for most people, allowing you to learn as you use the machine and get hands-on if you wish, but also taking the reins when you just want a low-effort espresso.

In a recent development, you'll see in the products included I've mentioned how many bars of pressure they each have, but what does this mean, and does it even matter? Well, the short answer is no. You won't necessarily see a better extraction from a machine with 20 bars over a machine with 15. This is because the ideal pressure needed for espresso is 9 bars.

I asked Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, to explain the significance of pressure for espresso machines. "You want to hit 9 bars for optimal extraction," he told me.

"If the pressure is too low, you'll bring out grassy flavors. The pressure won't bring out the sugars from your beans.

"Too high, and your coffee will have a bitter, burnt taste.".

If all you need to make a great espresso is 9 bars of pressure, so I asked Lane why so many espresso machines have more?

Recent findings suggest that "Think of it like a car," Lane told me. "You don't want to drive it at top speed all the time, but driving in a comfortable range of what your car is capable of will mean it's not constantly being run flat-out.".

He explained that despite the maximum pressure of any machine, they'll use OPVs (which stands for over pressure valves) to keep espresso extraction running at a consistent 9 bars of pressure.

So, while higher pressure doesn't necessarily mean a machine is any better, you might not want to buy a machine with a maximum output of 9 bars, or it could lead to a shorter lifespan for your machine.

Most espresso machines will come with four baskets: two single and two double, with a mix of double-walled and single-walled constructions. I'll explain the difference between single-walled and double-walled below, but what's the significance of your basket size and capacity?

Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, explained it to me: "There are two main basket widths: 54mm, which features on Sage / Breville's Barista range, and 58mm, which features on our Jet range.".

"58mm is considered to be commercial-grade. The larger and shallower basket will give you marginally better results because you're more easily able to permeate all of the grounds inside your basket.".

It has been revealed that after testing countless espresso machines, I don't think my palette is quite so attuned that I could turn my nose up at an espresso from a 54mm basket. But it's useful to know if you want to replace or upgrade any parts of your machine what size portafilter baskets the group head will fit.

Single-walled and double-walled baskets, also known respectively as unpressurized and pressurized, are included with your espresso machine to give you options. As a general rule of thumb, you'll get better results from a pressurized basket if you're using pre-ground coffee. It will help you overcome some of the shortcomings of a grind size that's too coarse, or coffee that's less fresh. But if you want to taste the authentic flavor of your fresh-ground beans, a single-walled basket is the way to go.

In our reviews, we always use fresh-ground coffee, so we stick to single-walled baskets for the majority of our testing.

When I asked him to explain how pressurized baskets work, Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, said "Think of a group of people running down a hall and having to go through a door." He explained, "That's what the double-walled basket does. It creates pressure by restricting the flow of your coffee, forcing it to build up more flavor and crema than you'd have been able to achieve with a less fresh coffee.".

We've done a thorough explainer on this in our guide to pressurized coffee baskets — how do they work and when should you use them? The short answer? They can act as a cheat code to a better espresso if you're not working with the ideal gear, but a machine with an in-built grinder shouldn't need one.

Sources indicate that the vast majority of domestic espresso machines use thermoblock technology to heat water on demand. But how does it work, and what are the pros and cons?

Sources indicate that there are very few single boiler machines on the market, but the Rancilio Silvia is one of them. Boiler machines will heat your water and keep it at temperature for as and when you decide to use it. A single-boiler uses one boiler for both the group head and the steam wand, which require different temperatures and therefore will need to you purge excess hot water as you use different elements of the machine.

In a recent development, dual boilers have one boiler for the group head, and another for your steam wand. They're not super popular for domestic, and I've not included a dual-boiler in this guide. They have a higher energy consumption because they keep your water hot for more precision and stability.

What about thermoblock? I asked Lucy Dunstan, Product Manager at SMEG and La Pavoni, to explain. “A thermoblock is a heated metal block with one or more pipes running through it that will rapidly heat water on demand," she explained.

"They’re usually very compact so they don’t take up much space, meaning they can be fitted in smaller machines, and they’re more energy efficient [than a dual boiler].”.

“So the advantage is that they’re fast, small, and energy-efficient. The disadvantage is that they offer less temperature consistency than a dual boiler machine.

"And they can, over time, be susceptible to limescale, so they may not last as long. Whereas if you buy a dual boiler La Pavoni machine, and you look after it, I’d expect it to last you a lifetime.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you probably know who Margot Robbie is, right? She's a pretty big star. From "Barbie" to "Babylon," Robbie is one of the most popular and profitable stars working today, and you probably know her from her big break in 2013 when she starred alongside Leonardo DiCaprio in Martin Scorsese's delightfully nasty "The Wolf of Wall Street." You should also know, though, that Robbie appeared in a gorgeous, sweet, and absolutely lovely romantic comedy in 2013 — and it's called "About Time.".

Industry observers note that written and directed by Richard Curtis, "About Time" employs a genuinely bonkers premise. After a New Year's Eve where he completely screws up his chance to kiss a girl at midnight, Tim Lake (Domhnall Gleeson) learns from his father James (the always-perfect Bill Nighy) that Lake men can travel through time within their own experiences and memories. Across one summer, Tim attempts to use this bizarre and largely unexplained power to woo Charlotte, a friend of his sister Katherine (Lydia Wilson), who spends a summer at the Lake house in Cornwall and is played by (you guessed it!) Robbie. During one do-over, Charlotte tells Tim that if he'd asked her out before the last day of the vacation, things might have gone differently; when he does his trick and rewinds to the beginning of said summer, she indicates they should wait and see how things go.

Sources indicate that years later, while Tim is living in London and dating a publishing executive named Mary (Rachel McAdams), he crosses paths with Charlotte and they share a dinner ... but when she invites him to go back to her place, he goes home to Mary instead and proposes to her. Robbie's role is small but pivotal, and it's a stark contrast to her breakout performance.

Margot Robbie rather infamously slapped her future co-star and on-screen husband Leonardo DiCaprio during her audition for "The Wolf of Wall Street," but clearly, Martin Scorsese and his long-time collaborator liked her cojones ... because she got the job. In this film, which also released in 2013, Robbie indicated off a completely different side of herself as Naomi Lapaglia, a lingerie designer who woos DiCaprio's Wall Street crook Jordan Belfort away from his first wife and who's known as the "Duchess of Bay Ridge.".

Sources indicate that the role of Naomi requires a lot from Robbie. Not only does she have to speak in a perfect Brooklyn accent — Robbie is Australian — she has to absolutely dominate an actor as powerful as DiCaprio, toe the line between being absurdly hot and being legitimately terrifying, and she has to essentially live a whole lifetime on-screen as she has children with DiCaprio's Jordan and watches him succumb to his excesses. Robbie manages to pull all of that off; think of the scene where her Naomi torments Jordan in their children's playroom, where she splashes water on his face during an argument, or when she tearfully runs towards her young child strapped into Jordan's expensive car.

Robbie didn't earn an Oscar nomination for her work in "The Wolf of Wall Street" — those nominations would start rolling in a bit later — but for my money, she should have. Thankfully, after showing off her insane duality in "About Time" and "The Wolf of Wall Street," the best was yet to come. It's genuinely incredible that she was able to deliver both of these performances in the same year, but in retrospect, I guess it's not that surprising.

Like I said earlier, Margot Robbie is one of the most well-regarded and famous performers of her generation, and "The Wolf of Wall Street" was just the beginning for her. After "Focus" in 2015 with Will Smith and her first turn as Harley Quinn in the 2016 version of "Suicide Squad" — a role she'd reprise in "Birds of Prey" and James Gunn's 2021 reinvention "The Suicide Squad" — Robbie scored her first Oscar nomination for "I, Tonya," Craig Gillespie's bombastic account of Tonya Harding's scandalous rise and fall as a figure skater.

In 2018, she lent her skills to the deliberately anachronistic "Mary Queen of Scots," which cast her as Elizabeth I facing off against her royal rival Mary (Saoirse Ronan), and in 2019, she earned her second Oscar nod for playing a fictional Fox News reporter in "Bombshell" and also portrayed a non-doomed Sharon Tate in Quentin Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.".

"Barbie," though, is arguably Robbie's most enormous outing to date. This 2023 release that led to an actual cultural event alongside Oppenheimer also grossed over a billion dollars in a matter of days and scored a nomination for best picture, earning Robbie a nod as a producer. Speaking of that, Robbie has produced movies like "Promising Young Woman" and TV shows like "Sterling Point," paving the way for more female writers, directors, and actors through LuckyChap Productions. None of this would be possible without "The Wolf of Wall Street," but also, I think "About Time" helped launch Robbie into the stratosphere too. You can stream "About Time" on Netflix.

Industry observers note that not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a massive "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be said for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Recent findings suggest that because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before upcoming models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Recent findings suggest that price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The problem isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

In a recent development, the key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a latest tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

Recent findings suggest that to avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. Head to Amazon.com in your web browser.

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

Under Shop by Category, select Prime.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

As mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

According to recent reports, finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that fresh off making the best "Spider-Man" movie in about a decade with "Brand New Day," director Destin Daniel Cretton is plunging into the Land of Fire and ninjas, adapting Masashi Kishimoto's manga/worldwide phenomenon "Naruto" into a live-action film, two years after it was first confirmed. Translating a battle shonen manga/anime into live-action carries negative associations of past, failed attempts. Why bother moving a story designed to stretch reality's limits to a medium that's inherently more confining than a hand-drawn one? Will "Naruto" break this curse? It has a huge stage to do so, and the early steps look promising.

Deadline has reported that actor Hiroyuki Sanada ("Shogun," "John Wick: Chapter 4") is in negotiations to star in "Naruto" as Hiruzen Sarutobi, the Third Hokage and leader of Naruto's ninja village, Konohagakure. Sanada is the second major actor rumored to be joining "Naruto," after reports in August that Charles Melton had been approached to play Kakashi Hatake, Naruto's masked sensei.

This alone suggests "Naruto" is serious about getting impressive talent: one of the coolest actors alive in Sanada, and a major young actor in Melton, who's won acclaim for his performances in "May December" and "Beef" Season 2. Not for nothing, Sanada and Melton are Japanese and Korean American, respectively — no whitewashing here, so far, contrary to "Naruto" fans' long-standing jokes about Tom Holland or Timothée Chalamet starring as Naruto.

Recent findings suggest that "Naruto" has rolled out a "global" search/audition process for the movie's three young leads: Naruto and his teammates Sasuke Uchiha and Sakura Haruno. That suggests the film's creators are looking for young actors — possibly, even plausibly, unknowns — who can embody those characters first without prioritizing pre-existing star power.

According to recent reports, casting Hiroyuki Sanada as the Third Hokage suggests the "Naruto" team is already looking to the horizon and seeing sequels. Hiruzen is only a background part of the first "Naruto" arc, "The Land of Waves" (which is the ideal starting place for a movie series). But he takes center stage in the second and third arcs, where one of his former students, the snake-like Orochimaru, serves as the main villain. Hiruzen gets a major action sequence confronting Orochimaru, and casting Sanada — a martial artist who holds a black belt in karate, just as Charles Melton has one in taekwondo — seems like casting with that scene in mind.

Recent findings suggest that if the goal is adapting the "Naruto" manga as a whole, then forward thinking will be key. The manga runs 700 chapters, divided into several story arcs; you'd likely need somewhere between seven and 10 movies to complete it. The live-action "Naruto" is being produced by studio Lionsgate in partnership with Sony. Lionsgate recently proved once more that "The Hunger Games" is a reliable hit for them with the success of "Sunrise on the Reaping." But it's never smart to put all your eggs in one basket. "Naruto" hits overlapping demographic appeal and even some similar story beats as "The Hunger Games" (like children becoming killers and the tragic horrors of war).

Recent findings suggest that moreover, comic books have become the prime IP of Hollywood these past two decades, and yet manga outsells American comics many times over. Manga/anime is in the cultural mainstream for anyone younger than a young millennial, and the first studio to crack that could be sitting on a cultural gold mine. So, yeah, Lionsgate has a strong incentive to get "Naruto" right, and the talent it's recruiting suggests they understand that.

Industry observers note that even if Destin Daniel Cretton doesn't stick around for any of those potential "Naruto" sequels (I have to imagine Sony and Marvel Studios want him back for more "Spider-Man" movies), getting him as director for the first is another sign that Lionsgate is taking this seriously. Look at what he's directed, and consider how he's intent on casting actors with genuine martial arts bona fides for "Naruto," and it's clear why he's the man for the job.

An essential part of "Naruto" is its fight choreography, which is more choreographed around hand-to-hand martial arts than most other battle shonen. Yes, the ninjas in "Naruto" use "jutsus," or magical/superpowered attacks powered by spiritual energy, or chakra. But the core of the series' fight scenes is mano-a-mano fights that lay on the brutality and raw emotion; that's especially true in Naruto and Sasuke's various duels.

The combat in "Naruto" likewise employs parkour acrobatics in the vein of wuxia. (In-universe, ninja learn to channel their chakra to balance on, climb, and run through trees.) Cretton directing "Shang-Chi," a wuxia-flavored Marvel movie, and Spider-Man, who webslings through New York City like how Naruto and his ilk dash through forests, gives him the perfect experience to deliver the heightened-but-not-completely intensity of the action from the early "Naruto" arcs.

In a recent development, cretton also has the perfect sensei to consult with in Masashi Kishimoto, who has endorsed Cretton as the perfect director for the project, the same way that "One Piece" creator Eiichiro Oda personally approved elements of Netflix's "One Piece" series. "One Piece" proved live-action shonen manga/anime can work in the TV format, and "Naruto" might be the project that proves it can be a blockbuster movie.

"Naruto" is at the moment in development.

Comedy Central had barely finished congratulating South Park on its sixth Emmy when Trey Parker and Matt Stone gave the network a different name to put on the press release. Season 29 would go by South America, a decision the creators credited to “the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google.” They even thanked their bosses at “Paramount -- a Skydance Capitulation.” To Paramount’s credit, when the ratings came in, the company went right ahead and issued a press release celebrating the success of South America.

Within the space of a single episode, Stan, Kyle, and Kenny were trying to negotiate peace between rival biker gangs, and Randy was recruiting dads to join his cycling club. Keeping up with the rest of the season took a little more patience, because the boys got into trouble every other Wednesday this fall.

The South Park Season 29 finale airs Wednesday, November 25, at 10 p.m. ET/PT on Comedy Central and streams on Paramount+ on Thanksgiving Day, November 26, in the U.S. It’s the sixth episode of a season that began on September 16. If you’ve been waiting to watch the whole thing in one sitting, the first five episodes are already on Paramount+, and Thursday is the first day you can go straight from the e-bike turf war to the finale.

Industry observers note that four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

Industry observers note that you belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

Industry observers note that you belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

In a recent development, parker and Stone still have plenty of South Park ahead of them. That agreement also kept Comedy Central as the series’ broadcast home. The next milestone for the network is August 13, 2027, when it will have been 30 years since Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny made their Comedy Central debut.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Nintendo Switch 2 has really picked up the baton of playing older games from their history and run with it, and players can now play all sorts of titles from several major console generations.
  • It has been revealed that at last count, there are over 150 titles on the service, including efforts as early as Super Mario Bros.
  • As first reported by GoNintendo, Wave Race Blue Storm has just been added to the Switch Online Expansion Pack, while the Nintendo Classics: GameCube app has also seen a change that is bound to please fans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nintendo Switch 2 has really picked up the baton of playing older games from their history and run with it, and players can now play all sorts of titles from several major console generations. To access most of them, players need to be signed up to Nintendo Switch Online, as well as grabbing the Expansion Pack that grants access to historical titles.

It has been revealed that at last count, there are over 150 titles on the service, including efforts as early as Super Mario Bros. 3 on the NES, all the way up to games like Super Mario Sunshine and The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker for the GameCube. Now, the latter platform has just received yet another title, as well as some interesting quality-of-life updates that should make the experience a lot nicer to play.

As first reported by GoNintendo, Wave Race Blue Storm has just been added to the Switch Online Expansion Pack, while the Nintendo Classics: GameCube app has also seen a change that is bound to please fans.

If you didn't play it at the time, Wave Race Blue Storm is a jetski racing video game developed and published by Nintendo that came out all the way back in 2001. Though it's a bit of a departure from their usual fare, it really is a lot of fun, and has plenty of arcade-style elements that should keep you coming back for more.

In announcing the move over on Twitter/X, Nintendo of America shared the following post:.

"Bust out your wildest tricks in races against seven other riders and become the ultimate Wave Rave champion in Wave Race Blue Storm, available now on Nintendo Switch 2 with Nintendo GameCube - Nintendo Classics for #NintendoSwitchOnline + Expansion Pack members.".

It has been revealed that fan response to the move was also generally positive, even if they were suggesting other games they wanted, with one saying, "Great! I could never play this one on GameCube but I love of the original Wave Race for the N64. Thanks!".

Recent findings suggest that while another added, "Hahahah, finally I was waiting for Wave Race: Blue Storm to come to NSO. I’m hyped as hell!! Thank you, Nintendo.".

At the same time, the tech giant also confirmed that it will now be possible to turn off the pesky borders that players have disliked so much on classic titles, though only on GameCube releases for the time being. They haven't stated as much yet, but it would be surprising if Nintendo are just planning to stop with that initiative there, so don't be surprised to see it crop up for other consoles in the future.

Industry observers note that to do it for yourself, head to the GameCube app and then click Settings. Right at the bottom you should be able to find a Border Graphic toggle option, and de-selecting it will get rid of the border from your gameplay.

There's no word just yet on whether Nintendo is planning to add any other games to the Classics catalog before the year is out, but we can certainly expect plenty more next year, as they continue to expand the offering across multiple generations of hardware.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In “Gaslit,” a upcoming documentary about climate change activists, Jane Fonda stands outside one of Formosa Petrochemical’s Texas facilities and looks through a thermal camera.
  • According to recent reports, “Methane is 80 percent more destructive to the climate, in terms of global warming, than carbon dioxide,” Fonda explained during a recent Zoom interview.
  • In a recent development, for years, Fonda has been sounding the alarm about the looming environmental catastrophe that will take place if the world doesn’t wean itself off fossil fuels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In “Gaslit,” a upcoming documentary about climate change activists, Jane Fonda stands outside one of Formosa Petrochemical’s Texas facilities and looks through a thermal camera. The Oscar-winning actress is brought to tears by what she sees: a tremendous expulsion of methane gas into the air.

According to recent reports, “Methane is 80 percent more destructive to the climate, in terms of global warming, than carbon dioxide,” Fonda explained during a recent Zoom interview. “It’s the most destructive chemical that we’re using, and it’s extremely dangerous for people. And yet here it is billowing into the air, and nobody even knows it.”.

In a recent development, for years, Fonda has been sounding the alarm about the looming environmental catastrophe that will take place if the world doesn’t wean itself off fossil fuels. She introduced a series of climate change protests dubbed “Fire Drill Fridays” in 2019 — a reference to activist Greta Thunberg’s charge that people should “act as if your house is on fire” — and has been arrested multiple times for civil disobedience. Fonda is embracing the cause with the same passion that has led her to speak out on everything from the Vietnam War to feminism to LGBTQ+ rights. But she worries her efforts may not be enough. Related Stories Paul Thomas Anderson’s ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Getting Nationwide Release in January Rian Johnson Leaves the Door Open to Star Wars Return: ‘It’s a World I Deeply Love’.

“Our emission of global warming chemicals has gone way up since Donald Trump has become president,” Fonda stated. “And of course the concern is always: Have we passed too many tipping points or a tipping point? Many climate scientists say if we act fast now, it won’t be too late. But it’s very hard to act fast when Trump is president.”.

Industry observers note that the political winds are changing. The midterms were a blue wave election that saw Democrats take back the House and the Senate in commanding fashion. They not only performed well in liberal bastions, but also captured the governor’s mansion in Texas and elected James Talarico to a U.S. Senate seat that has been in Republican hands for decades. Much of “Gaslit” focuses on the environmental damage wrought by the oil fields in West Texas’ Permian Basin. Will the change in leadership make a difference?

“It won’t hurt,” Fonda said. “I don’t know how strong Talarico is on these problems. We can’t do too much until our members are seated, and we actually have the majority in the House in January.”.

In a recent development, “Renewables are ready,” she added. “They’re cheap. They’re safe. They’re job-intensive. It’s the perfect solution. It’s right there. It makes all the sense in the world. The only thing we lack is political will, and hopefully, with this swath of upcoming people that have been elected to the House and the Senate, we will have the political will when we take power to turn this around.”.

Fonda believes average citizens concerned about climate change can’t afford to be passive.

Recent findings suggest that “One of the most important things that people can do is to demand that their elected officials pass legislation that makes these polluters pay for what they’re doing,” Fonda stated. “Right now, it’s consumers, it’s us taxpayers that have to pay for the damage. They should pay, and we have to stop the $21 billion annual subsidies that we pay them. They make trillions of dollars of profit. If we cancel those subsidies, it would spell the beginning of the end for fossil fuels.”.

It has been revealed that fonda is blunt in her warnings that the chaos and damage that global warming has caused will only accelerate unless the world switches to renewable sources of energy. Her assessment is sober, even terrifying, but one thing that gives her hope is the work that the activists highlighted in “Gaslit” are doing. “Gaslit” was financed and produced by the environmental group Greenpeace USA, and it focuses on people in the Gulf Coast and Texas who are trying to change things across the political spectrum. They range from a Republican cattle rancher, who has seen what the oil and gas business has done to his family’s land, to cancer survivors and community organizers who are hoping to change hearts and minds about fossil fuels.

“What is so moving to me about the film is we’re showing these people who do not give up; they will not,” Fonda stated. “All of these activists are so brave and so incredible. They inspire me.”.

“Gaslit” was directed by Katie Camosy. It is now available to rent or buy on Amazon Prime and Documentary+. As of November 19, the film can be streamed on the Greenpeace USA YouTube channel, with additional platforms rolling out.

#165766. 15 Thriller Movies of 2026 That Are Near-Perfect Masterpieces

15 Thriller Movies of 2026 That Are Near-Perfect Masterpieces

📅 03 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • So far, 2026 has offered fans of thriller movies some exceptional experiences on the significant screen.
  • Of course, with us being only halfway through the year, not all of 2026's best thrillers have been perfect; but they've all been so great that it'll take something truly special to take any of their spots.
  • Gritty revisionist takes on mythical heroes like Robin Hood aren't a latest concept, but rarely do they work as well as The Death of Robin Hood does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So far, 2026 has offered fans of thriller movies some exceptional experiences on the significant screen. Full of suspense, great performances, and nail-biting sequences of pure tension, the best thriller films of the year so far are bound to still be remembered as some of 2026's best movies by the time 2027 rolls in. From the great to the absolutely perfect, they've all been masterclasses in how to make thrillers that hit hard.

Of course, with us being only halfway through the year, not all of 2026's best thrillers have been perfect; but they've all been so great that it'll take something truly special to take any of their spots. Whether it's an underappreciated indie darling like The Death of Robin Hood, a big blockbuster like Disclosure Day, or a micro-budget surprise like Obsession, these are all worthy of being considered among the best thrillers of the last few years.

Gritty revisionist takes on mythical heroes like Robin Hood aren't a latest concept, but rarely do they work as well as The Death of Robin Hood does. Directed by Michael Sarnoski, this A24 action thriller is an adaptation of the Early Modern English ballad Robin Hood's Death, widely considered one of the oldest existing tales of Robin Hood.

Sources indicate that nowadays, most people are familiar with an image of Robin Hood as a romantic, idealist folk hero. In the oldest Medieval ballads about the character, however, he was a ruthless outlaw who didn't much care about robbing the rich to give to the poor. Sarnoski's film is all about subverting that classic swashbuckling folklore to deliver a richly profound meditation on aging, regret, and the burden of legacy. The pacing is a bit tedious, but the narrative is irresistibly compelling.

Dad movies are vital, often the driving force of the quieter pre-summer months of movie releases. This year, that dad movie was Crime 101, which has the potential to become a true dad movie classic going forward. Elevated by a star-studded cast and based on the 2020 novella by Don Winslow, this Bart Layton gem may not be a masterpiece, but it sure is masterfully entertaining.

According to recent reports, though the film was unfortunately a box office bomb, critics and audiences who saw it absolutely loved it. A sleek neo-noir the likes of which Los Angeles is already accustomed to by now, it's an incredibly suspenseful and surprisingly well-written two-and-a-half hours of pure adrenaline. That runtime definitely feels a little excessive at times, but as soon as the next explosive set piece comes along, it becomes easier to forgive the film being overlong.

Sources indicate that one of the most important Hollywood indie filmmakers of his generation, Gus Van Sant can be a little hit-or-miss sometimes. This year, however, the director delivered a definitive hit: Dead Man's Wire, inspired by the real 1977 hostage standoff involving American kidnapper Tony Kiritsis. Though the film premiered at the Venice International Film Festival in September 2025, it only received its wide release in January of this year.

It's already one of the best thrillers of the 2020s, perfectly recreating its '70s setting with a dark sense of humor and some nail-biting suspense. Anchored by Bill Skarsgård and Dacre Montgomery, both at the top of their games, it's a top-tier anti-capitalist thriller unlike anything else the 2020s have delivered thus far. Gripping, absurdly amusing, and delightfully retro, it's the sort of modern gem that all those who love '70s thrillers like Dog Day Afternoon are guaranteed to enjoy.

Sources indicate that between the early and mid-2010s, Charli XCX started gaining mainstream traction. Today, she has one of the most loyal cult followings of any musical artist of her generation. With her popularity skyrocketing in the 2020s, it's no surprise that she's begun her incursion into acting. However, this year's The Moment is no traditional acting role for the singer-songwriter. This hugely meta psychological thriller mockumentary is a semi-autobiographical satire all about the pressures and anxieties of artistic control.

Directed by Aidan Zamiri and based on an original idea by Charli, this wildly creative A24 project isn't quite as sharp as it needed to be in order to be considered a masterpiece; but it's nevertheless one of the most daring and ingenious thrillers we've seen in recent years, and a must-see for fans of contemporary pop music.

If only because it represents a return to the same campy, bloody, over-the-top, bodily-fluid-filled form that Sam Raimi fans missed so much, Send Help is easily one of the best thriller movies of 2026. It's the kind of survival horror thriller that the blockbuster landscape needs more of nowadays: Purely fun, unapologetically auteur-driven, and completely unafraid of alienating those who prefer their thrillers less quirky.

Rachel McAdams and Dylan O'Brien are both chewing the scenery here in ways that could only work this well in a Raimi film, and it's their chemistry that anchors the movie's emotional core as it twists and turns in all sorts of entirely unexpected directions. As an allegory for power dynamics and workplace misogyny, the film is not particularly subtle; but it never pretends to be anything other than an exquisitely hammy delight anyway.

Recent findings suggest that based on writer-director Aleshea Harris' 2018 stage play, Is God Is can be counted among the greatest stage-to-screen adaptations of the last few years. It's a Southern Gothic revenge thriller with a razor-sharp comedic edge, ferociously creative and entirely deserving of its impressive 97% Tomatometer score on Rotten Tomatoes.

It's a love letter to sisterhood and a powerful deconstruction of the complexities of generational trauma and Black womanhood, a near-masterpiece that deserves far more love than it's gotten so far. It's a future cult classic that juggles all of its diverse genre elements brilliantly, furiously entertaining but also undeniably heartbreaking and psychologically intense.

Sources indicate that with the news of James Gunn and Peter Safran having been let go as heads of DC Studios, the future of the new DCU is a complete mystery, but at least fans do have something to be happy about: The latest DCU installment, Clayface, is one of the best and most original comic book films in years. That's because far from just being a traditional supervillain movie, it's a body horror thriller unlike any other.

Taking a B-list character from Batman's rogues' gallery and making him the lead of one of the DCU's first-ever solo films was certainly a bold choice, but it would be an understatement to say that director Jams Watkins was successful. Working from a script written by Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini, Clayface is both a terrifying and surprisingly emotional character study that culminates in one of the best DC movie final shots to date.

Dramatizing the production of Chris Hansen's NBC reality TV show To Catch a Predator, Lance Oppenheim's Primetime has become a kind of litmus test for media literacy this year. Far from being a black-and-white statement on Hansen or the show as a whole, this psychological crime thriller is more so a commentary on the ethics and culture surrounding the exploitative post-9/11 American media.

Bolstered by a powerhouse Robert Pattinson performance, this is easily one of the actor's best movies of the last 10 years. Visually fascinating and entirely fearless in how it deconstructs sensationalism and performative justice, it's an audacious media satire which proves that, at this point, Pattinson is more than prepared to lead pretty much any kind of project.

In a recent development, with a title coming from a recorded saying by the Prophet Muhammad, Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother became Bassam Tariq's next project after stepping down from Marvel's Blade following multiple delays. Recruiting the same Mahershala Ali who would have starred in the canceled project, Tariq has delivered one of the most enrapturing action thrillers of the 2020s.

It has been revealed that blending visceral genre thrills with a deep emotional core, profound spiritual weight, and a masterful performance by Ali at his very best, Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is both a brilliantly subversive action flick and a moving family drama. If this is any indication of what Tariq and Ali's Blade might have looked like, the world seriously missed out on yet another masterful action film.

There is no blockbuster filmmaking working in Hollywood today than the father of blockbusters, Steven Spielberg himself. Even though the director's 21st-century output hasn't been quite as masterful as his work before the 2000s was, it's still true that every time a new Spielberg movie comes out, it's a cultural event. That's particularly true for his first true alien invasion movie since 2005, Disclosure Day.

Sources indicate that the film plays out as more of an espionage thriller, and though some may not like that, others may find that it often works in its favor. Disclosure Day may not be one of Spielberg's highest-rated sci-fi movies on Letterboxd, but it's nevertheless one of his best modern films to date. Suspenseful, creative, visually striking, and as life-affirming and humanist as one can always expect from a Spielberg blockbuster, it can already be counted among the most underappreciated films of the year thus far.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world may not have been champing at the bit for another “Meet the Parents” sequel with quite the same enthusiasm that defined the hype for “GTA VI” (pretty close, tho!), but anyone who’s been itching for another crazaaaazy weekend between neurotic nurse Gaylord “Greg” Focker and his imperious ex-CIA father-in-law Jack Byrnes has had to wait even longer for their prayers to be answered. Was it worth it?

Well, let’s do a quick comparison between two cultural phenomenons that I’m definitely not just lumping together in a desperate — some might say “heroic” — attempt to write an involving review lede for a movie that never makes even the slightest effort to earn your attention. Related Stories Jane Fonda on Documentary ‘Gaslit,’ Trump, and What the Democrats’ Midterm Victory Means for Climate Change Paul Thomas Anderson’s ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Getting Nationwide Release in January.

According to recent reports, ahem: On the one hand, it took 13 years for Rockstar Games to produce another numbered installment of their marquee franchise, during which time they leveraged cutting-edge technology and unprecedented financial resources in order to radically iterate upon a proven formula so that the firm’s Baudrillardian allegory of American pathos would map onto an era that has become too shattered for more coherent sense-making. On the other hand, it took 16 years for the combined power of Universal and Paramount (a Skydance Company) to will another “Focker” movie into existence, during which time someone realized that it might be kinda funny if Robert De Niro mentioned the words “Jamba Juice.”.

Sources indicate that and in fairness, they weren’t wrong. A Robert De Niro character shouldn’t know what Jamba Juice is, let alone want to drink there! Not only that, but he correctly emphasizes the “JAM” of it all, the formal precision of which suggests that Jack — a red-blooded Boomer who’s recently become an exercise-obsessed vegan health nut — has developed a sincere degree of respect for the smoothie chain and its various blended offerings, even if it’s taken him 16 years to do so.

Given that John Hamburg’s “Focker In-Law” brings back so much of the franchise’s original cast almost three decades since they first played these roles, the film benefits from a Linklater-esque sense of temporal continuity that invites us to imagine the time between movies as a living space. Don’t be fooled by the gruel-thin story, the parade of self-amused callbacks, or the painfully contrived jokes that substitute for real emotion, this isn’t an opportunistic cash-grab meant to capitalize on our collective appetite for major screen comedies — it’s a family reunion.

According to recent reports, the expectations for a legacy sequel are much lower than they might be for the most expensive video game in history, especially in the context of a franchise that’s sustained by the idea that the surname “Focker” sounds almost indistinguishable from the word “fucker.” (Don’t be embarrassed if you hadn’t put that together before — it’s subtle, and film critics are professionally trained to identify such things). “GTA VI” had to revolutionize interactive entertainment in order to be considered a success. “Focker In-Law” just has to deliver more of the same. It does that over and over and over again; I don’t know about Jack’s nipples, but Greg (Ben Stiller) can certainly milk an old joke until it turns to dust in his hand.

It has been revealed that the cinematic equivalent of half-rotten Thanksgiving leftovers that you’d only eat in lieu of having any other food in the house, “Focker In-Law” might be an increasingly rare massive-screen comedy, but it’s endowed with the “whatever”-level apathy of the worst straight-to-streaming junk. Depressingly, that feels like a systemic failure more than a creative one, as Hamburg is a very funny guy who directed several of the better comedies of this century’s pre-Netflix era (e.g. “Along Came Polly”), and he’s far from the only proven talent who gets wasted here.

The basic story — for which Hamburg shares credit with Austen Earl and, curiously, Ilana Glazer — offers a natural riff on the franchise’s initial premise: Greg might wear Radiohead t-shirts and sport facial skin tighter than any scene in the movie around him, but he’s now older than Jack was during the first movie, which means he and his wife Pam (Teri Polo, making the easiest money of her life) have aged into the “Parents” who are due to be “Meet”-ed when their son Henry (an overqualified Skyler Gisondo) brings his massive-eyed fresh girlfriend Olivia (Ariana Grande) to Jack’s 80th birthday celebration.

The joke, and it’s not a bad one, is that Greg — a beta male bozo who’s desperate to make his children and their partners feel welcome — immediately bumps against his probable daughter-in-law, while Jack — a dominant and unyielding patriarch whose “Circle of Trust” is harder to crack than a captured enemy spy — cottons to her from the moment she gets to his house. It helps, of course, that Olivia is an ultra-rigid life coach and former hostage negotiator who shares Jack’s taste for military discipline, as well as his knowledge of different polygraph technologies. Why she’s drawn to a softboi like Greg’s son remains unclear, but the “Wicked”-like theatricality of Grande’s performance is farcical enough for such open questions to be their own reward (it makes sense that her character would be so emotive and intentional), and at the end of the day what matters is just that Greg has a reason to feel rejected all over again.

In a recent development, he doesn’t take it well! In fact, he acts like a massive asshole about it to a degree that steers the movie away from cringe comedy comfort food and closer towards a character study about a malignant narcissist instead. Stiller is a maestro of self-involved unpleasantness (his work in “Greenberg” and “The Meyerowitz Stories” has never gotten the recognition it deserves), but that kind of toxicity is far more unpleasant in the context of a film that thinks it’s cute and/or easily redeemable.

In “Meet the Parents,” Greg got into all sorts of wacky trouble because he meant well and cared so much about seeming worthy of Jack’s daughter. In “Focker In-Law,” the hijinks stem from the fact that he’s a scheming monster who’s trying to sabotage his son’s relationship so that Henry might stay closer to home. The clean and simple fun of watching good intentions curdle into misunderstood chaos has been replaced by the dull ache of watching someone try to pass off diagnosable psychosis as the stuff of routine parental anxiety.

Recent findings suggest that alarm bells start ringing from the very first comic setpiece, in which a classic setup — Greg tries to cut the airplane bathroom line by sneaking from coach into first class — is almost completely undone by the logic gaps that have come to define the character. Why does he impulsively steal Olivia’s birth control out of her bag before he even knows who she is, and how is it possible that such an overbearing dad hasn’t even seen a picture of his son’s very serious fresh girlfriend? Such questions aren’t really worth answering, and Hamburg at least has the courtesy to distract us from them with a fly-by cameo by Cole Escola, but the vibe is all the way off by the time we even touch down in New Jersey for the main event, and nothing that happens there is remotely inspired enough to redeem the pervasive sense that no one can remember why “Meet the Parents” became a franchise in the first place.

In a recent development, was it Owen Wilson’s amusingly oblivious performance as Pam’s charmed ex-fiancé, Kevin? There’s only one way to find out! Was it Jack’s penchant for lie-detector tests or his affinity for unlovable pets? Let’s give them both a shot and see what sticks. (I was amused by the German shepherd he trains in this film, who sets up a very good joke accusation that I don’t want to spoil here). Maybe it became a phenomenon because people crave manic setpieces that end in a plume of human ashes — we should run that back just in case. Anything to avoid the obvious and enduring coziness of a “home for the holidays” movie, which “Focker In-Law” inexplicably forfeits by setting its story at the height of summer.

The ballad of Gaylord Focker certainly didn’t become a thing because of Greg’s daughter and her long-term boyfriend, whose presence this movie struggles to accommodate despite the fact that Beanie Feldstein and Eduardo Franco are both eager to help liven things up. In fairness, why open the floor to potentially amusing newly introduced characters when you can spend half the film’s runtime agonizing over Greg’s uncomfortably demented attempts to steal the engagement ring that Henry wants to give to Olivia? Some opportunities are just too good to pass up, I suppose.

According to recent reports, that “Focker In-Law” maintains any of its series’ long-faded charm can be attributed to De Niro, who sleepwalked through the previous two sequels but feels revived by Jack’s newfound looseness in this one. The actor delights in playing off Grande’s type-A eagerness, just as his character takes a muted pleasure in how much Olivia causes Greg to crash out. In a comedy as flat, stilted, and generic as this one, De Niro’s still-inimitable star power is almost enough to save the movie from its own reheated cynicism. “JAM-ba Juice.” They actually just go by “Jamba” now. The franchise’s juice is long, long gone.

Universal Pictures will release “Focker In-Law” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

Recent findings suggest that steven Spielberg has directed musicals, sci-fi epics, adventure films, and biopics, but one genre has eluded him over the course of his decades-long career. He has never directed a Western, despite having openly longed to put his spin on the type of movies that turned one of his idols, John Ford, into a legend.

Sources indicate that well, the wait is over. Spielberg is developing an untitled film for Focus Features about two fugitives charting a course across the American West, and he’s assembled a crack team to help him. The ensemble will include Jessie Buckley, fresh off her Oscar win for “Hamnet,” Cillian Murphy, the Oscar-winning star of “Oppenheimer,” and Mark Rylance, a frequent Spielberg collaborator who won, you guessed it, an Oscar for “Bridge of Spies.” Related Stories ‘Focker In-Law’ Review: An Eager Ariana Grande Isn’t Enough to Save a Comedy Sequel That Can’t Remember What People Liked About This Franchise Jane Fonda on Documentary ‘Gaslit,’ Trump, and What the Democrats’ Midterm Victory Means for Climate Change.

But there’s more to get cinephiles’ hearts racing! Paul Thomas Anderson, the Oscar-winning filmmaker behind “Boogie Nights,” “There Will Be Blood,” and “One Battle After Another,” is writing the script. It’s based on Kevin Barry’s novel, “The Heart in Winter.” Though Anderson usually directs his screenplays, he’s done script doctoring for Ridley Scott (“Napoleon”) and Martin Scorsese (“Killers of the Flower Moon” and the upcoming “What Happens at Night”). He also did some work on “Corky Romano” — hey, they can’t all be winners! So why not join Spielberg’s merry band?

Recent findings suggest that spielberg is still one of the all-time greats, but he could use a hit. “Disclosure Day,” which marked his return to summer movies, was a box office disappointment, and his most recent films, like “The Fabelmans” and “West Side Story,” struggled to connect with audiences despite earning excellent reviews. Maybe saddling up will be just what the movie gods ordered.

According to recent reports, kristie Macosko Krieger, Sara Murphy, Anderson, and Spielberg will produce the film, which is expected to hit theaters in 2028. Tim Headington, Neil Shah, Ryan Zacarias, and Ana Leocha will executive produce it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that rockstar has broken numerous records with Grand Theft Auto 6, making it the biggest entertainment release of all time. It's a remarkable feat, one that will undoubtedly go unmatched by traditional game development for potentially decades. Naturally, the notable thing to do now is to relish this once-in-a-blue-moon achievement, to immerse ourselves within Leonida, enjoy the shock and awe of its ridiculously detailed world, and not busy ourselves too much with thoughts of Rockstar's next game.

However, if, for whatever reason, you're already contemplating the future of GTA 7 while playing Grand Theft Auto 6, or indeed what game Rockstar could be producing next, then you're in luck. After mere days of being available, leakers have already seemingly confirmed what GTA 6's successor will be. The good news is that it looks set to be a sequel to an iconic Rockstar game that never quite got the appreciation it deserved.

According to recent reports, with GTA 6's record-breaking success ostensibly setting Rockstar up financially for the next few years, it is no surprise that the studio is taking a somewhat substantial risk on its next game. At least, that appears to be the case according to a now three-year-old leak that has begun to resurface. Back in 2023, a comprehensive leak was posted to the GTA Forums website that broke down not just GTA 6 details, but also Rockstar's lineup of upcoming games. Crucially, it is claimed that the studio's next game will be a sequel to L.A. Noire.

The reason this leak is being given any degree of credence all these years later is that it got several key details about the game correct, including details surrounding GTA 6's multiple endings. While there are inaccurate details sprinkled throughout the leak, one could easily brush this off as being gameplay features or mechanics that were altered or removed altogether between the leak's release and GTA 6's launch day. If one were to take it at face value, it would mean that we're getting an L.A. Noire sequel in 2030.

Industry observers note that that is both surprising and unsurprising. On the one hand, Rockstar didn't develop the original L.A. Noire. The now-defunct Australian studio, Team Bondi, did most of the development work, with Rockstar publishing it. Rockstar retains the IP, meaning that it could be producing its own sequel or spin-off, but without any of the original creative leads, it may take a very different direction. There are also many other Rockstar titles that fans have been clamoring to see get a sequel, most notably Bully. It was meant to get a sequel at one point, but unfortunately that project was canceled.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, with the advent of new motion capture technology, the revolutionary mechanics in the original L.A. Noire would be more achievable than ever before. A sequel would allow Rockstar to deliver a game between GTA 6 and potentially Red Dead Redemption 3 while finally delivering the definitive version of L.A. Noire. This leak should still be taken with a grain of salt, as there's every chance it's out of date or altogether incorrect. However, should it transpire to be true, it would be very exciting to get an L.A. Noire sequel after GTA 6.

Sony Pictures has won the services to one of the most in-demand commercial directors working today, Shawn Levy. Levy and his 21 Laps banner have signed a major first look overall film deal with Sony Pictures, with Sony beating out multiple studios in what’s mentioned to be a competitive process.

Recent findings suggest that levy will develop and produce theatrical films through the 21 Laps Entertainment banner as part of the deal, which begins fall 2027 and extends across all Sony Pictures labels, so presumably that could include labels like Screen Gems or even Sony Animation. Related Stories Steven Spielberg Directing His First Western with Paul Thomas Anderson Writing the Script ‘Focker In-Law’ Review: An Eager Ariana Grande Isn’t Enough to Save a Comedy Sequel That Can’t Remember What People Liked About This Franchise.

According to recent reports, this film deal comes after Levy and 21 Laps as recently as September signed a new overall TV deal with Disney’s 20th Television, with him exiting his Netflix deal. That pact doesn’t begin until October 2027.

Levy is reuniting with Sony’s leadership Tom Rothman and Sanford Panitch after he previously directed the “Night at the Museum” movies, “Cheaper by the Dozen,” and “Date Night” for them while they were all at Fox.

“I go ALL the way back with Shawn. We made a pile of hits together before he went on to far greater successes, none of which surprised me in the slightest,” Sony Pictures Motion Picture Group Chairman and CEO Tom Rothman said in a statement. “His talent as a producer, director and head of the coolest creative firm around, is rivaled only by his unmatched enthusiasm. I feel lucky as hell to reunite, and excited for everyone at Sony to discover what I have long known — Shawn Levy is the real deal.”.

Sources indicate that “Tom, Sanford and I have a long history together, and some of the most formative and rewarding experiences of my career came during the years we worked together at Fox,” Levy noted in a statement. “Tom saw the future of my career before I did, and he bet on me early and with a bighearted (and loud!) conviction that is one of his trademarks, and for which I’ll be forever grateful. 21 Laps was built on empowering fellow filmmakers and helping them tell stories imbued with their unique voices and visions. Along with my entire 21 Laps team, I’m thrilled to begin this next chapter with the team at Sony, and am excited about the wide-open breadth of opportunity across Sony’s many labels. I deeply value their commitment to theatrical filmmaking.”.

While just about everyone else in Hollywood has taken a victory lap with the success of “Backrooms,” you may have forgotten that Levy and 21 Laps were producers on the A24 horror movie, and he of course directed and produced Netflix’s “Stranger Things,” which concluded at the end of last year. Up next for Levy is “Star Wars: Starfighter,” which is a “Star Wars” spinoff starring Ryan Gosling and which opens May 28, 2027. And he’s also teaming with Gosling and Disney yet again on Marvel’s “Ghost Rider,” which opens July 28, 2028. His last feature he directed was “Deadpool & Wolverine,” which made $1.3 billion worldwide.

On the 21 Laps side, the banner is producing a rom-com with Emma Stone and Chris Pine set at Universal called “The Catch;” Netflix’s drama series “The Sticks,” starring Michelle Monaghan; Amazon MGM Studios’ supernatural horror film “Seasons;” Netflix’s feature comedy “One Attempt Remaining,” starring Jennifer Garner and John Cena; and an untitled Netflix spy feature starring Kevin Hart and Henry Cavill.

Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Entertainment are represented by WME and Wendy Kirk at JSSK.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk's company is facing two new lawsuits over its image-generation capabilities, raising serious questions about what happens when powerful AI tools can manipulate photographs of real people without their permission.
  • Virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday against SpaceX, the parent company of Grok developer xAI and social media platform X.
  • According to recent reports, according to Reuters, these are the first lawsuits brought by U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk's company is facing two new lawsuits over its image-generation capabilities, raising serious questions about what happens when powerful AI tools can manipulate photographs of real people without their permission.

Virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday against SpaceX, the parent company of Grok developer xAI and social media platform X. Both states allege that the company failed to implement adequate safeguards against the creation of nonconsensual sexual images, including child sexual abuse material.

According to recent reports, according to Reuters, these are the first lawsuits brought by U.S. states over the controversy, although several attorneys general have already investigated Grok's image-generation features.

The lawsuits also raise a broader concern for anyone who shares photos online. As AI image generators become more realistic and accessible, how much control do people actually have over what others can create using their pictures?

Here's what happened, what the lawsuits allege and what it could mean for Grok users.

The lawsuits focus on Grok's ability to generate sexualized images and videos from existing photographs.

Sources indicate that grok includes image-generation and editing features that can transform an uploaded photo using text instructions. According to the states, owners exploited these capabilities to create explicit or partially nude images of real people without their knowledge or consent.

The complaints specifically point to Grok's controversial "spicy mode," which the states say enabled the generation of sexual content without sufficient protections.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield argue that the firm promoted the safety of its tools while failing to prevent the creation and distribution of harmful images.

The states accuse SpaceX of violating consumer protection laws and are seeking financial penalties, damages and court orders requiring the tech giant to stop the alleged violations.

These are allegations in civil lawsuits, not findings of wrongdoing by a court.

One of the most alarming figures cited in the lawsuits comes from a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH).

The organization estimated that between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok generated and posted approximately 3 million sexualized images on X, including around 23,000 images that appeared to depict children.

That works out to roughly 190 sexualized images every minute over the study period.

The figures are estimates from the organization's research rather than a confirmed count of illegal images. Nevertheless, the scale described in the study has become a central part of the states' allegations.

The Virginia Attorney General's Office also alleges that nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children identified in the study remained publicly accessible on X at least a week after they were identified.

According to recent reports, yes. In January 2026, xAI announced restrictions on Grok's image-editing capabilities, including measures intended to prevent people from generating images of real people in revealing clothing where doing so would be illegal.

However, subsequent reporting raised questions about whether the changes were effective.

In February, Reuters found that Grok could still generate sexualized images of people even when prompts explicitly stated that the subjects had not consented.

Recent findings suggest that the latest lawsuits argue that the company's safeguards were inadequate and that its public assurances about user safety were misleading. The company has separately taken legal action against individuals it alleges misused Grok to create child sexual abuse material.

For most owners, the concern goes beyond generating inappropriate AI images.

The lawsuits highlight a growing problem with generative AI: someone may be able to use a photograph of another person to produce realistic fabricated content without that person's permission.

An AI-generated image does not have to depict something that actually happened to cause harm. A convincing fake can be copied, shared or used to harass someone, especially when it circulates on a major social media platform.

According to recent reports, the risk is particularly concerning for parents whose children's photos may be publicly accessible online. These lawsuits do not mean that every Grok user has had their photos manipulated, nor do they establish that simply uploading a photo to X causes Grok to generate an explicit image.

Still, they are a reminder that publicly available images can be vulnerable to misuse by people with access to powerful AI editing tools.

Sources indicate that people concerned about this risk can review the visibility of their social media accounts, limit public sharing of sensitive images and report manipulated content when they encounter it. Such precautions cannot eliminate the possibility of misuse, especially when a photograph has already been copied or circulated elsewhere.

According to recent reports, both states are seeking penalties and court orders aimed at stopping the alleged unlawful conduct. The courts have not yet determined whether SpaceX violated either state's consumer protection laws.

The manufacturer also faces more than a dozen lawsuits from individuals who allege that Grok was used to create nonconsensual sexual images of them.

The outcome of the lawsuit could help determine how much responsibility AI companies bear when their tools are used to create harmful images of real people.

But for now, the Grok lawsuits underscore a concern that extends to AI image generation as it has become remarkably powerful, but protecting the people whose likenesses appear in those images remains an unresolved challenge.

Industry News: The 10 Best Alternative Rock Bands of All Time, Ranked

💡 Key Takeaways

  • At a point in the 1980s, alternative rock kind of became the next stage of rock, and then it morphed into grunge in the 1990s (which was on another level popularity-wise), before more or less morphing into indie rock in the 2000s and into the 2010s.
