📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that classic rock kind of came and went by the 1980s, after flourishing in the 1970s and beginning in the 1960s. That doesn’t mean rock itself died, nor that any rock made after the mid-1980s can’t call itself classic. It’s just classic rock is that beefy, grand, and popular kind, probably best exemplified by the likes of The Who, The Rolling Stones, some Pink Floyd, and (definitely) Led Zeppelin.

At a point in the 1980s, alternative rock kind of became the next stage of rock, and then it morphed into grunge in the 1990s (which was on another level popularity-wise), before more or less morphing into indie rock in the 2000s and into the 2010s. So, some of the best alternative rock bands of all time are a bit grunge, and some might technically fit into the indie wave to some extent, but it does nonetheless feel fair to consider all the bands below as alternative rock ones. Oh, and particularly great alternative rock bands at that, too.

Speaking of grunge and its relation to alternative rock, here’s Nirvana, a band that didn’t last long technically, but has undeniably endured well beyond the band and the way it ended when frontman/lead singer Kurt Cobain took his life in 1994. That event didn’t entirely end grunge, but Nirvana no longer being a thing definitely had an impact on the whole sub-genre, or strand of alternative rock.

Placing Nirvana low here might seem controversial, but it comes down to the discography being limited, and the first album (of three), Bleach, being not bad, but not quite great. The great albums, of course, are Nevermind and In Utero, and then the live album MTV Unplugged in New York shouldn’t be overlooked either, since that one is also phenomenal, albeit obviously more focused on acoustic/mellow rock over alternative rock, in its sound.

While The National are the newest band here, they’ve always sounded kind of old, but in a good way. “World-weary” is probably the way to put it that doesn’t run the risk of sounding like an insult. The label that might run the risk of sounding like more of an insult is to say The National are the best “sad divorced dad rock band” of the 21st century so far.

If you can take that as a compliment, please do, because making that kind of music and having it be both authentic and not annoying is a real skill. The weariness to The National’s music also contributes to them feeling a little less like an indie rock band than some of their contemporaries, and possibly more appealing to people out there (divorced dads or otherwise) who might be more familiar with some of the ’80s and ‘90s era bands being mentioned here otherwise.

Laugh at Weezer if you want, but a lot of the time, you're probably going to be laughing with them, or they’ll be laughing at you laughing at them, like, if you don’t think they're in on the joke. Weezer are a pretty ridiculous band, but the first two albums in their discography are untouchable, all to the extent that people are generally in agreement that they're excellent, and there’s only some division on the whole “which is better” debate between The Blue Album and Pinkerton.

Beyond that, things get wild. There are some pretty shoddy Weezer albums, but then some that come close to being so-bad-they're-good, if that’s even a phenomenon that can happen with albums. Then Maladroit, Everything Will Be Alright in the End, The White Album, and OK Human all have some great stuff on them, and even some of the other lesser Weezer albums in between all that might have a handful of decent tracks on them.

Well, a little of what can be stated about Nirvana can be said about Pixies, since there aren’t a huge number of absolutely essential albums within this band’s discography. And, like Weezer, the two all-timers were the first two albums the band put out, here being Surfer Rosa (1988) and then the even better Doolittle just one year later.

Doolittle is more approachable and somehow even more consistent, though it would be foolish to skip over Surfer Rosa entirely. Start with one or the other, and either way, you're winning. As for the band generally, Pixies definitely have a distinctively alternative rock sound, and kept doing their own weird thing into the 1990s and beyond, too (with the influence the band had on Nirvana, especially Kurt Cobain, also understandably getting talked about often).

In a recent development, if you want one adjective to best describe Sonic Youth, it’s probably “raw.” The band’s great and groundbreaking for sure, with early albums in the early 1980s, meaning they're especially influential as far as alternative rock bands go. The band didn’t peak until a little later, though, with the signature album of theirs coming out right as the 1980s were coming to an end: 1989’s Daydream Nation.

In a recent development, that was such a good year for unusual and/or alternative rock, seeing as Doolittle, Bleach, and one other massive rock album by The Cure (more on them shortly) came out in 1989. The closest Sonic Youth came to putting out something approachable and/or like a hit was in 1990, though, with Goo. That’s not a bad starting point, though if the length and ambition of Daydream Nation doesn’t intimidate you, that’s perhaps the best one to check out if you want to see what all the fuss is about.

Speaking of ambitious albums, The Smashing Pumpkins put out something kind of insane in 1995, but it really worked. That album was Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness, and at over two hours in length, it’s almost like a triple album, considering a good many albums of a more traditional length hover at around the 40-minute mark.

If Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness is a bit maximalist for you, the other contender for the crown of “best Smashing Pumpkins album” is, of course, 1993’s Siamese Dream, which is a definite alternative rock classic and a huge improvement on the band’s first album, 1991’s Gish. Albums #2 and #3 might not have ever been topped, but there is a good deal more music by this band beyond 1995, and quite a bit of that discography is worth exploring if you like this particular sound/era of rock music.

It has been revealed that R.E.M. never sounded as intense as Sonic Youth, but they're worth mentioning because they did the whole alternative rock thing quite early, with some of the band’s best material being from the early to mid-1980s. It does sound like a hipster thing to say, but sincerely, Murmur is the best showcase of what the band could do, especially lyrically, and also with pretty stripped-back and simple instrumentation overall.

It’s got a pure alternative rock thing in that way, and feels influential on the wave of indie rock a couple of decades later. But it’s Automatic for the People that was the hit R.E.M. album, and yes, that one’s pretty great too. Then, the 1982 EP Chronic Town is awesome, and albums-wise, the likes of Reckoning, Lifes Rich Pageant, and Document are all pretty much essential, too.

The Cure were briefly mentioned before, when talking about great albums from 1989, because Disintegration is easily one of that year’s best albums on account of it also being one of the best albums of all time. Calling it alternative rock and leaving it at that is underselling it, but it’s a kind of rock throughout, with a mix of lengthy and moodier songs alongside some more energetic ones.

It has been revealed that admittedly, a few of those livelier songs are also epic in length. Disintegration is just a monumental album in terms of its sound and also how long it goes for. And yet it’s just one album that makes The Cure worthy of being called one of the best alternative rock bands of all time (see also the likes of Seventeen Seconds, Faith, a 1981 album Google might not like me typing the name of, The Head on the Door, Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Wish, and even the quite recent Songs of a Lost World).

Industry observers note that sure, The Smiths ended a long time ago, as a band, but they’ve certainly endured. There were four studio albums released during the 1980s, and then there are some compilation albums that all feature a good many songs that were never on any of the main albums, so you do ultimately have quite a few hours' worth of songs here to dig through, and they're all pretty great, even with there being a certain sameness to things.

For a few great years, there was a phenomenal songwriting partnership between Johnny Marr and Morrissey.

It has been revealed that the sameness, though, is okay when a standard song by The Smiths is so high-quality. And admittedly, the band might be a little more pop or proto-indie than outright alternative rock, but it still feels like they qualify just well enough. For a few great years, there was a phenomenal songwriting partnership between Johnny Marr and Morrissey, with the pair also making for distinctive guitarists and vocalists, respectively.

Radiohead is one of those bands that feels hard to introduce, because what else can be said, at this point? The first album they released was an alternative rock and almost grunge sort of one (Pablo Honey), then they went into a Britpop thing for the much-improved The Bends, and then it was kind of anything goes after that. OK Computer is the band’s "most" alternative rock album, if that makes any sense, and then album #4, Kid A, is probably the least rock (alternative or otherwise) related.

Still, Radiohead has retained feeling like something of an alternative rock band, since they're almost always at least a little bit rock, and they very much do things their own way and ultimately prove influential, since other bands sometimes seem perfectly okay to play catch-up. It’s an easy pick, putting them #1 here, but they have probably been the most consistently impressive alternative rock band in relatively recent memory.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, don’t let the title fool you: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” might offer up a breezy, very fun-to-watch new entry into the life and times of titular (and fictitious) Hollywood stuntman, but co-star Elizabeth Debicki steals the show in David Fincher’s film (in addition to stealing the heart of Brad Pitt’s Cliff). Is it time to greenlight “The New Adventures of Karen Crosby”? We think so.

It has been revealed that the much-anticipated sequel to Quentin Tarantino’s “Once Upon in Hollywood” picks up nearly a decade after the Oscar-winning antics of the previous film, finding Cliff pursuing upcoming professional endeavors (film projecting! bartending! contract killing, kind of!). Stunt work? Eh, only when he feels like, and he certainly feels like after taking an unexpected meeting with Hollywood agent Karen Crosby (Debicki), whose grace and good humor instantly delight both Cliff and the audience. Related Stories Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Set Overall Film Deal at Sony Pictures Steven Spielberg Directing His First Western with Paul Thomas Anderson Writing the Script.

It has been revealed that tossed together by the wacky demands of Karen’s marquee client, actor Charlie Nelson (Scott Caan), the shaggy, Tarantino-penned “Cliff Booth” meanders its way through every corner of Hollywood, finding real emotional ballast and crackling chemistry every time Pitt and Debicki share the screen. Characteristically wordy and dense, we learn plenty about Karen along the way (including her early forays into film criticism and her current feelings about movies), and she wins Cliff’s heart by, well, literally and physically slapping the crap out of him.

Ahead, IndieWire catches up with the Aussie star (who gets to use her real accent this time) about Fincher’s film, from slapping her co-star to some serious ruminations on the instantly iconic “pig monologue speech.” No wonder Cliff went so crazy for Karen; she’s a delight.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: What was your relationship with “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” when the film came out in 2019?

Elizabeth Debicki: I went to see it in the cinema. I think I went by myself, which makes me think I must have been on a job. I was definitely in the States, maybe I was in L.A., and I went one afternoon. I went and sat in the cinema, and I loved it. It’s really vivid in my memory.

I didn’t watch it again before we made this for performance reasons. In a way, I realized I didn’t really need to because, [there’s] something about Quentin’s movies, they just kind of wedge themselves in your brain. I can literally see the Playboy Mansion scene. I can see the Manson kids driving up to the house. I can see Margaret Qualley’s feet on the dashboard. I can see everything.

So it sounds like you came into this as a Tarantino fan.

In a recent development, absolutely. Yeah. I mean, he’s seminal.

And to get Tarantino and Fincher is this incredible two-for-one.

Recent findings suggest that it’s funny, because obviously in the making of this, I had to sort of normalize that. And they helped me do that because they were, from the second I got onto set — which was a two-week rehearsal period where we really worked through the script — we had Quentin for that whole period. [It was] very, very collaborative.

A part of me wonders whether it was that thing where they have sat with the material for so long and had their full body relationship to it, and then I was fresh. I had my own thoughts and feelings. My memories of those rehearsal periods were really all three of them [Fincher, Tarantino, and Pitt] just turning to me and saying, “What do you think? What do you think?” The first time it happened, I was like, “Oh my God, what do I think?” After a little while, I started to actually say what I thought, which was great.

What was your audition process like?

I didn’t audition for this. David emailed me and asked me if I would be interested in playing a part. I remember he phrased it in an email as he hoped that I would consider playing a very tricky part in a film he was hoping to make in July. It was a very David-ism kind of email. I think it stated something like, “I hope you understand the seriousness of this conundrum,” or something. And I called him up and yeah, I was obviously ready to say, “I’ll do it.”.

Sources indicate that he was very, very insistent. He was like, “Wait, wait, wait. I really want to tell you everything about it.” Because at that point he and Quentin were doing a massive edit of the script. He couldn’t send it to me there and then.

In a recent development, karen is so singular, but she is in a familiar position if you’re working in Hollywood. Did you base any part of your performance on any agents or managers or publicists that you know or have encountered?

When I first read the script, there were things that just rang so true to me, and might seem outrageous for anyone or slightly absurd maybe for anyone who doesn’t work in this industry. The incredible pig scene where Cliff talks about killing a pig, and then the scene in the car where Karen indicates, “Now because of you, I now have to spend my entire morning finding a pig. That is not a joke, that is literally what I have to get up and do. And you know what? I had a lot of things I had to do, and it wasn’t find a pig. And now I have to drive your ass all the way to Marina del Rey because I have to just deliver you because that’s what my client needed.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s kind of this absurd ask, but it’s folded into “that’s what I need for my process.” Quentin and David, they’re so fascinating because they are Hollywood. They are Hollywood, and also they sit outside it, and they observe it from these very, very unique vantage points. Quentin, in particular, his love affair with L.A. is so profound, and with Hollywood. Part of the thing I loved about her too is that she’s sort of accidentally an agent, which is not frequently do you come across that. One of the things too that feels very human about her is that she sort of had this other dream, but she took one really bad knock, and it broke her heart, and she just buried it deep inside and then made decisions based off that.

When we get to that scene with Karen and Cliff when you’re talking about how Karen had this other career as a film critic, I how much of that was lifted from what would’ve been Quentin’s movie, “The Movie Critic”?

Industry observers note that I don’t know. I don’t actually know the answer to that question in terms of the parallel there. But I do love that in the middle of this film about 1977 in Hollywood, that there’s a really notable moment where we think about Pauline Kael, and we think about her and she lives in this film. I’m so glad that there’s this moment where my character gets to say, “Pauline Kael is my god,” because she was. She was incredible.

As Karen, you have this great monologue explaining to Cliff who you used to be, what had happened with that career path, how wonderful it was that Pauline supported you, and then it didn’t work out. And then you have another monologue about seeing movies as hamburgers. It’s a really funny tension for Karen, because the audience likely assumes she loves movies and does see them as art.

In a recent development, that’s right, there is a tension there. I feel like one of the things that Quentin can do so well, and kind of totally unique to his own brain, is that he sort of plucks an idea out of the zeitgeist, something that we’re all thinking about, and he feeds it through his characters in a way that feels very organic. This is a big conversation that people are having as the industry shifts and changes. It also was a huge conversation that was happening in 1977. There was this big question of, “Is that art still if it’s commercial, if its box office success equates to this?” I think that the dichotomy of what she believes in her heart and wants to be true and what she spouts in front of people, I sort of think both things are true at once, and I think that’s just the kind of human element.

Industry observers note that but I also think that it’s crucial to remember in that monologue that Charlie really pulls it out of her. She really doesn’t want to do the dance, the dancing monkey, or what did she say? “There’s a dancing bear aspect to your request,” I think is such a great line. But yeah, I think both things are true for her.

You have the sense she’s said this speech before, and again, maybe she doesn’t totally believe it, but Charlie just loves it and so she has to do it.

David and I spoke about it a lot, and we sort of landed on we feel like she did it once off the cuff, like at a table at the Emmys or the Globes, and everyone went, “Gee, Karen, that’s genius.” And Charlie heard it and went, “Yeah, that’s genius. She’s my agent, look how smart she is. She’s so great.” Then she’s done it one other time at a dinner. So, by the time we get to the pool, she’s like, “Oh, my God.” It’s becoming a routine against her will, which was also a really fun element to play with in terms of how much she does or doesn’t enjoy it, and finding that balance.

Do you personally read reviews of your work?

Has that always been the case for you?

Industry observers note that has it always been the case? [Smiles] I’m sure anyone who doesn’t read a review once read a bad review.

It doesn’t even have to be a bad one. What I learned is, you can read a review that is seemingly positive, but it might not be what you were trying to do, and then you feel heartbroken about that too. So yes, I really avoid it. Yeah.

In a recent development, you get to slap Brad Pitt a lot in this film. Was that hard to do?

Industry observers note that it’s a very beautiful face, and we had to do it. We had to do it. And Brad is a very good sport and a very good stuntman. I think that Brad was very, very comfortable, and I was very nervous. We shot the dialogue for two days, that we were just in almost this sort of trance of the two of them, and of the very unusual power dynamic that [they have]. One of the best things about that scene to me, which I didn’t analyze at the time, it’s so intricate the way that Quentin wrote it. It’s this moment where, in revealing what he wants, he becomes so vulnerable that the power dynamic kind of very subtly shifts in this kind of core foundational way between these two characters.

So, we shot that for two days and then all of a sudden it was like, “Oh, my God, it ends, and I need to figure out how to do this.” We had an amazing stunt coordinator on that job.

We had to do extremely complex things with people, but with me, I was like, “Hey Dave, could we just pop out the back there and have a little chat about the slap…?”.

Sources indicate that everyone knows that David likes to do a lot of takes. How many takes was the actual slapping?

Recent findings suggest that not so many! It was probably the least amount of takes we did. We probably did a couple, five, maybe six. And then I do remember that Brad sort of went, “OK, I think we got it. I think we’re good now,” and we moved on. But we did the inside [slap] first. It was such a joy to do. It’s such a happy memory. We filmed it, and then we all ran around to the monitor, and we watched it in playback, and we’re like, “Oh, my God, it’s so good.” And then we filmed it again. We were so pleased with ourselves. [Laughs].

What scenes did David ask for the most takes?

It has been revealed that the thing about the takes is, it’s coverage-dependent. So, if you have four actors in a scene, like the hamburger monologue, let’s say there’s four setups on each actor, you do 10 takes per setup. So, that becomes a lot.

Recent findings suggest that I will say that in the pig speech monologue, I don’t have a lot of lines, but we did just as much coverage on me as we did on Brad and Scott. That was one of my first days on set, and I remember thinking, “This is so, so unusual. Why is he doing this?” And then a couple weeks later, he showed me a kind of rough edit, and I thought, “Oh, my God, that’s why he did it.” He is using Karen as the kind of go-between. As David would always say, at least there’s one grown-up in the room, and it’s Karen.

So I do have this really funny memory too of doing that during the pig monologue scene. I was off-camera, or we were catching just the side of me; I was very much out of focus, and I took a drag of the cigarette, and I remember he gave me a note for that, something about the speed of it or the intention of it. And I remember thinking ….

Recent findings suggest that exactly! I was like, “You saw that?” And he was right, he was absolutely right, but I thought, “OK, this is not a set where we get away with anything.”.

It has been revealed that especially in that scene, you have these facial expressions where you are having the appropriate reaction to what we’re hearing, but in such a beautiful way. I think that’s when we all fall in love with Karen. We’re like, “She gets it. She knows how ridiculous this is,” but she is part of this world.

I’m particularly proud of the Tic Tac crunch; that was my prop idea, and I just thought we should end with her crunching down on something, because she’s so pissed about having to then go and spend her entire morning looking for a hog in Malibu Colony or something. Where is she even going to find that pig?

In a recent development, she did it. I mean, David and I would talk about that too. I’m like, “Do you think she did it or she sent Mallory, her assistant, to go do it?” Either way, someone did it, someone paid for it.

Speaking of falling in love with Karen, there’s been this sentiment circulating as people see the film that there is a real rom-com built into it with Cliff and Karen. Do you see it that way?

I don’t think it’s a rom-com, but I think it’s romantic, and I think they’re funny. Don’t get me wrong, rom-coms are my religion. Yesterday I was walking through New York, and I literally felt like I was in “You’ve Got Mail.” I was like, “This fall day, I need a bunch of sharpened pencils.” But I don’t think that this necessarily falls into that category. It’s sort of undefinable, indefinable, but I do think it’s really romantic. I felt that when we were playing it, and we really enjoyed that together.

Recent findings suggest that the romance of it is kind of surprising, because it surprises her. It’s sort of best case scenario romance, that you think you have it all together, and this person walks in that you absolutely dismiss in terms of that, and then little by little they just sort of reveal this thing. More beautifully, they pull something out of you. I didn’t necessarily intellectualize any of this while we were shooting it, it’s just that I can see that now retrospectively. Not that I read anything, but I am curious what people will make of them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Big Game is coming to the Big Screen. Technically the biggest screens.

Super Bowl LXI is set to play live on IMAX screens across North America, as well as in some international markets, specifically Australia, New Zealand, and Brazil. The game takes place on Sunday, February 14, 2027, or Valentine’s Day 2027, and now you can convince your partner that the Valentine’s Day date night is still alive because you can go out to the movie theater to watch the game instead of stay at home.

Recent findings suggest that IMAX will screen everything from the pregame and postgame coverage, the full four-hour presentation of the game itself, and of course the Halftime Show headlined by Jay-Z, all beginning at 6 pm ET. ESPN’s Monday Night Football broadcast team of Joe Buck, Troy Aikman, Lisa Salters, and Laura Rutledge will be the ones you hear in the theater, so no luck if you’re a Peyton and Eli or Pat McAfee fan. The only thing we don’t know is who’s playing in the game just yet, but this Chicago Bears fan is feeling pretty good about his team’s chances. Related Stories ‘Cliff Booth’ Star Elizabeth Debicki on Slapping Brad Pitt, ‘The Movie Critic,’ and the Rom-Com Question Shawn Levy and 21 Laps Set Overall Film Deal at Sony Pictures.

Recent findings suggest that tickets are expected to go on sale in January. Specific theater locations and ticketing information will be confirmed in the coming weeks.

Industry observers note that this is the first time IMAX is screening something as big as the Super Bowl, but it’s not the first time IMAX has played live sporting events in its theaters. IMAX also screened the opening ceremony for the Paris Olympics, it this year did a series of F1 races in partnership with Apple TV, and events like NHL games and even the NBA Finals have played internationally. This is on a much bigger scale as well, as this will be available in hundreds of IMAX screens across the country.

Sources indicate that ABC, Disney, and ESPN hadn’t been in the rotation for the Super Bowl for a long time, so they’ve been going all out for their first go around. Disney is making the game available via broadcast on ABC, as well as on ESPN and Univision, and also for streaming on Disney+. ESPN is also doing an alternate telecast on ESPN 2 with Peyton and Eli Manning as they do for “Monday Night Football” throughout the regular season. And it was previously confirmed that “The Pat McAfee Show” is getting in on the fun with its own Super Bowl show on ESPNU and “Playbook with Next Gen Stats” on NFL Network.

It has been revealed that this is really a boon for theaters to do added business on a day and weekend when most theaters are pretty empty and the upcoming movie options are few and far between. We’ll see though how the box office responds and how many people relocate their Super Bowl parties to their local multiplex.

In a recent development, “Watching the Super Bowl with your fellow fans is one of the great shared experiences in sports, and this first-of-its-kind collaboration with the NFL and IMAX takes it to a historic newly introduced scale,” said Ken Potrock, President, Major Event Integration for The Walt Disney Tech giant. “With ESPN’s first Super Bowl, we’re reaching fans across an unprecedented range of platforms and meeting them wherever they want to be, with unique moments that only Disney and ESPN can deliver.”.

Industry observers note that “The Super Bowl is a one-of-a-kind global cultural event imbued with spectacle, sound, drama, and heroes — all the makings of a great IMAX experience,” said Rich Gelfond, CEO of IMAX. “This is a milestone for IMAX that further elevates our standing as a premier global platform for entertainment and events, and we’re excited to work in partnership with Disney, ESPN and the NFL to give football fans an unforgettable night.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that faith Roswell is a Senior Writer on Screen Rant's Classic TV team. Since earning her degree in Creative Writing over a decade ago, Faith has written articles on film and TV from a variety of different angles. Faith now combines her knowledge of psychology with her love of monster movies to give more insight into what makes the best ones. You may have read her Screen Rant lists and features covering horror, sci-fi, and fantasy, or read her Amazon Top 10 book, "Movie Monsters of the Deep." Faith has had an extensive career as a writer, appearing on BBC live radio, researching true crime for Rotten Mango podcast, and writing for publications including Mental Floss, Atlas Obscura, and The Daily Jaws before beginning here at Screen Rant.

This article has some mild spoilers for the ending of the series being discussed.

Sources indicate that the best animated indicates in Netflix's history have been a surprisingly eclectic collection, but one has stood out for its visually stunning artwork and compelling story that has had viewers describing it as similar to both Shōgun and John Wick. This is an impressive comparison, with Shōgun revolutionizing the historical epic genre and John Wick becoming an iconic revenge story with a franchise that is still building on itself. Even so, Netflix's animated series is one of the greatest revenge sagas ever told, and fully deserves the comparison.

During Japan's Edo period, when relations with other countries were strictly limited, four white men remained behind, and one of these fathered Mizu. Suffering at the hands of her community, Mizu trained as a warrior and set out on a journey of revenge. This is the premise for Blue Eye Samurai, the multi-award-winning series that builds a fully tangible world and characters you care about in just eight episodes, while many TV series fail to do this in multiple seasons. Blue Eye Samurai can be binged in one sitting, but ended on a cliffhanger which will be resolved next year.

Blue Eye Samurai's ending saw Mizu boarding a ship and leaving Japan for London, seemingly a step closer to getting the revenge she is after. Of the four possible candidates for the identity of her father, Mizu killed one before the events of season 1, and has reluctantly spared the life of Fowler, the second possibility, as he knows where the other two men are hiding. With Taigen and Princess Akemi still in Edo, and Ringo believing that Mizu is dead, the series set itself up to continue the story in multiple locations if renewed for a second season.

According to recent reports, the series was renewed for its much-anticipated second season in 2023, and it has been confirmed that Blue Eye Samurai will officially return in January 2027, with six fresh episodes. The shorter season length has received a mixed reception from viewers and critics, but with episodes lasting almost an hour and with animation that takes a significant period of time, most are cautiously optimistic. Netflix has been criticized for canceling shows early, but the streaming platform has such faith in Blue Eye Samurai that the series has already been renewed for a third and final season.

Sources indicate that action shows tend to evoke a specific mental image, with plenty of grit and explosive live stunts. Unfortunately, this results in animated TV shows often being overlooked, but Blue Eye Samurai has quietly claimed a place among Netflix's best action series, with some even considering the show's eight episodes a worthy Game of Thrones replacement, which speaks to the quality of its worldbuilding, political intrigue, and character writing. The series has a well-deserved 97% and 93% Rotten Tomatoes rating from critics and audiences, respectively, and has attracted some of the world's best voice talent.

Blue Eye Samurai was nominated for seven Annie Awards, winning six of them.

It has been revealed that many characters in Blue Eye Samurai may sound familiar, with the voice cast including Maya Erskine (BoJack Horseman,) Masi Oka (Heroes,) George Takei (Star Trek,) and Kenneth Branagh (Oppenheimer,) and it is not surprising that the series has come from the writing team responsible for both Logan and Blade Runner 2029, as the show's emotional beats hit hard and the visuals feel grounded and cinematic rather than cartoonish. These are the aspects that give an action series the depth it needs to become more than an exciting spectacle, and Blue Eye Samurai surpasses even some of the greatest action reveals.

Rather than relying on fast editing and a punchy soundtrack, Blue Eye Samurai makes fighting look hard. Mizu is not a superhero, but a character who has been through immense emotional pain to get the expertise and skill she has. The show incorporates the blood and sweat of a battle while the tactics of winning do not go ignored. Putting this against a stunning backdrop and a mission that takes as much of Mizu's strength as the fight itself makes Blue Eye Samurai a success on multiple levels, and a legitimate successor to many better-known movie and TV franchises.

Director Andrey Zvyagintsev has worked with supervising re-recording mixer Andrey Dergachev for 20 years, since the director’s second film, “Banishment.” On each project, including their most recent portrait of a rotten marriage in a rotten world, “Minotaur,” they’ve tried to improve the sound design—using it as a hook that makes the film’s world feel more vital and alive for the audience.

It has been revealed that seriously, spoilers. This is never more true than in the absurdly sad and funny, then suddenly murderous confrontation between cuckolded husband Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) and his wife’s lover Anton (Yuriy Zavalnyouk) at the hinge point of “Minotaur.” Related Stories Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens ‘Cliff Booth’ Star Elizabeth Debicki on Slapping Brad Pitt, ‘The Movie Critic,’ and the Rom-Com Question.

Zvyagintsev and Dergachev generally strive to preserve as much authentic production sound from performances as possible. “On my third movie, ‘Elena,’ we recorded the live sound from shooting, and it’s maybe two or three phrases we had to rerecord, but otherwise the whole sound that you hear is fully recorded during the shooting,” Zvyagintsev told IndieWire on an upcoming episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “Our main purpose is to keep as much sound from the shooting as possible and not to add anything extra, and it was the same for ‘Minotaur.’”.

But for the moment that Gleb attacks Anton, and its aftermath, it was important to Zvyagintsev that the world beyond the apartment start intruding on Gleb — that even though he wants desperately to cover up what he’s done and make sure no one sees or learns about it, we hear dozens of ways in which he isn’t alone. That required a lot of work outside of the studio to record the background noises Zvyagintsev and Dergachev could then layer into the scene.

Sources indicate that “We were creating [background] sounds of the kids playing football in the backyard. We would spend the whole day recording the kids, how they’re speaking, the way they’re playing, people passing by on the street,” Zvyagintsev said. They also recorded different sound layers from Gleb’s luxury SUV, which they could deploy to create maximum panic in both Gleb and the audience.

Industry observers note that “The car signals, the leaves on the street, the birds — they all pronounced, and [emphasized] something. So we were modulating all those layers that we recorded, and then we combined them to create the atmosphere and to put it all in one place for the scene,” Zvyagintsev stated.

Sources indicate that there’s atmosphere from outside and from inside, as Zvyagintsev and Dergachev refused to let Gleb have a moment of peace on the soundtrack — until, as with all the cruel jokes of “Minotaur’s” filmmaking, he gets it in the worst way, at the worst possible moment. There’s a terrible silence once he’s struck Anton on the head with his own camera. And then the world comes rushing back in, even louder than before.

“We were trying to create this volume of sounds right after the hit. And then, when Anton is falling, there is this complete silence. And then somewhere far away we hear the car alarm and even more sounds that create this volume. This is what we were looking for,” Zvyagintsev noted.

According to recent reports, it was crucial to finesse the sound design of the sequence so as not to overplay it. Zvyagintsev initially wanted to add music to the moment, but had to hold himself back. “It was really tempting,” Zvyagintsev noted. “My composer Evgueni Galperine even wrote the music, which we added. But when we saw the result, we realized, and I understood that no, no, it has to be completely silent.”.

Industry observers note that silent as the grave, one might say. But it’s the sound design, the modulation between loudness and silence, that makes the moment so horrifying. Zvyagintsev and Dergachev did it by hand, just to make sure of it.

“Minotaur” is now playing in select theaters.

#165749. The 6 Most Uplifting War Movies of All Time, Ranked

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1391 w)

The 6 Most Uplifting War Movies of All Time, Ranked

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this is a difficult topic to tackle, because war movies don’t tend to be uplifting.
  • Sources indicate that with the war genre, plenty of these movies are anti-war, and so the likes of Grave of the Fireflies, Come and See, and All Quiet on the Western Front are about as far from inspiring and uplifting as movies get.
  • Charlie Chaplin was an exceptionally interesting figure during the 1930s and 1940s, since in the former decade, he held onto silent film as a whole medium for longer than most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this is a difficult topic to tackle, because war movies don’t tend to be uplifting. Like, if you're after movies that'll make you feel good, or at least a little better about the state of the world, you're going to be better off seeking out those belonging to other genres, like certain coming-of-age movies, romance films, or some comedies, for hopefully obvious reasons.

Sources indicate that with the war genre, plenty of these movies are anti-war, and so the likes of Grave of the Fireflies, Come and See, and All Quiet on the Western Front are about as far from inspiring and uplifting as movies get. But if you're after some great war movies that have uplifting qualities (even if you do have to take those uplifting parts with some inevitable heavy parts), the following ones might well end up scratching that admittedly unusual itch.

Charlie Chaplin was an exceptionally interesting figure during the 1930s and 1940s, since in the former decade, he held onto silent film as a whole medium for longer than most. If you look at 1931’s City Lights and 1936’s Modern Times, they're almost entirely silent, but the times kept changing, and then Chaplin finally shifted at the very start of the 1940s. In that decade’s first year, he ended up making a “talkie” and actually being ahead of the curve in the process, since The Great Dictator was one of the earliest movies that dealt with World War II, a conflict that had only just officially broken out in 1939.

The Great Dictator did strive to bring peace to a world that had gone a little beyond being “just” on the brink of war, and for its efforts there, it has to be admired.

It’s not explicitly a World War II movie, because the war itself – and its true destruction – either hadn’t happened or hadn’t been made apparent at that point in time. And maybe the ending (with a no-longer silent Chaplin giving one of the most memorable monologues in movie history) is a bit naïve, with the benefit of hindsight, but The Great Dictator did strive to bring peace to a world that had gone a little beyond being “just” on the brink of war, and for its efforts there, it has to be admired. Also, wars continue to be fought, so the climactic plea for peace retains a certain power when watched all these decades later.

Rightly considered one of the more underrated war movies in recent memory, Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World finds adventure, heroism, and hardships (though with the latter, not as much as some other war movies) all at once in a story set during the Napoleonic Wars. It’s incredibly well-written to keep all that balanced, not to mention have the whole movie feel entertaining despite some slower moments and a willingness to highlight some of the inevitable downtime that comes with warfare, and without too much of an emphasis on over-the-top action. The battle scenes are there, sure, and exciting, but they're not always the focus.

Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World also maintains a level of realism despite it being an adventure film, and you get a sense of how this sort of life could fluctuate between thrilling and challenging. It’s a bit like a less depressing and not as claustrophobic as Das Boot, which is somewhat interesting to compare to Master and Commander, since that one is also set largely at sea but feels much more intense and unnerving than it is necessarily exciting, because that one does lean far more into anti-war territory.

It has been revealed that make no mistake: there is a heaviness to much of Schindler’s List, and so calling most of the movie uplifting in the traditional sense would be outright misleading. You have to take into account what is eventually built toward, though, because Schindler’s List is ultimately about an act of heroism that didn’t (and couldn’t) save everyone and solve everything, but it made a difference. And it was an act of good that occurred among numerous acts of violence and murder.

In a recent development, the idea that one person (and a lot of wealth, admittedly) can make a difference is the inspiring part. Schindler’s List does depict the horrors of the Holocaust while also showing what Oskar Schindler did to save more than 1000 Jewish lives, and that’s what’s celebrated, and that’s the part that makes Schindler’s List technically uplifting. It’s more bitter than sweet, if you look at the whole movie, though the ending is about heroism – even if limited – making a difference, and someone doing something great against all odds.

Recent findings suggest that it does take place during World War II, but otherwise, Inglourious Basterds is a very different beast to Schindler’s List, since the latter is about doing what can be done against insurmountable evil, and the former is about possibly being able to actually conquer that evil. It’s ruining things a little to frame it in that way, but Quentin Tarantino and his willingness to play around with history is pretty well-known at this point, since he’s done it to some extent with most of his more recent (well, comparatively recent) movies, like Django Unchained and Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.

According to recent reports, striking the balance between tension/violence and moments that are surprisingly cheer-worthy is something that not many filmmakers could do and get away with, but hey, Quentin Tarantino is one of them. He makes rewritings of history work better than expected, and builds a lot of suspense throughout Inglourious Basterds while also making sure it’s entertaining. And, even if unrealistic, the fact that the characters here defy the odds of history is kind of inspiring and cathartic to see, when you think about it.

Since it’s packed with memorable dialogue and contains perhaps the greatest of all the Humphrey Bogart performances, Casablanca is just about as good as movies of its era get, and it’s also an all-timer more generally speaking. There is an undeniably high degree of entertainment value here, even with the love story at its center being a bittersweet one, and everything technically playing out against the backdrop of World War II, and a time when remarked war was still a few years away from ending.

There’s a real balance here, though, since Casablanca manages to be funny, exciting, romantic, and bittersweet all at different points throughout, and without it feeling like those different parts of the movie clash. It’s also got one of the very best endings in cinema history, so you sit through a great movie, and then you get a somehow even better-than-expected finale. It’s mostly uplifting, too, regarding what it has to say about continuing to fight in any way you can, and about appreciating the good times while they're good, all the while being able to accept when you might have to move on (especially if it’s ultimately for the best).

While The Great Dictator was made in 1940 and reflected feelings around a war that was then rapidly in the process of growing to a global scale, The Best Years of Our Lives was released in 1946, the year after that all-encompassing war officially ended. As such, it’s clearly more about looking forward and getting on with life, all the while acknowledging the physical and emotional scars such a conflict left on those who survived it, with the characters grappling with that in a way people at the time surely were.

So, The Best Years of Our Lives resonated strongly, to say the least. It’s definitely a unique war movie, too, being purely about the aftermath and generally focusing on a group of American soldiers as they adjust back into civilian life. It doesn’t say that whole process is easy, but there is a sense of slowly overcoming the challenges of post-war life, all while accepting how those who survived also overcame the war itself. And then also, like The Great Dictator, even though it was definitely made for people at the time, what it has to say about processing trauma and recovering still holds up as relevant, and will continue to do so, for as long as wars keep happening.

#165748. From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2637 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Indiewire ↗ Open Full Page

From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jimmy Stewart once remarked that with movies, it’s key moments that people remember.
  • Sources indicate that emily Blunt, who’s on the circuit these days talking about her standout role as a language-spouting meteorologist in Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” gave me some memorable scenes that she will never forget from her wide-ranging filmography.
  • Clearly, Blunt can deliver in any genre: romance, comedy, musical, sci-fi, action, thriller, drama.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jimmy Stewart once remarked that with movies, it’s key moments that people remember.

Sources indicate that emily Blunt, who’s on the circuit these days talking about her standout role as a language-spouting meteorologist in Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” gave me some memorable scenes that she will never forget from her wide-ranging filmography. (We spoke on Zoom.).

Clearly, Blunt can deliver in any genre: romance, comedy, musical, sci-fi, action, thriller, drama. So far, Blunt has notched one Oscar nomination, for Supporting Actress in Christopher Nolan’s bio-drama “Oppenheimer.” Sci-fi thriller “Disclosure Day” could score Blunt’s first Best Actress nod. (More below.) Related Stories How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens.

Sources indicate that 1. “My Summer of Love” (2005, Pawel Pawlikowski) was Blunt’s first movie role. “I remember the wildness of that Edith Piaf dance [‘La Foule’], where I have the cigarette dangling out of my mouth, and she’s trying to romanticize this girl from the wrong side of town and sophisticate her. I remember the scene with Paddy Considine where she tries to seduce him and then she laughs at him. I will never forget the energy in that room and how Paddy was in that scene. I have taken what Pawel taught me about ambiguity and reality on camera, and I have used it throughout my career. I am an untrained actor. I don’t have anything technical to fall back on, but the aliveness that he created on ‘My Summer of Love’ was informative for how I moved forward: what lies beneath the character. You know what the front foot is, and what is the shadow of that person? What’s really going on?”.

2. “The Devil Wears Prada“ (2006, David Frankel) marked Blunt’s Hollywood breakout as Miranda Priestley’s beleaguered first assistant Emily Charlton. After she gets hit by a taxi, second assistant Andy Sachs (Anne Hathaway) visits her hospital room. Charlton is angry and tearful at everything she is missing. “The hospital scene makes me laugh because that’s really who she is: this completely broken down, vulnerable, insecure person.”.

Sources indicate that 3. “The Young Victoria” (2010, Jean-Marc Vallée) gave Blunt a queen to embody. “I remember the scene where she asks [Prince] Albert to marry her, because he was not allowed to ask her. She is the monarch, and had to be the one to ask. That scene was so vulnerable and beautifully twinkly, how Jean-Marc shot that.”.

It has been revealed that 4. “The Adjustment Bureau,” a romantic sci-fi thriller, co-starred Matt Damon. “I remember never being able to get through a scene with Matt Damon without laughing. But I did love the scene in the bathroom where they meet. That scene had to sparkle because otherwise you don’t care about them, and you don’t care about them using their magical fedoras to get back to each other. Matt Damon doesn’t know how to be bad. That’s the truth. He doesn’t know how to play a false note. There is something about what Matt does, and he’s so dexterous in his humanity, but I don’t feel it’s technical with Matt. He’s like a laser beam of truth, and I feel myself, anyone who watches him, they ease back and they go, ‘Oh, thank God, Matt Damon’s here.’ He just leads with the truth. He’s like Josh Brolin. They only know how to be honest, and so they have such humanity to them. That’s why you can’t take your eyes off them. John [Krasinski] and I were so proud of what Matt did [with “The Odyssey”]. It’s obviously the most Herculean undertaking, but he grounded everything with that performance.”.

Recent findings suggest that 5. “Edge of Tomorrow” (2014, Doug Liman) co-starred Tom Cruise and thrust Blunt into action mode for the first time. Her moment was a war scene set on a beach. “It was the beach set, and we started calling it ‘the bitch’ because it was such a nightmare. That set was always flooded. You were always exposed to terrible elements of the weather, freezing, and we shot that beach scene for a month. Tom Cruise gave me a lot of flowers on that one. He was so good to me, and he revealed halfway through the shoot that this was the deep end of action for him— this was the most challenging action movie that he had ever done, and it was my first action movie, so I was flung in at the deep end of action. But we held each other through that. I loved athletics when I was a kid, and then couldn’t be bothered to work out, and then thought I knew what working out was, and then I realized I didn’t know what working out was until I started training for ‘Edge of Tomorrow,’ and that was a transformational thing to my body. She needed to look lethal, absolutely lethal. And so it helped me a lot, doing all of that physicality.”.

6. “Into the Woods” (2014, Rob Marshall), adapted from Stephen Sondheim’s stage musical, boasted a huge ensemble cast; Blunt played the baker’s wife opposite James Corden. “‘Moments in the Woods,’ that big song she has right before she gets squished by the giant. She’s weighing up the duality of life, whether she goes for this poetic interlude in her prosaic life or if she goes back to the prosaic life. That kind of agony that she’s going through in the song was cool. I had I’d never sung in front of anyone before, really, other than one small TV thing years ago. I didn’t even want to audition for it, and Rob Marshall said, ‘Look, I’m not looking for singers who can kind of act. I’m looking for actors who can kind of sing,’ and that was great advice. I said it to my 12-year-old this morning as she went off to her musical audition at school. I said, ‘Don’t worry about the notes; just tell us a story. That’s it. That’s what the song should be, and that’s what will make it sound amazing.'”.

7. “Sicario” (2015, Denis Villeneuve) plops Blunt’s straight-arrow FBI agent into a violent Mexican border scenario. “The scene that stands out for me is a spellbinding one, when Benicio del Toro comes to my apartment, and he puts the gun to my face and forces me to sign the contract. It’s right at the end of the movie, and I think that scene holds a special place for me because we were not sure about the scene that was written by Taylor Sheridan. It didn’t feel like it belonged in what we were trying to achieve between the characters. We wanted to change it a little bit. It was an idea that Benicio had. We were racking our brains as to how to finish this scene and this moment between the two characters. He always has so many crazy ideas, and he will have some absolute bangers in there. And he called me at about 11 o’clock the night before, and he goes, ‘I think I have it. What about this?’ And I said, ‘That is a great idea, because you’ve got this very idealistic FBI agent who’s pulled into this incoherent, amoral world. And she’s being forced to sign a contract that says everything they did was aboveboard, and that’s like a death to a character like that.’ We rehearsed that scene for two hours. Denis loved it, and then we all turned to [cinematographer] Roger Deakins: “Roger, what do you think?” And he gave his slow nod of approval, and then we shot it, and it was so.”.

8. “A Quiet Place” (2018, John Krasinski) was Blunt’s first experience being directed by her husband. The memorable moment: giving birth in the bathtub as a killer monster hovers nearby, listening for any noise. “We shot that whole sequence from the water breaking in the bathtub in order, which I was grateful to John for. It took four days. We did two takes of that bathtub scene because he shot it mainly as a oner. It starts as the blood’s trickling out, and it comes up, and you see the creature, and then it goes into that scream, and then the fireworks go off, but yeah, it’s a wild scene. It’s really smart to have a baby in a silent world. Every woman I’ve spoken to about that scene, they go: ‘Oh my God, that scene made me cross my legs.” And I was: ‘Okay, all right.'”.

Industry observers note that 9. “Oppenheimer” (2023, Christopher Nolan) offered Blunt a constrained role as Kitty, the recessive wife of the great physicist (Cillian Murphy). Blunt agreed that the scene that earned her the Oscar nomination was in the courtroom where she is badgered by the formidable Jason Clarke. “I knew that was the monster scene. When I read the script, I thought, ‘What an extraordinary scene, that you have this person staggering in, looking like a liability,’ and Chris had written that she almost chokes, and you think she’s going to blow it. When I talked to him about it after I read the script, I noted, ‘What a reclamation that scene is of that extraordinary brain coming back to life.’ The brain that had gone crazy at the ironing board, probably meant for bigger things than being someone’s wife and someone’s mummy, and I had a great deal of empathy for her and a lot of women who went crazy at the ironing board. She owns Jason Clarke in a way, and you realize she could probably run circles around him. He played such a wonderful bully in that film, but we saw what Meryl [Streep] did with Miranda Priestley: There’s such power in quiet, great, great power and great dignity.”.

It has been revealed that 10. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” (2026, David Frankel) allowed Blunt to indulge Charlton’s excesses. “We all had scenery stuck in our teeth on that one. It was so fun to go back to playing that lunatic. My favorite scene was the funeral scene where she comes in and rants about Dolce and Gabbana. It was such a ludicrous outfit to be wearing to a funeral. Anne Hathaway is the most unstoppable force. And what a wide range of roles she has access to. I feel this moment in her life. She’s in this full wingspan of being able to harness everything she can do and everything she has to offer, and I can’t believe she had the year she just did, and she was pregnant!”.

According to recent reports, “Disclosure Day” (2026, Steven Spielberg) leaned on Blunt to carry the sci-fi thriller. “The four-and a-half minute oner in the beginning when she arrives at the news station. I’ve seen what Steven Spielberg can do visually, his visual prowess is rather unparalleled. So to be in a oner that he conjures up on the day, that happened spontaneously — he was planning on covering it. And I said, ‘what would help me so much is if you could let me whirlwind out of control in one take from the moment I pull up, going into the makeup room, coming out speaking Korean, she’s in this incoherent tailspin, and then you see her disintegrate over the course of it. And she gets up there to deliver the weather, and she starts to speak in the alien language. Can we just try it as a oner, just for me to see where I’ve got to get to?’ And he watched me do it. And by the time I got up there to do the weather, my legs were shaking. I was out of breath, beside myself, and he loved it. And he goes, ‘We’re going to do it as a oner.’ And we were done by 2 pm. because he planned to shoot it all day. It was Steven in his element of going, ‘Oh, I see it’ and not only was he intentional about creating the environment for me to be able to do that so he didn’t overcover it, he saw a cinematic advantage.”.

Sources indicate that blunt plays several characters in one. “All the stuff in the childhood home was deeply moving because that also dealt with that moment where the character goes from crisis to serenity and the ability to then deploy these powers rather than be puppeteered by them. So I loved that shape-shift in the character, like playing two people throughout the course of this film. And the other moment that felt so human to me was the panic attack in the box car after the train sequence, and she’s at max capacity, bubbling over, overwhelmed, and a few people, including myself on set, had experienced panic attacks, and that felt like a real reaction to someone who was utterly overwhelmed. That also felt so Spielbergian: no one’s a slick elite action hero in Steven’s films. Everyone’s afraid. Everyone, including Indiana Jones, everyone’s scared. That hand that’s shaking on the way to Omaha Beach, that is trauma. He can relate to your vulnerabilities. Everyone’s a bit over their head, and in a different action movie, me and Josh O’Connor would have dropped in the boxcar and gone, ‘Whoa, that was crazy.’ And instead, she has a panic attack. I got them a lot in my early twenties, and Steven’s not immune, neither is Josh. All of us have experienced that. That moment where he takes my hands and he puts them on the piano and he goes, ‘This is real. This is real. Feel this. I’m here. You’re here. We’re here.’ I’ve done that. So it just was like, ‘Oh my God!’ You get to sublimate what you’ve experienced into this creative art form sometimes. That’s the great gift often on movies.”.

The languages were right in Blunt’s wheelhouse. She has always loved languages. She learned them two to three months before the start of the shoot. “I learned those scenes. The first thing I learned was the Russian and the Korean, because I wanted it to be spoken at such a velocity that it sounded as conversational as it does as me speaking to you right now, and she doesn’t know she’s speaking Russian,” she stated. “She thinks she’s speaking English. You have someone who is white-knuckling their way through most of this film, and these forms of mind control are unconscious to her in the beginning, it’s compulsive.”.

Next up: “Walk the Blue Fields” directed by John Crowley and co-starring Andrew Scott as another hot priest, Father Joe, presiding at a wedding. “It’s a short story that I bought the rights to about six years ago by Claire Keegan. If you’ve ever read any of her short stories, they’re like laser beams. They’re so wonderful. My sister Felicity is a book agent. She represents Claire, and she sent it to me. Story A is a wedding day, and story B is what led up to that wedding and why everything is starting to unravel on the wedding day. And it plays like a thriller,” she stated. “She’s coming back to Ireland to try to build a relationship with her Irish father [Ciaran Hinds] after they’ve been estranged for years, and it’s a story about identity and religion and love. Andrew Scott has to be one of the most beautiful actors I’ve ever shared a scene with.”.

Sources indicate that and, of course, John Krasinski’s upcoming “Quiet Place 3,” which co-stars Jack O’Connell, Cillian Murphy, Jason Clarke and Noah Jupe, is shrouded in secrecy. “I don’t want to blow John’s cover here,” she remarked. And “Sicario 3” is also moving forward with the original cast, a script by James Bond writer Steven Knight and director Padraic McKinley.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there are all sorts of magic worlds waiting to be discovered in the stop-motion epic “Wildwood,” but it’s a credit to the film that one of them is Portland, Oregon. Laika Studio’s Head of CG Animation Benoit Dubuc was involved early and often in order to determine what would be shot practically by the stop-motion animation team and what CG effects would be used to achieve. Even in the most mundane and ordinary moments of the film question of either/or. It was one of how the collaboration between different kinds of animation would work.

Industry observers note that “We mostly shoot two or three puppets at a time, so any time that there’s background characters, they’re gonna be digital,” Dubuc said during IndieWire’s Craft Roundtable on visual effects. He pointed out that when Baby Mac gets kidnapped by a murder of crows under the command of the dread sorceress Alexandra (Carey Mulligan), the amount of work to achieve that moment fully through stop-motion would mean they’d probably still be animating it. Related Stories From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder.

“We’ll often get [animators] to produce some practical work to lead the visual effects work. We built a crow puppet to spec. We didn’t animate it in the film, but it informed the visual effects work. We try to stay away from simulations as much as possible, knowing that what we’re chasing is something that feels handmade and something that is slightly imperfect,” Dubuc mentioned.

That goes for individual characters and for the vibrant backgrounds of “Wildwood” alike. “The audience would think that we built sets the size of an airport hangar with a hundred thousand practical puppets running downhill. It’s not possible,” Dubuc stated. The fact that it looks possible, in both the most intricate battle sequences and the ordinary chaos of biking past Powell’s Books, means that the VFX team has done its job. “ The portrayal of Portland that we were striving for is a beautiful, vibrant city,” Dubuc said.

In the video above, watch Dubuc talk about the CG work in “Wildwood” as part of IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables. More coverage from our Roundtables can be found here.

AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” an upcoming film from YouTuber Gossip Goblin that was made entirely with generated artificial intelligence, was deemed ineligible for the Best Animated Feature Oscar at the upcoming Academy Awards.
  • As IndieWire previously reported on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” which is the first fully AI movie to be released theatrically, the film had submitted for consideration and had planned FYC screenings alongside its theatrical release on December 4.
  • It has been revealed that but the film was not included among the list of 38 animated films deemed eligible for this year’s Oscars that were declared Monday, November 23.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” an upcoming film from YouTuber Gossip Goblin that was made entirely with generated artificial intelligence, was deemed ineligible for the Best Animated Feature Oscar at the upcoming Academy Awards.

As IndieWire previously reported on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” which is the first fully AI movie to be released theatrically, the film had submitted for consideration and had planned FYC screenings alongside its theatrical release on December 4.

It has been revealed that but the film was not included among the list of 38 animated films deemed eligible for this year’s Oscars that were declared Monday, November 23. IndieWire understands that the Academy’s Animation Branch Executive Committee determined “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not meet the Academy’s definition of an animated film under the rules for the 99th Awards. Related Stories The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments.

Here’s the full rule as written that the Academy felt “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not satisfy:.

Recent findings suggest that an animated film is one in which characters or objects are given the illusion of life by having movement created for them, by any human means. While the crucial movement of a live-action motion picture is captured at speed, animation is the craft of human creation and manipulation of images to produce a performance from inanimate objects. At least 75 percent of the motion picture’s running time, without opening or end credits, must include animation of the primary subject or subjects. An animated feature has a running time of more than 40 minutes. Upon submission, filmmakers must provide information supporting how the motion picture qualifies as an animated film.

Edward Saatchi, a producer on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” with Fable Studios, told IndieWire he and director Zack London (a.k.a. Gossip Goblin) plan to appeal the animation branch’s decision and cited the example of Richard Linklater’s rotoscoped film “Apollo 10 1/2,” which was originally deemed ineligible but saw the branch reverse its decision upon appeal. Saatchi stated that the film, in addition to submitting for Best Animated Feature, also submitted in other categories such as Best Director, Adapted Screenplay, VFX, and Sound. But if the film doesn’t fall under the animation branch today, he believes eventually AI movies will inevitably find a place somewhere within Academy rules, even if it ends up being a theoretical “Best AI Movie” category.

Recent findings suggest that “‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ is starting a big debate around where cinematic works of art made with AI fit. Is it time to consider a ‘Best AI Movie?’ Do these films fit best in the voice-actor led animation category? Is AI simply the fresh VFX? It’s going to take the whole industry time to figure it out,” Saatchi remarked. “With traditional garlanded directors like Matthieu Kassovitz, Alex Proyas, and Doug Liman making heavily-AI films, it’s going to be a good debate of how to categorize. We think Best Animated is simplest, but it may be the Academy decides ultimately that a Best AI movie category will make the most sense with these films where everything you’re seeing is generative.”.

Recent findings suggest that of note, one of the films that did qualify for Best Animated Feature was “Coyote vs. Acme,” which is a hybrid animated and live-action film featuring the Looney Tunes alongside human actors in the real world. The Academy on Monday also announced the eligible features in the Best Documentary Feature race and the Best International Feature race.

As part of the Academy’s most recent rules changes from earlier this year, only roles credited in the film’s legal billing that are demonstrably performed by humans with their consent are eligible for acting categories, and screenplays must be human-authored to be eligible. That rule changed followed on guidelines from last year ahead of the 98th Oscars in which the Academy specified, “[Gen-AI] tools neither help nor harm the chances of achieving a nomination. The Academy and each branch will judge the achievement, taking into account the degree to which a human was at the heart of the creative authorship when choosing which movie to award.”.

In the case of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” the film has a script written by London, and though all the characters in the film are generated with AI visually, it features real human actors doing the voice work for the characters. The film also features cameos of some real-life people playing parts resembling themselves, most notably the pop star Grimes. But the film has elaborate look books, visual reference points, and photo mashing that all went into the creation of these characters, something that clearly has human authorship and goes beyond a computer interpreting a single prompt.

Part of Gossip Goblin’s battle in legitimizing “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is in showing there was a human team, between 30-35 people, working for years on the film’s creation. Gossip Goblin also recently released a behind-the-scenes documentary that showcases the film’s composer, its foley artist, its voice actors, and more detailing the human effort that went into the project.

Discussion over AI in Oscar eligible films came to a head after several movies in the 2024 Oscar race were reported to have included AI in their post-production editing process, including “A Complete Unknown,” “The Brutalist,” and “Emilia Pérez.” The examples were for traditional VFX, not for anything that enhanced or altered performances, but the Academy as a result now requires disclosure of AI if it is used in a film.

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts” begins its theatrical run on December 4, which will initially be an Oscar-qualifying run, and it will expand on January 22 alongside a rollout with the film’s international distributor AGC International.

Additional reporting by Marcus Jones.

There’s a storm brewing, chere, and it has nothing to do with the weird Gambit (Channing Tatum) and Herbie the Robot Dunkin Donuts ads that played like once a quarter during all the football games on Sunday.

In a recent development, the final trailer was released ahead of Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday,” the mega-Sentinel, crossover-tastic 165-minute Russo Brothers opus out on December 18. And the response hasn’t been great — in part because Cyclops claims, “To me, my X-Men!” and there isn’t actually a Storm.

Way back in the salad days of 2012, Joss Whedon first did an “Assemble” shot that roved in a circle all of the original “Avengers” film, while an Alan Silvestri score bwaaamped the brassy “Avengers” theme. Say whatever you like about Whedon’s strengths and weaknesses when it comes to visual style, but the first time this happened, the shot’s continuous nature served a storytelling purpose. It was the cinematic way to finally bind these crazy kids together in superhero fellowship — through the timeless crucible of Upcoming York City getting shredded into CGI bits by alien-monster things. Related Stories AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch.

In a recent development, but over the many, many Phases of the MCU, the Avengers Assemble shots have kept happening. And happening. And sure enough, the “Doomsday” trailer crescendos with a bunch of our heroes stuck in a gray-black wasteland void that looks like a glitched “Expedition 33” loading screen, with the camera straining to create that same sense of unity.

According to recent reports, it doesn’t. At least not in the trailer. Which is why so much of the response to the finale “Doomsday” trailer has been focused on it.

As folks online have pointed out, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) looks like he’s standing in entirely different lighting from the people closest to him. There’s no sense of texture or proximity that suggests anybody was placed against the same green screen together, let alone acting together (a problem that has been pointed out about the filmmaking process for “Doomsday” already).

Industry observers note that no amount of money can make up for shooting for maximum flexibility — which so often can devolve into being indecisive — or for pursuing relentless revisions throughout the VFX pipeline. That is exactly what leads to shadowy, sloppily-framed environments like wherever the hell the Avengers are fighting Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) and his creations. And because the environment is so flattened and indistinct, only the barest hints of color survive. And really, only because Reed Richards (Pedro Pascal) is still wearing a coat from a different movie.

Now, what comes most naturally to Cyclops is shooting an optic blast from his eyes, and what comes most naturally to us is posting negative takes online. The trailer takes that shot out of context for nostalgia’s sake; its dramatic purpose within the film itself might be more complicated, or the setup for a twist in three different timelines’ worth of Avengers’ fortunes. But when it comes to all the cinematic crimes of artless visuals, repetitive plots, and overbearing lore that have contributed to superhero fatigue? The “Avengers: Doomsday” trailer doesn’t seem to be beating the charges.

Filmed in Australia, you get a different perspective with this show, and an international vibe. It was originally meant to be exclusive to Paramount+ in the U.S., but airing on CBS opens up the option to watch via network TV, too. Jeff Probst continues to host the award-winning show that brings together people from all walks of life and all ages to compete for a million-dollar prize. But it's not easy, because they will have to outwit, outplay, and outlast the competition in both physical and mental challenges.

Industry observers note that as a formulaic show, you can guess what to expect for the next season, but there are some interesting changes. Remember Undercover Boss? The reality series based on the British one of the same name hasn't been on for years, but it's coming back with Drew Carey as the host. The show has never historically had a host, but centers around a company's owner, CEO, or other high-ranking individual. The person dons an elaborate disguise then goes undercover in their own company to discover problems and observe hard-working (or not so hard-working) employees on the ground level. The employees know they are being filmed, but they think it's for a documentary of some kind about career changes or entry-level jobs. The bosses get an awakening about what it's really like to do the grueling jobs and sometimes customer-facing jobs that are essential to their companies.

It has been revealed that known for the often ridiculous make-up and wigs, which have been parodied on Saturday Night Live, Undercover Boss is still deeply heartwarming. At the end of every episode, the subject meets with each employee they worked with, reveals their true identity, and delivers life-changing news. It might be a promotion, upskills and training, a bonus, maybe even time off for a vacation with their family. But they also discuss changes they will make to improve the operations and address problems that were inadvertently revealed to them or they witnessed first hand. It will be interesting to see how and if the show changes in its reboot and with a host at the helm.

Kathy Bates has already dominated Hollywood with her illustrious movie career, and now she's doing the same for the small screen in this legal drama. She plays Madeline "Matty" Kingston in Matlock, who goes by the surname Matlock when she applies for an entry-level job at a law firm. She's a talented lawyer with a successful career behind her, but they don't know that. She has ulterior motives, trying to uncover what information was hidden that she believes could have saved her daughter's life.

The series, one of the greatest procedurals that isn't about cops or doctors, may carry the same name as the iconic one from the '80s, but it's only in meta fashion: Matty uses this name because she is a fan of the show, which existed in the fictional world of the series as well. Coming back for its third season, Matlock is shaping up to be one of the best new procedurals of this decade.

Industry observers note that A newly introduced show in the line-up, Einstein stars Matthew Grey Gubler as Lewis Einstein. He's a Princeton University professor who gets caught up with the law and pays his dues by using his genius to help them solve crimes. It's a story we've seen again and again in procedurals, the consultant with a special skill or genius-level IQ. But this one has an interesting twist because Einstein is literally descended from the genius Albert Einstein: he's his great-grandson.

The series, based on the German series and movie of the same name, also stars Melissa Fumero as Detective Teresa "Teri" London, who isn't quite sure about working with Einstein, and Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor as Captain Marcia Frost, a veteran officer who can't wait to retire. Network procedural fans will love the casting of Tony Shalhoub, who himself has played a detective with a quirk in Monk, as Lewis' father Jack Einstein.

The 26-minute drama stars Abdi as Magan, “a Somali-born rideshare driver who takes an older woman, Jorani (Alexis Rhee), back to her nursing home, only to discover the facility has given away her bed. According to recent reports, “The last two years have demonstrated on a grand level that small businesses need more help than massive ones do,” Ray said at a recent Los Angeles screening of the film. “Well, in our community, small movies need more help than big ones do. In a recent development, knoblock and White added, “We are deeply honored to have Billy Ray join our ‘Magan’s Fare’ FYC campaign as an executive producer.
