💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the arrival of GTA VI on the scene has been just as significant as most people were expecting it to be, blowing past all sorts of records in its first few days.
  • In a recent development, at the same time, the game is now in the hands of over 40 million players, a total that very few titles manage to achieve in their entire lifespans, let alone in less than a week.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the arrival of GTA VI on the scene has been just as significant as most people were expecting it to be, blowing past all sorts of records in its first few days. It generated more than $3 billion dollars on its first day out in the wild, making it comfortably the biggest media release of all time in any medium, and that number has only gone up significantly since.

In a recent development, at the same time, the game is now in the hands of over 40 million players, a total that very few titles manage to achieve in their entire lifespans, let alone in less than a week. Reviews were also extraordinarily high, and it currently sits as the highest rated game on Metacritic in terms of professional appraisals.

With all of that success, PlayStation still serves as the official partner platform for the game, and Sony are hard at work trying to differentiate their offering from the competition to make that partnership more than a simple title. Now, the latest of those steps has gone live via an update, and it allows consumers to get involved in the fun in more ways than ever.

In a recent development, as first reported by PushSquare, GTA VI has now been updated to support PS Plus Premium cloud streaming directly to the PS5 and PS Portal. That noted, the game has not been added to the PS Plus catalog more generally, and you will still need to have an owned copy of the game in your library to take advantage of the upcoming update.

According to recent reports, streaming directly to the PlayStation Portal is undoubtedly a big deal, and taking the game to other rooms or away from the main television (when others want to use it) is going to be a major quality-of-life improvement for those who are locked in to completing it. There also isn't a limit to how long you can stream for as a Premium member, so you should be able to explore Vice City to your heart's content.

Xbox fans don't need to be too upset, though, as the game is also available to stream for those with access to an owned copy of GTA VI and an active Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscription. Those in charge of proceedings did recently change the terms of service for game streaming, so players have a maximum of 15 hours available per month. More can be bought ad-hoc, though it will generally be a cheaper and better idea to play it in the traditional manner.

It has been revealed that one advantage that Xbox players do have is that, despite the PlayStation being Rockstar's console of choice for the game, it currently seems to be performing best on Xbox Series X. The frame rate drops are notably lower, and though the Series X and Pro maintain 30 FPS relatively well, the lows are still marginally better on Microsoft's hardware.

As for GTA VI players, they're continuing to explore the enormously detailed world that Rockstar has created, and there are likely hundreds of hours of things to do before all is noted and done. That will then leave the Online modes as the next port of call, and who knows what kind of chaos that will bring.

Many of the best phones and best laptops often claim to reach speedy charging levels — like how my Motorola Razr Fold is advertised to have 80W charging — so the screen on the charger shows the exact real-time wattage going through each of its three USB-C ports. Ultimately, it’s the peace of mind of knowing it can charge all the gadgets I carry on me that wins me over — including my laptop. Depending on which one I decide to bring on a given day, smaller travel chargers often struggle to keep up, but thanks to its 100W charging output, the PicoGo Pro easily handles power-hungry laptops like a MacBook Pro or Googlebook alongside my iPhone 18 Pro and camera. At its $59 regular price, it’s already a solid upgrade — but a discount that brings it down to $41 for Black Friday is a no-brainer if you want to lighten your load.

According to recent reports, perhaps my favorite upgrade? The art library has expanded from a few hundred to over 1,000 complimentary choices.

So if you, like me, would rather have art than a giant blank screen as your living room centerpiece, this is the Black Friday TV deal worth considering.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harry Potter fans are counting down the days for HBO's highly anticipated upcoming adaptation, which will finally bring back the iconic fantasy story after more than a decade since the original film series concluded. It's difficult to overstate the cultural impact of J.K. Rowling's original novels, which have sold hundreds of millions of copies worldwide since the publication of Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone in 1997.

For nearly 30 years, generations of readers have grown up alongside Harry, Ron, and Hermione, with the books inspiring countless young readers to fall in love with fantasy literature. While there's plenty to look forward to with HBO's upcoming adaptation, there's also something special about discovering an entirely new magical world for the first time.

Anyone looking to recapture that feeling of reading Harry Potter for the first time will want to keep an eye out for an exciting new fantasy adventure from author Thomas Taylor.

Recent findings suggest that thomas Taylor's The Lantern and the Labyrinth is slated for release on April 8, 2027, through Penguin Random House's Puffin imprint in the UK. The 400-page novel marks the beginning of an entirely new fantasy series titled The Faerwell Lantern, with hardcover, ebook, and audiobook editions already listed for pre-order.

According to the official book description, Taylor's upcoming novel explores "magic, courage and the boundless possibilities of the imagination." The story follows a young protagonist named Tom who inadvertently discovers the boundary separating the ordinary world from Faery, a magical realm inhabited by supernatural creatures.

[The Lantern and the Labyrinth is] a dangerous magical world full of trolls, ghosts, dragons, and things from the darkest corners of the imagination.

Tom becomes an apprentice to a mysterious organization known as the Esotericals, whose intentions are called into question after he befriends a young witch named Persistence and her magical companion, Mortimer. Meanwhile, a terrifying entity known as the Smothering Dark threatens both worlds. The publisher describes the adventure as "rich, epic, immersive and exciting.".

Taylor has also confirmed that the novel is part of a three-book publishing deal with Puffin Press, revealing in his May 2026 newsletter that he was already editing the sequel, tentatively titled The Book of Everafter.

According to recent reports, taylor is perhaps best known for his award-winning Eerie-on-Sea series, which debuted in 2019 with Malamander and spanned five novels, concluding with Mermedusa in 2023. The series has enjoyed considerable international success, selling over half a million copies worldwide and being translated into 20 languages. Taylor has also written and illustrated numerous children's picture books and provided illustrations for Marcus Sedgwick's graphic novel Scarlett Hart: Monster Hunter.

In a recent development, interestingly, Taylor actually has a significant connection to the Harry Potter franchise itself. His very first professional illustration commission after graduating from art school was the now-iconic cover artwork for the original British edition of Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone in 1997.

According to recent reports, nearly three decades later, the artist responsible for many readers' very first visual glimpse of Harry Potter is embarking on an ambitious upcoming magical adventure of his own. With HBO's adaptation set to introduce another generation to the Wizarding World, 2027 is shaping up to be an exciting year for fantasy fans, and The Lantern and the Labyrinth is certainly worth keeping on your radar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that over the last two years, AI greed has been largely to blame for rising prices across the tech world, from video game consoles to phones and laptops. It may have just claimed another victim, like Jason slowly tromping through Camp Crystal Lake.

A new report from the Korean publication ETNews claims that Samsung will be shifting from an annual release of its Galaxy Watch lineup to a biennial cycle. By skipping 2027, the Galaxy Watch 10 would be the first one to not be released annually since Samsung debuted its first Galaxy smartwatch in 2018.

Industry observers note that now, as ETNews points out, "chipflation" is only partially to blame for this potential shift. However, it's certainly a major portion of it.

Sources indicate that samsung's Mobile eXperience (MX) division, responsible for the tech giant's smartphones, wearables, and more, has posted for profit losses for two quarters. The whole division is going through some major restructuring. That starts with Won-Joon Choi who was just announced as the new head of MX, less than four days ago.

Choi was previously the division's COO and led the debuts of the S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8 series.

Tom's Guide reached out to Samsung for confirmation but did not receive a response in time for publication. We will patch this article if the company responds.

The decision to delay the next Galaxy Watch is part of an aggressive push to make Samsung's mobile division more profitable. Part of that is streamlining the organization's product lineup.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The increased prices of RAM and other key components have severely cut into Samsung's costs. Much of it is driven by Samsung's own chip fabrication division, which has fed into the AI chip frenzy.

Sources indicate that already, the firm is reportedly cutting smartphone shipments by 30% with a focus on high-end models. A focus on premium, high-end models isn't latest; other companies like Lenovo have already pursued it this year.

But also, the Galaxy Watch 9, a perfectly solid smartwatch, didn't move the needle when it debuted this summer. Plus, it suffered from a price hike as well. We praised the health insights that Samsung hasn't paywalled, unlike rivals, but at the end of the day its a more expensive Galaxy Watch 8. We didn't even include it in our picks for best smartwatch, a rarity for Samsung's usually excellent wearable.

“As hardware innovation has reached a mature stage, the company appears to have concluded that releasing new products every year is no longer cost-effective," industry insiders told ETNews.

According to ETNews, the gap year could be filled in by fresh software updates and enhancements to existing health tracking features.

Also, Samsung may release its own Galaxy Fit model à la the recently released Google Fitbit Edge and Fitbit Air. Samsung has had versions, but nothing new has really hit in the last three years. Though at the beginning of November, a new fitness track was leaked as potential rival to the Fitbit Edge.

Perhaps, RAMageddon aside, this should be the model. In recent years, excitement for new phones, watches, and other annual tech hasn't really hit because, like EA Sports' ongoing Madden franchise, these iterative updates typically don't really justify the cost of upgrading.

Besides, Samsung already does this with the "Classic" model and the newer Galaxy Watch Ultra high-end watch, both of which are on two year cycles.

A year or more of development time could finally bring about true innovation and change.

Tech Report: This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos.
  • In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity.
  • Sources indicate that to buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first revealed. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

Sources indicate that to buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you noted) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.).

All the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.).

Recent findings suggest that there’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can proposal them better next time.

It has been revealed that you’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

According to recent reports, but this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.).

Industry observers note that the Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

Recent findings suggest that I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I noted it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

#165715. Gemini Notebook's Newly introduced Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

Gemini Notebook's Newly introduced Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses.
  • Recent findings suggest that that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code.
  • According to recent reports, website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all owners, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something upcoming. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

Recent findings suggest that that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

According to recent reports, website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all owners, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app. You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

Recent findings suggest that to make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

According to recent reports, with a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but notes you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection.".

The finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a latest window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

Sources indicate that for something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

In a recent development, maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a significant family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

In a recent development, it looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

The 7 Greatest Movie Masterpieces Over 3 Hours, Ranked

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1494 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that three hours.
  • Industry observers note that to be crystal clear, the movies on this list must truly surpass three hours in length.
  • Industry observers note that when people think of Lawrence of Arabia, they tend to envision the spectacular sweeping shots of the desert.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that three hours. 180 minutes. 10,800 seconds. Imagine every one of them being perfect. There is nothing in cinema quite like a truly great epic. The perfect marriage of narrative might, filmmaking craft, and creative ambition commands the screen, compels the audience, and applies the monumental runtime to extracting thematic depth and conjuring awe-inspiring scale.

Industry observers note that to be crystal clear, the movies on this list must truly surpass three hours in length. As great as they are, The Godfather (175 minutes), Patton (172 minutes), and even the first two The Lord of the Rings movies (178 and 179 minutes respectively) have not been considered for this list, nor have extended editions or director’s cuts. Even with such omissions, the best movies that do cross the 180-minute mark encompass cinematic artistry and grandiosity at their most earnest, standing at the pinnacle of the form, for all 10,800+ seconds of their runtime.

Industry observers note that when people think of Lawrence of Arabia, they tend to envision the spectacular sweeping shots of the desert. David Lean’s descent into the harsh landscape is as gorgeous as it is grueling, with cinematographer Freddie Young capturing a sense of man’s smallness amid an enormous backdrop of sand dunes and blue skies. However, Lawrence of Arabia isn’t just a procession of pretty pictures; it is a profound character study that thrives off the back of Peter O’Toole’s performance and Lean’s endeavor to make every second of the 226-minute runtime count.

The biographical epic follows T. E. Lawrence, a lieutenant in the British Army tasked with uniting the feuding Arab tribes to fight as one force against the Turks as WWI rages on. However, as Lawrence befriends the Arabs, the movie shifts away from being a traditional war epic and becomes an enticing, morally complex exploration of hubris, duty, loyalty, and individualism. Ego, eccentricity, and emotional turmoil play as much a part in Lawrence’s journey as his far-famed tactical nous and military exploits. It culminates in one of Hollywood’s most quintessential achievements, an ageless icon of cinematic majesty.

It has been revealed that it may seem disingenuous to put an entire trilogy in one spot, but the criminally underrated The Human Condition is a masterpiece of international cinema that never dips in quality. Each of the three films is three hours long in its own right. Watching the full story from beginning to end takes 579 minutes (just over nine-and-a-half hours), but it is worth every second of the commitment as it delivers one of the most emotionally raw and powerful anti-war tales ever put to screen.

It is a towering tale of idealism and humanity clashing with the machine-like brutality of totalitarianism. The saga follows a conscientious objector from Japan as he is embroiled in WWII, with everything from POW camps to the front lines of the Pacific Theater corroding his resolve and his philosophical convictions. It’s a tragic odyssey of morality in the face of compliance and destruction, one steeped in a very real sense of disillusionment courtesy of director Masaki Kobayashi and star Tatsuya Nakadai’s own wartime emotions.

Recent findings suggest that breathtaking from its opening frame to its last, Barry Lyndon is revered as being one of the most picturesque and painterly movies ever made. Stanley Kubrick’s visionary brilliance and cinematographer John Alcott’s expertise combine to realize an astonishing creative vision that seeks to imitate 18th-century art with natural lighting and ravishing production design. The result is defining of cinematic majesty, and yet there is so much more to the 1975 historical epic than just its lauded visual display.

Industry observers note that it is a satirical meditation on status that undercuts the idea of elitism with Redmond Barry’s (Ryan O’Neal) unabashed opportunism. The Irish rogue climbs the social ladder any way he can; he longs to be a "gentleman" and doesn't care how much he has to steal, cheat, and fight to achieve it. The realization of this pendulum of prosperity is patient, to be sure, but the meticulous pacing is imbued with a sense of gravitas. It makes Barry Lyndon ceaselessly hypnotic across its 185-minute runtime. It is arguably even more compelling today given its cynical dissection of class structure and the ageless beauty of its technical artistry.

Industry observers note that A frightfully devastating deep-dive into the horrors of the Holocaust, Schindler’s List is understandably viewed by many as being a quintessential cinematic masterpiece that they will only watch once. It dramatizes the heroics of Oskar Schindler (Liam Neeson), a charismatic Nazi Party member who uses his influence to recruit prisoners in the concentration camps as workers in his factories. Under the guise of maintaining productivity, Schindler negotiates to ensure his workers remain unharmed, thus saving hundreds of innocent lives.

It has been revealed that schindler’s cunning and courage are hallmarks of the film, but so much of its dramatic urgency comes from the succinct brutality with which it depicts violence, inhumanity, and death in the camps. It is a display of piercing, soul-shaking power, and it is perhaps the single greatest testament to Steven Spielberg’s genius as a filmmaker, a harrowing achievement that uses everything from John Williams’ haunting score to subtle glimpses of color amid the black-and-white cinematography to enrapture viewers in its terrible potency.

According to recent reports, were the extended editions to be considered for this list, The Lord of the Rings as a trilogy could easily have featured, and very high up. As it stands, however, The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King was the only movie of the three to release in cinemas with a runtime surpassing three hours (201 minutes to be exact). It marks the climactic triumph of Peter Jackson’s stunning adaptation of J. R. R. Tolkien’s famous fantasy novels, and it follows Frodo Baggins (Elijah Wood) completing his perilous journey to Mount Doom while the other members of the Fellowship prepare to meet Mordor’s forces in battle.

In a recent development, every single aspect of production is handled with astute mastery. The practical filmmaking and digital effects work wonderfully in tandem. The acting is faultless across the board. The set design and production value are still astonishing today. And Howard Shore’s score imbues every major sequence with the rousing triumph and tender humanity it requires. Peter Jackson delivers one of the most engrossing epic movies of all time, arguably the defining masterpiece of fantasy cinema. In both its own right and as the climax of the trilogy, The Return of the King presents 201 minutes of cinematic majesty.

Is it one of those rare sequels that surpasses its predecessor? Well, that is up to each individual to decide. There is no doubt The Godfather Part II is a bigger picture, not only in how it adds almost half an hour to the original’s 175-minute runtime, but also in how it splits its narrative focus across two major plot threads decades apart. In the aftermath of The Godfather, Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) encounters opposition as he tries to expand his family’s crime empire. At the start of the 20th century, a young Vito Corleone (Robert De Niro) begins to rise up the ranks of the criminal world of Newly introduced York City.

Francis Ford Coppola’s ability to seamlessly interweave the dual stories while using them both as thematic catalysts exploring opposite sides of the darkness of the American dream is impeccable. Vito uses crime as a pathway to a life beyond poverty, while Michael’s enterprising ambition threatens to spell the end of his family empire. Gordon Willis’ gorgeous cinematography and Nino Rota’s haunting score only heighten this piercing narrative focus. It makes The Godfather Part II a compelling epic that still stands at the pinnacle of crime cinema 52 years on from its release.

According to recent reports, it is 72 years old, and it has spawned hundreds of imitators over the decades, many of them being admirable movies too. The fact remains that Seven Samurai is an unsurpassed masterpiece, not only of action-adventure filmmaking, but of cinema at large as well. Japanese maestro Akira Kurosawa is at his absolute best in every shot of the 207-minute picture, from his trademark use of nature as a visual storytelling tool to the sweeping grandeur of the camera movements, and even to the precision of the framing and blocking.

Industry observers note that kurosawa’s ability to combine the epic with the intimate is on full display as well, with the heroism of seven samurai agreeing to help a poor village defend itself from bandits being beautifully offset by quiet meditations on honor and morality. It takes great care to explore the complex and often distrustful dynamic between peasants and samurai as well, with the uneasy tension buoyed by the urgency of the training. Seven Samurai takes its time developing these dynamics and ideas, and when the time does finally come for action, it is astonishing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this week’s slate of newly introduced movies across the best streaming services is set, and with 14 new arrivals, you've got plenty of options to consider. That’s why I’ve combed through the full list and picked out some highlights on platforms including Netflix, HBO Max, Hulu and Apple TV.

It has been revealed that the biggest newcomer this week is actually on premium streaming. The movie that everybody has been talking about will be available to watch at home; I, of course, refer to “You Can See Everything.” Alternatively, Netflix has a fresh WWII movie, HBO Max has a fantastical adventure great for young’uns, and Hulu has an entertaining buddy-style action-comedy.

Below you’ll find more details on my recommendations this week, followed by a full list of all the new movies heading to streaming services this week. We also have a guide to the top TV demonstrates you can watch in the coming days.

I finally got to see “You Can See Everything” over the weekend (thanks to its delayed international rollout). And even with high expectations because of the incredible word-of-mouth I’d seen on social media for weeks, it still blew me away. It’s being touted as one of the year’s best movies, and holds a 97% score on Rotten Tomatoes, with an equally strong viewer rating of 95%. A shoo-in for awards season, it's one of 2026's most buzzy new releases.

Take it from me: This is a doc where the less you know before watching, the better. So, to avoid spoiling anything, I’ll keep the following outline vague. Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, it follows the infamous fraudster Elizabeth Holmes 34 days before she’s due to be sent to prison. Holmes allows a film crew to document her daily life, but what starts as a simple documentary warps into something significantly more complex.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 24.

In a recent development, starring Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson and Tom Francis, it follows a quartet of promising young football players who park their athletic dreams to enlist in the United States Marine Corps during WWII. On the front lines, they face numerous hardships but also participate in a football game that became known as “The Mosquito Bowl” ahead of the Battle of Okinawa. Which, for a moment, let these troops forget the horrors of war.

Watch on Netflix starting November 25.

Sources indicate that “The Way of the Warrior Kid” so closely resembles “The Karate Kid” that I half-wonder if it’s legally actionable. The inspiration for Apple’s upcoming coming-of-age drama movie is so clear that even the title doesn’t try to hide it. But imitation is the sincerest form of flattery. I can’t say this Apple original looks like a critical darling-in-waiting, but hopefully it’ll offer some feel-good fun. And surely it can’t be received worse than the 2010 “Karate Kid” reboot, right?

Chris Pratt stars as Uncle Jake, a US Navy SEAL staying with his older sister, Sarah (Linda Cardellini), over the summer after being injured in the line of duty. Taking his nephew, Marc (Jude Hill), under his wing, Jake resolves to help him learn to stand up for himself against a pack of school-year bullies. Cue the epic training montage and scenes of family bonding.

Watch on Apple TV starting November 25.

I’ve got a personal reason to recommend “The Magic Faraway Tree.” The original Enid Blyton books were a childhood favorite, so seeing characters like Moonface (Nonso Anozie) and Saucepan Man (Dustin Demri-Burns) on the big screen transported me to a simpler time. The fantasy adventure is a whimsical ride, and clearly made with younger viewers in mind. Grown-ups might find it a little too simplistic, but if you’ve got young kids, I bet they’ll love it. Just don’t blame me if they want to watch it on repeat for weeks.

Starring Andrew Garfield, Claire Foy, Nicola Coughlan and Rebecca Ferguson (who’s deliciously wicked as the villain, Dame Snap), “The Magic Faraway Tree” sees a family move from the big city to the countryside in hopes of a simpler, technology-free life. Once in their new digs, the family’s three children discover a magical tree full of quirky inhabitants, and if that wasn’t exciting enough, the tree can also transport them to dazzling fantasy lands.

Watch on HBO Max starting November 27.

I can’t say that Alan Ritchson and Owen Wilson would have been my first choice if you’d asked me to assemble a dream duo for a “buddy” action movie, but it’s a combination that works surprisingly well in practice. Which isn’t to say “Runner” is flawless; the plot is very pedestrian, but the action is entertaining, and Ritchson and Wilson’s dynamic is great.

Sources indicate that ritchson plays a former soldier, now working as a “runner,” essentially a courier for high-value items, both legal and illegal. Tasked with making a critical medical delivery, he reluctantly teams up with an unlikely ally, Wilson’s Ben Bishop. A young girl’s life hangs in the balance, and the job is complicated when the pair become the target of a criminal cartel. “Runner” is a fast-paced action-comedy, with a pair of likable leads. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other demonstrates dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It promptly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

Sources indicate that A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

According to recent reports, A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Sources indicate that mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that quickly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

It has been revealed that peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The latest Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

Four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rick Berman says he got over Star Trek fans giving him grief about ruining the franchise "a long time ago.".
  • Berman was selected by Paramount as Star Trek executive producer in 1987, and he fully inherited Gene Roddenberry's mantle after the creator's death in 1991.
  • It has been revealed that rick Berman was a guest of two of his former employees, Brent Spiner and Jonathan Frakes, on their podcast, Dropping Names...
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rick Berman says he got over Star Trek fans giving him grief about ruining the franchise "a long time ago.".

Berman was selected by Paramount as Star Trek executive producer in 1987, and he fully inherited Gene Roddenberry's mantle after the creator's death in 1991. Under Berman's aegis, the Star Trek franchise rapidly expanded with Star Trek: The Next Generation, Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, Star Trek: Voyager, and Star Trek: Enterprise, as well as four TNG feature films. In the 18 years Rick Berman ran Star Trek, fans took issue with many of his decisions, but time is the fire in which those complaints burn, to paraphrase Star Trek Generations' villain, Dr. Tolian Soran (Malcolm McDowell).

It has been revealed that rick Berman was a guest of two of his former employees, Brent Spiner and Jonathan Frakes, on their podcast, Dropping Names... And Other Things. As actors and as a director, Spiner and Frakes played key roles in executive producer Alex Kurtzman's era of Star Trek on Paramount+, and they discussed the "grief" fans gave Berman that he "ruined Star Trek," which is now mainly directed at Kurtzman. Today, fans are sentimental about the "Berman era." Read their quotes below:.

Brent Spiner: “You got so much grief through the years…”.

Rick Berman: “Wait, what grief are you referring to?”.

Brent Spiner: “Grief just because ‘You ruined Star Trek.’ You got that moniker.”.

Jonathan Frakes: “Now, they want they cherish [the Berman era]: ‘We’ve gotta get back to the Berman era.’”.

Brent Spiner: “They call it the Berman years. Come on! It went to J.J. [Abrams], and everybody was down on J.J. until it became Alex [Kurtzman]. Whoever holds the mantle has ruined the entire enterprise.”.

Rick Berman: “I got over that a long time ago.”.

Brent Spiner: “But so have the fans, because they’ve come full circle that the Berman years were wonderful.”.

This part of Dropping Names... with Rick Berman begins at the 19:00 mark:.

Recent findings suggest that brent Spiner is right that "whoever holds the mantle" as the person making the substantial creative decisions about Star Trek bears the brunt of ire from unhappy fans. After 60 years, Star Trek fans span different generations, with conflicting ideas of what Star Trek is "supposed to be." However, a sizable segment now looks past the flaws of Rick Berman's era and holds up his run as the gold standard of what Star Trek is "supposed to be.".

From 1987 to 2005, Berman oversaw more than 600 episodes across four Star Trek TV series, as well as four Star Trek: The Next Generation movies. Many of the decisions Berman was responsible for that were controversial at the time, such as the first Black and female captains to lead Star Trek series and making Enterprise a prequel, for example, are now widely accepted. Time has diluted much of the ire once directed at Berman in the pre-social-media age.

Industry observers note that for longtime Trekkers, the Berman era is now a golden age when Star Trek series ran for seven seasons with 22 to 26 episodes a season. It was a dearly missed abundance compared to how relatively little Star Trek there is in the streaming era. Berman's shows are also held up to have superior writing and better stories, with the characters' Shakespearean-like dialogue more musical to the ears than the modern vernacular in Paramount+'s Star Trek shows.

Time will tell if, 20 years from now, Alex Kurtzman's era, and the highlights and movie he oversaw, will be as fondly remembered as Rick Berman's Star Trek is today. History seems to bear that out, and many fans are already poised to be against the next era of Star Trek coming under Skydance. The good old days of Rick Berman's 18 years of running Star Trek may be remembered as even more halcyon in the years to come.

The Star Trek TV series and movies executive produced by Rick Berman are streaming on Paramount+.

#165708. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer states it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big concerns.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Recent findings suggest that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer states it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big concerns.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Recent findings suggest that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he indicates he has identified the next massive shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to substantial problems in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

Sources indicate that the great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

According to recent reports, andrew Ng: This is a massive question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

In a recent development, ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a latest paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

According to recent reports, ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

It has been revealed that having noted that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of people, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of customers.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

Recent findings suggest that “In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from substantial data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

Recent findings suggest that I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and mentioned, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Industry observers note that over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing latest here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Recent findings suggest that ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

Recent findings suggest that the data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

Recent findings suggest that you often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from major data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand fresh model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For substantial data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Recent findings suggest that could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

According to recent reports, ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Latest tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an notable piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is vital, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention swiftly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

In a recent development, for example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an key tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Recent findings suggest that ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

In a recent development, “In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion people. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

In a recent development, to make these challenges more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a organization approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

In a recent development, how do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Industry observers note that ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and enhancement the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion owners. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Recent findings suggest that ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale has officially started—but keeping track of the best discounts yet to land and figuring out which deals are worthwhile can be a challenge. As an alternative, you can have Alexa give you a heads-up about deals on products you already know you want to purchase, so you don’t have to spend time sorting through the noise.

According to recent reports, then head to the Alexa mobile app and go to More in the top left (the three horizontal lines) > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping and toggle on Deal Recommendations under the Shopping Recommendations options. This ensures you’ll receive notifications for items that appear in your shopping activity.

If Alexa finds an upcoming deal on something in your Saved for Later, your Wish List, or in your Shopping Cart, you’ll receive a pop-up alert on your Echo Show display or see a yellow light ring on your Echo speaker. You can also ask, “Alexa, what are my notifications?” to hear a list of deals it has compiled thus far. You can also say "Alexa, let me know when [product name] goes on sale.".

Alexa can detect deals up to 24 hours in advance, so you can either ask it to remind you again when a deal starts or request that it buy the item when the deal goes live. Simply say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” and it’ll charge the default payment and send the item to the default delivery address on your account.

I tested the iPhone 17, 17e, 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and Duo — here’s what I’d buy for Black Friday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The single biggest shopping day of the year is almost here, and you’ve probably seen many offers claiming to be some of the best iPhone Black Friday deals around.
  • Industry observers note that the beauty of Apple’s current lineup is that it’s the most diverse it’s ever been, covering different form factors and budgets — so I’m pitting the iPhone 17, 17e, Air, 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and Duo against each other.
  • Having tested all of them, I’ll break down which iPhones are actually worth your money this Black Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The single biggest shopping day of the year is almost here, and you’ve probably seen many offers claiming to be some of the best iPhone Black Friday deals around. But before you make an impulsive decision, it’s worth knowing which of the current models is actually worth your money.

Industry observers note that the beauty of Apple’s current lineup is that it’s the most diverse it’s ever been, covering different form factors and budgets — so I’m pitting the iPhone 17, 17e, Air, 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and Duo against each other. With Black Friday deals rolling out across major carriers and retailers, it’s pretty tricky determining which one of them is the right fit.

Having tested all of them, I’ll break down which iPhones are actually worth your money this Black Friday.

6.1-inch Super Retina XDR display (2,532 x 1,170).
