In a recent development, frankly, the iPhone 17e is the one I’d recommend buying the least. What makes it an even tougher sell is that it rolled out at $599 earlier this year, but has since been given a $100 price hike that brings it to $699. Despite that, the iPhone 17e remains the most affordable entry point into Apple’s current lineup if you’re buying unlocked without any carrier deals or bundles attached.

It has been revealed that it covers the basics of what I’d want in a modern iPhone, like 256GB of starting storage, all-day battery life, speedy A19 performance, and a pocket-friendly build. Even though it runs iOS 27 just like all the others, it doesn’t make the cut for Siri AI — which is a bummer if you want a smarter, more proactive assistant. At the same time, it’s the only iPhone in the stable that is still stuck with a 60Hz refresh rate.

In a recent development, in terms of utility, you’re only getting a single 48MP main camera on the back — though I can’t overlook the fact that it performs well above average, including in low light. In fact, I was surprised in my iPhone 17e vs Pixel 10a face-off how its single rear camera held up.

But as I stated at the beginning, I can’t recommend getting this one knowing that the next model in the lineup exists.

If there’s one model in the lineup that hits the sweet spot for almost everyone, it’s the iPhone 17 — and yes, it too got a $100 price hike a couple of months back that now puts it at $899. Even with that increase, it’s easy for me to recommend for a number of reasons.

For that small jump over the iPhone 17e, you get a vastly smoother 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display, faster 35W wired and 25W MagSafe charging, and way better color options to choose from. Sure, it’s running the same A19 chip as the iPhone 17e, but its faster 120Hz refresh rate makes a huge difference in making UI animations look and feel smoother.

More importantly, the iPhone 17 delivers a far more satisfying camera experience. Pairing its 48MP main sensor with a dedicated 48MP ultrawide lens, this setup gives me more creative flexibility with my shots. I’ve broken down everything about them in my iPhone 17 vs. iPhone 17e face-off, which resulted in a lopsided win for the iPhone 17.

Sources indicate that when it debuted, I had so much excitement and buzz for the iPhone Air — until I actually started using it. As impressive as its 5.6mm titanium frame feels in the hand, the iPhone Air is another model that’s tough for me to recommend — especially now that Apple’s $100 price hike pushes its starting cost to a steep $1,099.

Industry observers note that you’re paying a serious premium strictly for thinness, while getting less functionality compared to the rest of the group. It doesn’t help either that the iPhone 17 sits below it at $200 less.

It has been revealed that the biggest trade-offs show up in daily use. Even though you get a gorgeous 6.5-inch 120Hz OLED display and speedy A19 Pro performance, its battery capacity is dramatically limited by its razor-thin profile — resulting in noticeably shorter battery life and slower charging than the rest of the lineup. Worse yet, it’s also stuck with just a single 48MP rear camera like the iPhone 17e. You don’t get an ultrawide lens, no macro shots, or definitely no telephoto zoom on a phone that costs $1,000-plus. We've even put its camera to the test against the iPhone 17e and I was shocked by how the iPhone Air barely came out on top.

Don’t get me wrong, I miss the days of thin and light phones, but when I’ve gotten accustomed to modern phones that pack dual cameras and easily get me through an 8-hour work shift without worrying about running out of juice, it’s so hard to go back to anything less.

Without question, I’d recommend looking out for Black Friday deals on the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. If you want the best of what Apple makes, both the $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro and $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max earn an easy recommendation from me. Yes, Apple hit both models with a $100 price hike this year and added a bit of heft — but they justify their premiums.

For starters, they’re packing a blazing-fast A20 Pro chip under the hood, offering access to the full Siri AI suite, and sporting a triple-48MP camera system headlined by a versatile fresh variable-aperture main lens.

No matter which one you end up getting, I love the fact that Apple still gave both phones identical camera hardware, 60W wired charging, and Pro Controls that make them more of a photographer’s camera. While the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max inherently has the bigger screen and battery, I personally find the smaller iPhone 18 Pro much easier to handle. Ultimately, choosing between them comes down purely to size preference.

Either way, you won’t question the decision to buy either one. And quite frankly, they’re well worth the cost over the iPhone Air.

Recent findings suggest that apple’s first foldable is easily the most exciting iPhone in years, and despite its steep $1,999 starting price, I still recommend buying it if you want a compact phone that unfolds into a mini tablet. Its sturdy titanium frame, nearly invisible crease, and nano-texture inner display, make it feel far more refined than a typical first-generation device.

It has been revealed that having a pocketable 5.4-inch outer screen is great for when I want to use it one-handed, and I also love how it opens into a 7.6-inch canvas unfolded with intuitive split-screen multitasking in iOS 27. Not only does its unique design make it perfect for creators who want to shoot videos of themselves by pairing the outer screen with the superior rear cameras, but it’s also an absolute powerhouse for everyday productivity — something none of the others can match to the same degree.

Of course, you still have to accept a few trade-offs compared to the $1,299 iPhone 18 Pro Max. You’re giving up Face ID, a dedicated telephoto zoom lens, no variable aperture, and no Pro Controls, while some third-party apps still aren’t fully optimized for the wider inner display.

Even with those compromises, nothing else in Apple’s lineup matches the Duo’s versatility — and if you can soften the blow with a Black Friday trade-in deal, I don’t think you’ll regret the purchase.

Delta-E color accuracy (lower is better).

When it comes to outdoor visibility, the iPhone Duo takes the crown with a blinding peak brightness of 2,558 nits. It’s an intriguing find because of its nano-texture display. While it’s still viewable outdoors, it lacks the contrast and vibrant color tones of the Pro models — with the iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone 18 Pro topping out at an impressive 2,326 nits and 2,314 nits, respectively.

Stepping down to the middle of the pack, the iPhone Air reached 1,678 nits, while the standard iPhone 17 hit 1,505 nits. I think both are plenty bright for everyday outdoor use. Unsurprisingly, the iPhone 17e trails the entire group at 1,002 nits.

Geekbench 6 (single-core/multi-core).

3DMark Wild Life Original Unlimited (score/fps).

Our benchmark testing draws a clear line between Apple’s A19-powered models and the newer A20 Pro flagships. The iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo all run on the A20 Pro chip — and, as a result, deliver class-leading CPU speeds, with Geekbench 6 scores clustering tightly around 4,700 single-core and 12,700 multi-core.

On the graphics front, the iPhone 18 Pro edges out the pack in 3DMark Wild Life Original Unlimited with a score of 38,667, just ahead of the 18 Pro Max at 38,474 and the Duo at 36,515.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the A19-equipped iPhone 17e and iPhone 17 trail noticeably behind in both CPU and GPU performance, while the A19 Pro inside the iPhone Air offers only a slight uptick over the standard 17. Even so, all three handle everyday apps effortlessly.

Average Battery life (Hrs:Mins).

According to recent reports, if battery endurance is notable to you, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max truly separate themselves from the rest of the pack. In our battery test, the iPhone 18 Pro Max led the way with an average of 18 hours and 27 minutes, while the smaller iPhone 18 Pro wasn’t far behind at 16 hours and 17 minutes.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the rest of the lineup clusters tightly around the 12.5- to 13.5-hour mark. The iPhone Duo edges out the non-Pro models at an average of 13 hours and 20 minutes, while the iPhone 17 and iPhone Air came in at over 12 hours.

Recent findings suggest that at the end of the day, I recommend looking out for Black Friday deals on the iPhone 17, iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and the iPhone Duo. While the iPhone 17 is a great entry point for everyday people and the iPhone Duo delivers unmatched foldable versatility, the iPhone 18 Pro takes the crown as the best overall balance and value of the bunch.

You get the exact same blazing-fast A20 Pro performance, variable-aperture triple-camera system, and speedy 60W charging as the pricier iPhone 18 Pro Max — all in a much easier-to-handle size that saves you $100 upfront. Unless you specifically crave a massive screen or a folding display, the iPhone 18 Pro is the one I’d look out for Black Friday.

For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

Industry observers note that I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):.

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

According to recent reports, amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

Industry observers note that sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

In a recent development, amazon Health: Prime users get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance plans, too.

Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

Amazon Luna: A cloud gaming platform that offers upcoming free games every month, free downloadable PC games, content, a monthly Twitch channel subscription, and a free channel subscription on Twitch each month for Prime Members.

Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, anthropic just introduced Claude Ship, a new AI tool that takes Claude's coding capabilities a step further.

  • It has been revealed that claude can now handle much of that process automatically.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, anthropic just introduced Claude Ship, a new AI tool that takes Claude's coding capabilities a step further. Instead of simply writing code, Claude can now review it, find problems, make corrections and even approve changes without requiring someone to supervise every step. So whether you're developing an app or creating a website, Claude will check its own work to ensure you're crafting the best design. Just confirmed Monday, Claude Ship is designed to tackle one of the more frustrating parts of software development.

It has been revealed that but writing code is only part of what it can do. Before an revision can go live, someone typically needs to review it, check for errors and approve the changes.

It has been revealed that claude can now handle much of that process automatically. For developers, that could mean spending less time reviewing code and more time building upcoming features. But even for people experimenting with AI to create their own apps or websites, it's another example of how swiftly Claude is becoming capable of doing work that once required multiple people.

Claude Ship combines three AI-powered tools that work together to move software updates through the approval process.

In a recent development, the first, Code Review, examines proposed changes and looks for potential bugs or other problems. It was already available before today's announcement.

According to recent reports, the second, PR Steward, is upcoming and takes things further. When Claude finds an issue, PR Steward can work on fixing it rather than simply alerting the developer. It can also respond to failed automated tests, conflicting code changes and feedback from human reviewers.

Finally, Claude Approvals determines whether a change is ready to be approved.

There's an key catch; Claude doesn't get unlimited authority to approve whatever it wants. That's a good thing! Anyone using this feature can establish their own rules about which changes AI can approve and which require a human reviewer.

For example, a small documentation correction might be approved automatically, while a change involving sensitive financial information could still require human oversight.

Developers can also tell Claude to stop working on a particular task even if it was not listed as needing approval previously.

Arguably the most interesting part of the announcement is how anyone can use Claude Ship directly from Claude Code.

A new /ship command starts the process. Claude can push the changes to GitHub, open a pull request, review the code and address problems that come up along the way.

Recent findings suggest that A pull request is essentially a proposed upgrade to a software project. Normally, it needs to pass through several checks before becoming part of the finished product.

Rather than having to return repeatedly to fix problems or respond to comments, developers can leave Claude working on those tasks while they move on to something else.

Anthropic notes the technology has already changed how its own Claude Code team works.

According to the manufacturer, the number of pull requests merged by the team more than doubled between June and September, while the share of those changes that later needed to be reverted fell by more than 40%.

Those are Anthropic's internal results, however, and they don't guarantee other teams will see the same improvements.

Industry observers note that like most advanced Claude features, Claude Ship will first roll out to Claude Team customers working with GitHub repositories. However, the existing Code Review feature is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals remain in beta.This isn't a feature that someone using the free Claude chatbot can immediately try. So if you don't have a Team or Enterprise subscription, this is a good time to discover more about what Claude Code can do. Because vibe coding has become so integrated into many workflows, the more you can practice and feel comfortable with it, the more productive you might be.

Sources indicate that usage is billed according to the amount of AI processing required, so the cost can vary depending on how many changes Claude reviews and how much work it performs. Organizations can establish spending limits to keep costs under control.

Claude Ship is another sign of how AI coding tools are evolving beyond assistants that simply respond to instructions.

Instead of asking Claude to write a piece of code and then taking over, developers can increasingly hand off larger portions of the software development process.

Industry observers note that don't let the possibilities of this upcoming feature fool you; this doesn't eliminate the need for human oversight. Anthropic acknowledges that Claude Ship can still miss bugs, security vulnerabilities and other problems, making careful approval policies key.

According to recent reports, still, the direction is clear. AI is moving from helping people write software to taking responsibility for more of the work required to finish it. For everyday owners, it's worth keeping an eye out for this feature to eventually come to lower subscription tiers.

When GTA 6 finally dropped last week after more than a decade of waiting, I knew playing it on a standard TV setup wasn't going to cut it.

Sources indicate that that is why I finally set up the Philips Smart LED Screen Sync behind my TV. Built on Philips' more budget-friendly smart lighting line, it is discounted right now for Black Friday — and I know this because I was manning the Amazon live blog when I spotted it.

Even better, the kit bundles both the screen-reading sensor and a four-sided RGBIC lightstrip right in the box.

I finally installed this Philips screen-sync LED strip behind my TV, and it’s a total game-changer. Pairing reactive ambient lighting with GTA 6 right after launch adds a whole fresh layer of immersion that makes every session feel unreal.

Recent findings suggest that I will admit I was skeptical about how painless the installation would be when all I wanted to do was jump into the game. Fortunately, the whole process took less than ten minutes. You stick the four-sided lightstrip around the back of your TV, perch the compact fisheye camera on top of the bezel, and let the app run an automatic calibration.

It maps the corners of your display on its own, though you can tweak the anchor points manually if your TV sits at an awkward angle. Because it relies on an optical fisheye lens to read the screen in real time rather than intercepting an HDMI signal, there is also zero input lag added to your console and no need to worry about bandwidth bottlenecks.

The WiZ app is where you can customise how it looks. I found after having a play around that Vibrant mode is my personal favorite, especially once you nudge the Saturation and Intensity sliders up so the colors really pop.

When they first lit up, electric pink and cyan neon signs bled softly out from the left edge of the frame while warm, syrupy golden-hour skies glow across the top, wrapping your whole field of vision in atmosphere. Everything you're playing, suddenly, feels so much more real.

Sources indicate that beyond looking incredible, that responsive halo actually cut down on my eye strain. I tend to game late into the night and already suffer from dry eyes, so the contrast of a bright screen in a dark room normally wears me out pretty fast. I didn't have any of that once I set these up, though, as the glow softens the glare and gives my eyes a break.

Is a camera mounted on top of your TV slightly less sleek than a hidden HDMI box? Sure. Does a dark room keep the color tracking noticeably more accurate than broad daylight? Definitely. Yet it completely changes how a game feels (and don't even get me started on how good it makes movies look!).

Throw in the fact that it is marked down right now for Black Friday, and it is hands down one of the best TV upgrades you can make.

#165690. Industry News: These 14 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Industry News: These 14 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1481 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov.
  • Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program.
  • Sources indicate that the iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the tech giant's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this upgrade isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially rolls out the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger challenges. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

Sources indicate that the iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the tech giant's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this latest feature here.

In a recent development, iOS 27.3 also comes with a new setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Currently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the big screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a fresh set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the tech giant is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,.

The organization generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these fresh Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

In a recent development, despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing fresh abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These newly introduced actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

It has been revealed that apple started testing its newly introduced Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

In a recent development, continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a upcoming Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Apple is also testing a upcoming Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Industry observers note that another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Recent findings suggest that apple is also testing latest StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with massive iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability right now works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

In a recent development, if you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

Recent findings suggest that if you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the fresh updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in a upcoming interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month.
  • Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.
  • In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in a upcoming interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:.

Sources indicate that we were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:.

Industry observers note that when we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a major way on newly introduced and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:.

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are upcoming or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe stated “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very vital to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe stated he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:.

Sources indicate that we could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The matter of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:.

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a company and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift….

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Christmas is not too far away, which means it’s the perfect time to start working your way through some festive movies.
  • Whether you’re in the mood for a feel-good romantic comedy, a laugh-out-loud festive adventure or a classic Christmas favorite, there’s something for every kind of movie night.
  • So grab a blanket, make yourself a hot chocolate and settle in for a little holiday movie marathon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christmas is not too far away, which means it’s the perfect time to start working your way through some festive movies. The season has already begun for me, and I always love having a Christmas movie playing in the background while I get on with things. Thankfully, you don’t have to look far for something to watch, as Prime Video has plenty of holiday treats worth adding to your watchlist.

Whether you’re in the mood for a feel-good romantic comedy, a laugh-out-loud festive adventure or a classic Christmas favorite, there’s something for every kind of movie night. I’ve rounded up five of the best Christmas movies to stream on Prime Video right now, including a few familiar gems and some newer releases you might have missed.

So grab a blanket, make yourself a hot chocolate and settle in for a little holiday movie marathon.

Sources indicate that of course, we had to start with one of the most iconic Christmas movies of all time. “Elf” has become a modern holiday staple, and a massive part of its charm comes from Jon Favreau and Will Ferrell’s approach to the comedy. The film holds a real nostalgic festive look and includes plenty of cozy moments and wonderfully silly humor. Favreau also recognized the value of letting improvised scenes breathe, including Buddy’s hilarious deadpan exchange with a colleague in the office mailroom. It's the contrast between Buddy’s childlike enthusiasm and everyone else’s everyday cynicism that makes the comedy work so well.

After accidentally crawling into Santa’s sack as a baby, Buddy (Will Ferrell) is transported to the North Pole, where he’s raised by Santa’s elves. However, after discovering he’s actually human, the adult Buddy sets off for Latest York City to find his biological father, Walter Hobbs (James Caan), a workaholic children’s book publisher who has no idea he exists. Wearing his full elf outfit, Buddy struggles to fit into the busy city while getting to know his new family, including his younger half-brother Michael (Daniel Tay). Along the way, he also catches the attention of department-store employee Jovie (Zooey Deschanel).

Industry observers note that “Scrooged” is a great choice if you prefer your Christmas movies with a slightly darker edge. Starring Bill Murray, this modern take on Charles Dickens’ “A Christmas Carol” swaps traditional festive sweetness for sharp comedy, media satire and plenty of cynical laughs. It might have divided audiences when it first arrived, but it’s since become a cult Christmas favorite, and definitely one I add to my watchlist this time of year. I also appreciate how it balances its darker comedy with some genuinely heartfelt moments. Think of it as the perfect anti-Hallmark holiday movie.

Recent findings suggest that frank Cross (Bill Murray) is a ruthless and cynical television executive preparing a lavish live broadcast of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol on Christmas Eve. More interested in ratings than giving his employees time off, Frank has little patience for anyone who gets in his way. But his looks are interrupted when the ghost of his former mentor appears, warning him that three spirits will soon pay him a visit. Over the course of the night, the Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Future take Frank on a series of unexpected journeys, forcing him to confront his childhood, his relationships and what lies ahead if he continues down his current path.

It has been revealed that “Red One” might have divided critics, but there’s plenty of festive fun to be had in this substantial-budget Christmas action-comedy. Dwayne Johnson and Chris Evans make an entertaining double act, with their buddy-comedy chemistry helping the film through some of its cheesier moments. J.K. Simmons is another highlight as a surprisingly buff and wonderfully enthusiastic Santa Claus. It’s not exactly subtle, but I found it an enjoyable seasonal watch, especially if you like a generous dose of action and silliness in Christmas flicks.

According to recent reports, when Santa Claus (J.K. Simmons), also known by his codename Red One, is kidnapped from the North Pole just days before Christmas, it’s up to his head of security, Callum Drift (Dwayne Johnson), to bring him home. With Christmas Eve fast approaching, Callum reluctantly joins forces with Jack O’Malley (Chris Evans), a notorious bounty hunter and hacker whose actions inadvertently exposed Santa’s secret location. Together, the unlikely pair embark on a globe-trotting rescue mission, travelling across the world and encountering all sorts of mythical creatures along the way.

George Bailey (James Stewart) is a businessman living in the small town of Bedford Falls who has spent much of his life putting his own ambitions aside to help others. But when a financial crisis threatens his family business on Christmas Eve, George finds himself facing the possibility of losing everything. Overwhelmed by his circumstances, he begins to question what the world would look like if he had never been born. That’s when Clarence, a guardian angel hoping to earn his wings, arrives to show George an alternate version of Bedford Falls, where he discovers just how differently things might have turned out without him.

In a recent development, it’s also that time of year when streaming services start rolling out their festive originals, and Prime Video is getting into the Christmas spirit with “Clashing Through the Snow.” Starring Christopher Briney from “The Summer I Turned Pretty” and Michelle Randolph, this cozy romantic comedy has all the ingredients for an enjoyable holiday watch. It has the classic enemies-to-lovers setup, which gives the central relationship plenty of room for bickering and romantic tension. Add in a snowy road trip and two appealing leads, and there’s plenty to enjoy. The timing is also spot on, arriving just as Thanksgiving week kicks off.

Sources indicate that in “Clashing Through the Snow,” rival publishing editors Ryan Mitchell (Christopher Briney) and Hannah Hendricks (Michelle Randolph) find themselves competing for their jobs after their organization announces budget cuts. Both are sent to Fresh York to secure a major book deal that could save their careers, but their aims take a turn when a Christmas snowstorm grounds their flight. With no other way to reach the city in time, the pair are forced to share a rental car and embark on a cross-country road trip together. Along the way, unexpected detours, roadside mishaps and encounters with strangers make their journey far more complicated than either anticipated.

In a recent development, alix is a Senior Streaming Writer at Tom’s Guide, which basically means watching the best movies and TV shows and then writing about them. It’s a dream job for someone who’s been obsessed with storytelling since she first figured out how to work a remote.

Before joining Tom’s Guide, Alix honed her skills as a staff writer with outlets like Screen Rant and Bough Digital, where she discovered her love for the entertainment industry.

It has been revealed that she heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

But while I rely on this wonder formula to silence creaky door hinges and loosen stubborn, rusty screws, I started wondering what else is hiding in this iconic blue-and-yellow can.

As it turns out, its superpowers go far beyond basic home repairs, including one unexpected chore. Next time you need to clean your windows, go grab a can of WD-40.

According to recent reports, WD-40 has been around since the 1950s. While my creaky joints don’t quite go back that far, I clearly remember it being a staple in my dad’s garage. The second anything needed lubricating, out came that familiar can of spray.

Originally invented as a rust-prevention solvent for the aerospace industry, its usefulness has since expanded into the domestic market, making it a well-known household staple. Instead of sitting on your tool shelf, you’re now just as likely to find it lurking in a cleaning cupboard.

WD-40 is an amazing household cleaning product to keep in your kitchen. When lightly sprayed on a stainless steel surface, like a refrigerator or dishwasher and wiped away with a microfiber cloth, it will remove unsightly fingerprints, smudges and water spots. For this reason, it’s also handy to have in the bathroom to remove water marks off shower screens.

It’s also pretty useful when you’re cleaning your windows, especially when they are covered in bird droppings. What’s more, once the bird poop is dried on, it’s even more difficult to remove, which is when WD-40 works its magic.

It has been revealed that you can’t be without a can of WD-40 in your tool kit. This budget-friendly, multi-purpose lubricant spray comes with a smart straw for precise targeting. The handy spray stops squeaks, drives out moisture, cleans and protects, loosens rusted parts and frees sticky mechanisms.

When birds have pelted your windows with droppings, you’ll need something a bit stronger than elbow grease to remove them if the poop has dried on.

2. Spray a small amount on the bird-stained area and leave it for a few minutes.

In a recent development, 3. Take a clean microfiber cloth and wipe away the mess.

4. Finish off by cleaning the area with a mild soap, this will rinse away any oily residue left behind from the WD-40.

Sources indicate that I’m certainly not on standby to clean my windows as soon as the birds have pelted them, which means by the time I notice the mess, the bird poop is already dried on. But at this point, plain water won’t do.

WD-40 says the stubborn crust, mixed with solid waste and digestive grit, resists plain water, whereas spraying it with the solvent and lubricant works beneath the dried layer to soften what is clinging to the surface.

Using the spray also helps to protect your glass, as scrubbing at the muck can cause scratches.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a 10-page ruling from the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, the justices found that the 2024 lawsuit filed by Tuff City Records against Universal Music Publishing failed to state a viable claim. The ruling found that the two songs “are not substantially similar as a matter of law.”.

“The works as a whole are distinct,” the ruling obtained by Rolling Stone reads. “The songs differ in their lyrics, melody, genre, subject matter, and overall sound.”.

Industry observers note that the Honey Drippers released “Impeach the President” in 1973, and it swiftly became a Nixon-era protest anthem with a distinctive drum break that would become widely sampled by artists including Janet Jackson, J. Cole, and Doja Cat.

In filing its appeal, Tuff City argued that the lower court used an incorrect legal standard to compare “Real Love” with “Impeach the President.” The appellate court disagreed.

Industry observers note that “While ‘Impeach the President’ and ‘Real Love’ share certain percussive elements, other elements are notably different, such as open versus closed hi-hats and distinct snare and kick drum rhythms,” the ruling states. “The songs’ ‘total concept and overall feel’ reinforce the conclusion that the works at issue are not substantially similar.”.

Agreeing with the district court, the ruling found that “Impeach the President” is a protest song that “fits squarely within the soul/funk genre,” whereas “Real Love” is a “hip-hop soul song about heartbreak, not politics.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

It has been revealed that hillel I. Parness, a lawyer for Tuff City, remarked the organization was “very disappointed” by Monday’s ruling and “will be seeking further judicial review.” He described “Impeach the President” as one of the “most widely- and consistently-sampled songs from the classic hip-hop era” and warned that the decision could have far-reaching implications for the genre. “Allowing Universal publishing’s refusal to pay for its undisputed sampling to stand would upend decades of law, and decades of industry practice, all designed around ensuring that creators and owners are paid for the use of samples, even if the samples themselves are then reconfigured,” Parness noted in a statement to Rolling Stone.

Lawyers for Universal did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • Industry observers note that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

Industry observers note that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

According to recent reports, A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn swiftly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Recent findings suggest that miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

In a recent development, during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Industry observers note that druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

Industry observers note that an image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly reveals Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

It has been revealed that he insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs demonstrates the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Industry observers note that despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

It has been revealed that the corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

It has been revealed that to observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most notable processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

Sources indicate that that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

In a recent development, space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very swiftly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she indicates, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

According to recent reports, it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

According to recent reports, habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” states Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

Recent findings suggest that the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

Sources indicate that to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller claims. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

Sources indicate that but duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller indicates wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller notes with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

According to recent reports, the countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

It has been revealed that among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Recent findings suggest that those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Industry observers note that around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller notes with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

Industry observers note that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

Industry observers note that “Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” states Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as swiftly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller states. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

It has been revealed that but for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

'Wifi Motion Sensing' Can Track Everything You Do Through Your Router

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simple wifi feature could let ISPs track your location and movement patterns within your home.
  • Industry observers note that while the technology isn’t universally implemented just yet and is typically opt-in only (smart home owners might want the movement tracking feature for lights and heating), it presents quite a few privacy risks.
  • It has been revealed that wifi routers rely on radio signals to connect wirelessly to your devices and appliances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple wifi feature could let ISPs track your location and movement patterns within your home. "Wifi motion sensing" turns your ISP’s router into a motion detector, letting providers know exactly how many people are in the house, where they are situated, individual movement patterns, and, in some cases, even body shapes that could approximate a person’s identity.

Industry observers note that while the technology isn’t universally implemented just yet and is typically opt-in only (smart home owners might want the movement tracking feature for lights and heating), it presents quite a few privacy risks. So here’s how wifi routers sense motion, what they can do with it, who has access to the data, and how you can disable it.

It has been revealed that wifi routers rely on radio signals to connect wirelessly to your devices and appliances. Those same radio signals are also absorbed and reflected by the human body as they travel in all directions from the router. With the right software, ISPs can track how those wifi signals travel around your room, which can be studied to detect presence and sense motion patterns.

As long as your ISP’s router model supports this feature natively, it doesn’t require any additional hardware to be installed in your home. For example, Xfinity’s version of the feature pairs your router with five other connected appliances in your room to create oval-shaped sensing zones that can track your presence and movement within those spaces.

According to recent reports, it isn’t a fresh feature, either—companies like Cognitive Systems and Origin Wireless that supply networking hardware to ISPs have been offering wifi motion sensing for years now, while early research prototypes from the MIT date back at least as far as 2015. In 2025, IEEE updated its Wi-Fi 802.11 standard to include motion sensing and lay out the architectural guidelines for it, which makes it likely that even more routers will now ship with the feature.

Recent findings suggest that in its current consumer form, wifi motion sensing can help you control smart home apparatus like lights or thermostats, get pet safety notifications on your phone, set up a fall alert system for elderly consumers, and trigger appliances remotely based on human presence. But enabling it carries risks.

According to recent reports, most providers, including Cognitive Systems, claim that the technology isn’t sensitive to identity and can’t be used to track specific individuals. But even if true, that’s more likely to be a product decision rather than a technical limitation. Karlsruhe Institute researchers have shown that even ordinary wifi signals can identify individuals with a 99.5% accuracy.

Industry observers note that also worth noting: ISPs’ legal wording suggests that they may disclose the collected and stored motion data at any time to law enforcement, government agencies, regulators, and courts in response to subpoenas or during an emergency. ISPs may also retain your motion data in the cloud long-term in case they are required to facilitate a subpoena in the future.

As far as major ISPs are concerned, Xfinity (Comcast) is the only broadband provider that currently offers this feature across its commercial routers on the XB7, XB8, XB9, XB10, MXB1, and XER10 gateways. It’s opted out by default, but in case you or a family member already switched it on, you can disable it again by navigating to Home > WiFi Motion on the Xfinity app, click on the gear icon on the live view page, and tap Remove WiFi Motion.

Verizon Fios customers also had access to a Home Awareness feature on their routers that could be toggled on or off using the MyFios app, but that’s since been discontinued. In an official disclosure published shortly after the discontinuation, Verizon notified customers that it has deleted all associated movement logs from this service and no longer retains any motion data from people.

It has been revealed that but there are other regional ISPs that offer it, too. For example, Breezeline (Atlantic Broadband) offers a feature called Motion within its Plume-powered application that alerts customers when movement is detected in their homes, among its other features. MidCo, a telecom manufacturer in the Upper Midwest, has a feature called Sense which can be toggled on or off using the MidCo Wi-Fi app. Plume, ADT-owned Origin Wireless, and Airties—all of whom supply technology to ISPs—have also been marketing motion sensing to customers for the last few years.

If you’re unsure if your wifi router or ISP has motion sensing features or opts you in by default, look for a feature called “Sense,” “Motion,” or equivalent in your broadband’s mobile app. Exact steps differ greatly from one ISP to another, so it’s best not to assume that they will all opt you out by default, or that they collect the same types of data. With the 802.11bf enhancement to IEEE standards in 2025, this technology will be accessible to even more router manufacturers, so expect adoption to grow among internet providers as well.
